(d) Pathway ranking: A scoring system is applied to synthesis routes to evaluate their reliability and effectiveness, ranking them accordingly.

RetrobioCat [\[8\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0008) is a template-based retrobiosynthesis tool that utilizes human expert-curated templates. The tool compiles enzymatic reactions from the literature into an in-house database, categorizing reactions based on enzyme types to facilitate template extraction and enzyme identification. Through a community-driven platform, users can explore synthesis routes for target molecules and contribute to expanding the reaction template database.

ASKCOS [\[9\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0009) is an example of a tool that extracts reaction templates from databases. Built upon a previous chemical retrosynthesis tool, ASKCOS [\[9\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0009) extracts enzymatic reaction templates from the BKMS [\[36\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0036) database and integrates them into a chemoenzymatic synthesis tool. A prioritization mechanism selects templates for each step from a combined chemical and biological reaction library. In a comparison between chemical and biological synthesis approaches, some pathways were found exclusively through enzymatic reactions. Additionally, chemoenzymatic synthesis planning predicted shorter synthetic routes compared to traditional chemical synthesis planning methods.

 

### 6.2.2 Template-Free Tools

In contrast to template-based methods, template-free tools utilize machine learning (ML) algorithms to predict precursors for a given target molecule ([Figure 6.1](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0001)b). While the output of template-based methods is deterministic after designing and selecting reaction templates, ML-based methods offer greater tunability. The representation of molecules, selection of algorithms, and techniques used in the training process all contribute to prediction performance. The reaction database is typically divided into training, validation, and test subsets, with prediction performance evaluated based on the model's ability to reproduce reactions in the test set. Molecules can be represented as SMILES [\[34\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0034) strings or drawn as graphs to encode structural information. Since retrosynthesis outputs are chemical structures, several factors must be considered to ensure their validity, including bond formation rules, structural thermodynamic stability, and isomerization effects. To address these issues, filters can be applied to eliminate invalid structures before generating the final output. Beyond that, due to the presence of recurring reaction types in the database, ML models may develop biases toward certain reaction types or specific transformations. Proper categorization and weighting of the database can help achieve a more balanced reaction output.

Rxn4chemistry [\[10\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0010), developed by IBM, is the first ML-based retrobiosynthesis tool. It uses reactions from the ECREACT database [\[10\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0010) for training. Chemicals are represented as SMILES and tokenized into an end-to-end transformer architecture for both forward and backward synthesis predictions. Notably, to expand the dataset and incorporate chemical knowledge into model training, reactions from the USPTO [\[6\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0006) chemical database were included using multitask transfer learning. On the Rxn4chemistry website, if a retrosynthesis route could not be found using enzymatic pathways, a supplementary chemical route is suggested instead. As the first ML-based retrosynthesis tool, Rxn4chemistry [\[10\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0010) demonstrated promising results while also identifying incorrect predictions in its published work, highlighting limitations and areas for further improvement.

Another ML-based tool, BioNavi-NP [\[11\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0011), focuses on natural product synthesis. Recognizing the issue of limited biological reaction data, BioNavi-NP implemented data augmentation techniques. Specifically, it uses the DNP database to represent natural products and calculates molecular similarities between reactions in the USPTO [\[6\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0006) dataset and compounds in the DNP dataset. Reactions with high similarity are added to the training set, and enhanced performance has been observed with the expanded database.

 

### 6.2.3 Searching Algorithm

In retrosynthesis, some tools focus on single-step synthesis, aiming to achieve high reproducibility and accuracy. However, designing a complete synthesis pathway for practical applications and industrial-scale synthesis requires multistep synthesis routes ([Figure 6.1](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0001)c). Since each target molecule can have multiple predicted precursors, the number of possible synthesis routes grows exponentially with each additional step. Therefore, rather than simply linking single-step reactions together, a multistep synthesis algorithm must balance route quality and computational efficiency. Starting from the target molecule, various precursor candidates can be generated. To reduce computational costs, the most promising precursor is selected for expansion at each step. During this process, the reliability and effectiveness of each reaction are evaluated and compared. Reliability is often determined by the degree of similarity to known reaction templates or established reaction rules, while effectiveness can be assessed using synthetic complexity scores, which will be discussed in detail in [Section 2.4](#c02.xhtml#c02-sec-0031). After these evaluations, the next node(s) are selected for expansion, and the process continues until commercially available compounds are reached.

The MCTS [\[37\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0037) is a widely used decision-making algorithm that determines the optimal next move based on probabilistic exploration. In retrosynthesis, AiZynthFinder [\[12\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0012) was the first tool to apply MCTS for retrosynthesis planning, following a process of selection, expansion, simulation, and backpropagation. In this framework, an initial molecule is selected for expansion, generating potential precursors. The search tree is explored through simulations, where each branch is evaluated to determine whether it leads to viable starting materials or requires further expansion. The calculation results help guide the search, allowing pathways to be ranked based on likelihood and feasibility.

Retro\* [\[11\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0011) is another multistep retrosynthesis search method that follows a best-first search strategy with a neural network-guided bias. It structures the retrosynthesis problem as an AND-OR search tree, where molecules represent OR nodes and reaction steps represent AND nodes. Retro\* utilizes a learned value function to guide node selection, prioritizing high-quality and low-cost reaction pathways. The cost function is derived from a transformer-based neural network, which assigns confidence scores to reaction feasibility. A pathway is expanded iteratively, and at each step, the most statistically favorable precursor is selected based on reaction likelihood and synthetic accessibility. Once a complete pathway to available starting materials is found, it is recorded, and the search continues to identify alternative routes.

 

### 6.2.4 Ranking

Appropriate ranking of synthesis routes is crucial both in the process of expanding the search tree and in presenting the final list of synthesis routes. Since multiple synthesis routes can be predicted, a reliable scoring system helps users select the best prediction, reducing time spent on experimental validation and applications ([Figure 6.1](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0001)d). In synthesis route ranking, reliability represents the confidence in the predicted reaction and is often measured by the similarity between templates and reactions. Additionally, since forward reaction prediction generally has higher accuracy than retrosynthesis planning, a forward reaction predictor can be used to verify the predicted results and identify potential side reactions. Effectiveness in retrosynthesis can be defined by whether the predicted routes lead to commercially available compounds, and several scoring metrics have been developed to evaluate this aspect. The most well-known metric is the SCScore [\[13\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0013), which introduces the concept of synthetic complexity for ranking synthesis routes. In practical applications, additional factors must be considered, including the cost of starting materials, the overall cost of the synthesis route, the yield of each step, and the toxicity of reagents used. To enable a more comprehensive evaluation, relevant data can be extracted from online literature databases and assigned different ranking weights.

The SCScore [\[13\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0013) is widely used in retrosynthesis, and both RetrobioCat [\[8\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0008) and Rxn4chemistry [\[10\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0010) utilize it for route ranking. This scoring system is based on the concept of synthetic complexity. Specifically, reactants and products in a reaction are analyzed, and products are considered synthetically more complex than reactants. All compounds are classified on a gradient from 1 to 5 according to their synthetic complexity. In route ranking, reactions that proceed from a synthetically more complex molecule to a simpler one are preferred, and scores are accumulated to determine the overall synthetic complexity of a given route.

The SAscore [\[14\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0014), on the other hand, evaluates whether a compound is easy to synthesize, recognizing that some complex structures can be formed through simple reactions. This approach involves fragmenting molecules from the PubChem database and calculating fragmentation scores under the assumption that easily synthesized substructures appear more frequently in the database. Additionally, complex molecular features, such as rings and stereocenters, are considered by applying penalty scores to these structures in the SAscore calculation.

 

## 6.3 Enzyme Selection and Optimization

Once a biochemical pathway is designed for a target molecule via retrobiosynthesis, selecting appropriate enzymes for the pathway becomes crucial to ensuring that each step in the pathway is feasible and efficient [\[38\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0038). Unlike traditional synthetic chemistry, where chemical catalysts may provide broad reactivity, enzymes exhibit high specificity, regioselectivity, and stereoselectivity, making them particularly valuable for synthesizing complex molecules with minimal side reactions. Moreover, identifying the suitable enzyme for a given transformation ensures overall process efficiency. In this section, we provide a high-level overview and in-depth technical details on how AI/ML tools can be used for enzyme selection and optimization. We focus on four key aspects: predicting enzyme substrate specificity and catalytic efficiency, engineering enzyme variants with improved properties, and designing novel enzymes *de novo* ([Figure 6.2](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0002)). These approaches complement the enzyme discovery tools that are described in [Chapters 4](#c04.xhtml) and [5](#c05.xhtml).

![Figure 6.2 Overview of the enzyme selection and optimization. Enzyme selection begins with a database of known enzymes, which are assessed for substrate specificity and catalytic efficiency. In enzyme engineering, candidate enzymes undergo refinement through optimization to enhance their properties. Concurrently, de novo enzyme design leverages generative AI to create novel enzyme structures and sequences tailored for specific substrates or reactions.](images/c06f002.png)

Figure 6.2 Overview of the enzyme selection and optimization. Enzyme selection begins with a database of known enzymes, which are assessed for substrate specificity and catalytic efficiency. In enzyme engineering, candidate enzymes undergo refinement through optimization to enhance their properties. Concurrently, *de novo* enzyme design leverages generative AI to create novel enzyme structures and sequences tailored for specific substrates or reactions.

 

### 6.3.1 Enzyme Substrate Specificity

Enzyme substrate specificity refers to an enzyme's ability to recognize and act on particular substrates. In retrobiosynthesis, selecting an enzyme is a critical step to ensure the feasibility of predicted reactions. Traditionally, enzyme selection relied on sequence or substrate similarity searches in databases (e.g. using tools like BLAST [\[39\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0039) against BRENDA [\[28\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0028) or UniProt [\[40\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0040)). While useful, similarity-based methods can miss enzymes with low sequence identity but suitable activity. AI/ML enhances the predictive power by learning complex patterns that dominate enzyme–substrate interactions. By training on known enzyme–substrate pairs, AI/ML models can generalize and predict whether a given enzyme will accept a novel substrate, enabling *in silico* screening of enzymes for predicted reactions in retrobiosynthesis.

Moving beyond EC number-based enzyme classification, which indicates what type of reaction an enzyme can conduct, enzyme substrate specificity prediction models are required to predict enzyme compatibility with a given substrate. Several AI/ML-based approaches have been proposed to generalize enzyme-substrate interactions across diverse enzyme families. Selenzyme is an enzyme selection tool that recommends candidates for a reaction based on sequence homology, reaction similarity, and phylogenetic distance [\[15\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0015). It is integrated into synthetic biology workflows for metabolic pathway optimization. Mellor et al. built a Gaussian process for enzyme search [\[41\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0041). Their work introduced a semi-supervised Gaussian process model that assigns probability scores for enzyme-catalyzed reactions based on reaction fingerprints and enzyme sequence similarity. The model successfully identified novel *E. coli* enzymes involved in metabolite transformations. Overall, sequence-based AI/ML predictors provide a rapid way to screen candidate enzymes for a novel substrate, representing an invaluable tool in retrosynthesis planning.

Recently, protein language models, like evolutionary scale modeling (ESM) [\[42\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0042), have significantly advanced sequence-based models to predict enzyme substrate specificity. The enzyme-substrate prediction (ESP) model employs a modified transformer architecture to predict enzyme-substrate relationships [\[16\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0016). Unlike traditional models that rely on explicit structural information, ESP derives sequence-based embeddings of enzymes, capturing functional features from protein language models. It addresses the challenge of imbalanced datasets by augmenting training with randomly sampled small molecules as non-substrates, achieving 91% accuracy across various enzyme families. In addition, the molecule-enzyme interaction (MEI) model integrates both enzyme sequence data and small-molecule atomic environments using hierarchical neural networks with attention mechanisms [\[17\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0017). This approach significantly outperforms conventional compound-protein interaction (CPI) models, which struggle with enzyme promiscuity. The model successfully predicts CYP450 enzyme activity and enzymatic degradation of complex plastics with an accuracy of 90.5%.

When high-resolution enzyme structures (experimental or predicted) are available, structure-based methods can refine specificity predictions. Molecular docking simulations such as AutoDock [\[18\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0018) have long been used to evaluate enzyme–ligand binding. Mou et al. integrated ligand docking, structural modeling, and physicochemical descriptors with AI/ML models (random forests, support vector machines, and gradient-boosted trees) [\[43\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0043). The approach yielded an 82% accuracy in predicting the substrate scope of bacterial nitrilases.

Overall, combining sequence-derived patterns, structural modeling (docking or AlphaFold-predicted structures), and modern AI/ML yields powerful predictors of enzyme–substrate specificity. These tools enable retrosynthesis planners to select enzymes likely to catalyze a given reaction *in silico*, narrowing down candidates before any lab experiments.

 

### 6.3.2 Enzyme Catalytic Efficiency

Once the candidate enzyme is identified for a reaction, the next challenge is to ensure the reaction proceeds at a desirable rate. Catalytic efficiency encompasses the kinetic parameters (turnover number *k*[cat], Michaelis constant *K*[m], and catalytic efficiency *k*[cat]*/K*[m]) and how readily an enzyme converts substrates to products. Improving catalytic activity often involves understanding the reaction's energy barrier and the enzyme's dynamics. Computational chemistry methods like quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics (QM/MM) can explicitly calculate transition state energies for enzyme-catalyzed reactions, and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations reveal how enzyme conformational changes affect catalysis [\[44\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0044). However, these physics-based methods are time-consuming and not feasible for screening large mutant libraries or many enzyme–substrate combinations. AI/ML offers faster predictive models by learning from either experimental kinetic data or high-level theoretical calculations. In this way, AI/ML can guide enzyme optimization by predicting which mutations or conditions will increase catalytic efficiency, all before actual wet-lab testing.

A growing area of AI/ML research is the prediction of enzyme kinetic parameters directly from enzyme and substrate features. Recent deep learning models have achieved promising results in this area. CatPred is a comprehensive deep learning framework designed for predicting *k*[cat], *K*[m], and inhibition constants (*K*[i]) values of enzymes [\[19\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0019). It employs pretrained protein language models (pLMs) and three-dimensional structural features to improve generalization, particularly on out-of-distribution samples. Unlike previous methods that struggle with generalization, CatPred incorporates uncertainty quantification techniques to assess prediction reliability. In addition, DLKcat employs a combination of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for enzyme sequence processing and graph neural networks (GNNs) for substrate structure representation [\[20\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0020). It has been applied for large-scale *k*[cat] predictions across 343 yeast species and successfully parameterized enzyme-constrained metabolic models. DLKcat achieves high predictive accuracy and even captures the impact of enzyme mutations on catalytic turnover, making it useful for enzyme engineering applications. Similarly, Kroll et al. developed a deep learning model for predicting *K*[m] values using a combination of a graph neural network for molecular fingerprints and a deep representation of enzyme amino acid sequences [\[45\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0045). Their approach successfully generalizes to genome-scale predictions for 47 model organisms, making it a valuable tool for metabolic modeling and systems biology.

Ensemble learning techniques, particularly gradient-boosted trees, have demonstrated strong performance in predicting enzyme kinetic parameters by leveraging pretrained language models and biochemical features. UniKP integrates multiple AI/ML models and pretrained language models to predict *k*[cat], *K*[m], and *k*[cat]/*K*[m] from enzyme sequences and substrate structures [\[21\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0021). It employs an ensemble-based regression approach, outperforming previous models by systematically considering environmental factors such as pH and temperature. Additionally, UniKP incorporates re-weighting methods to improve prediction accuracy for high-value kinetic parameters, addressing a key limitation in many AI/ML models. On the other hand, TurNuP predicts *k*[cat] by utilizing transformer neural networks to extract enzyme sequence features and employs differential reaction fingerprints to encode complete reaction information [\[22\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0022). Compared to traditional models, TurNuP shows superior generalization to enzymes with low sequence similarity to training data. The model has been successfully applied to parameterize metabolic models, improving predictions of proteome allocation.

These studies highlight that, given enough training data, AI/ML models can serve as surrogates for laborious enzyme kinetics experiments. For retrosynthesis, such models can rank enzyme candidates not just on whether they *can* catalyze a reaction, but how efficiently they will likely do so, focusing attention on the most catalytically competent options.

 

### 6.3.3 Enzyme Engineering

Enzyme engineering involves modifying an enzyme to enhance its performance. For instance, improving activity, selectivity, stability, or altering its substrate scope. In AI/ML-enabled retrosynthesis, once an enzyme is chosen for a step, one might engineer it to better fit the process requirements (e.g. higher turnover, tolerance to solvents, or acceptance of a non-natural substrate). AI/ML has emerged as a powerful tool to navigate the immense sequence space of possible enzyme variants. Instead of random or exhaustive mutagenesis, AI/ML-guided enzyme engineering uses data-driven models to prioritize mutations or designs likely to yield improvement.

The general workflow of ML-guided directed evolution (MLDE) involves: (1) generating an initial diverse library and measuring activities (the experimental data), (2) training an AI/ML model (such as a regression model or classifier, potentially a neural network) on that data to learn sequence–function relationships, and (3) using the model to propose the next set of variants expected to have even better activity. The proposed variants are then tested experimentally, new data are gathered, and the cycle repeats. By prioritizing beneficial mutations, AI/ML-guided approaches can explore sequence space more broadly rather than greedily following just the best current variant. This mitigates the risk of missing global optima. Yang et al. demonstrated the promise of this paradigm, showing that ML models could guide directed evolution to improve enzyme activity while using fewer screening iterations [\[46\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0046). As a concrete example, an AI/ML-guided evolution of Sortase A was able to find improved variants more efficiently than traditional methods by training a Bayesian model [\[47\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0047). Similarly, a recent study used an MLDE approach to evolve a ketoreductase with enhanced diastereoselectivity for a drug intermediate, successfully identifying highly selective variants [\[48\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0048). These successes illustrate how data-driven models can accelerate enzyme optimization, effectively reducing the experimenta*l*burden while achieving equal or better improvements.

 

### 6.3.4 *De Novo* Enzyme Design and Discovery

Despite the expanding repertoire of natural enzymes, retrosynthetic plans sometimes require reactions for which no known enzymes exist or no enzymes are efficient enough. In such cases, the ability to design new enzymes *de novo* – essentially inventing biocatalysts for “new-to-nature” reactions – is a game-changer. Traditional enzyme engineering starts from an existing protein scaffold, but *de novo* enzyme design aims to create an enzyme from scratch to catalyze a desired reaction. This is an enormously complex task: it requires imagining a protein structure that can bind the substrates in the correct orientation, stabilize the transition state of the reaction, and perform necessary catalytic chemistry, all while folding into a stable, expressible protein. Early efforts in *de novo* enzyme design (before the deep learning era) showed that it is possible in principle. For example, Röthlisberger et al. designed a novel enzyme for the Kemp elimination reaction by computationally inserting a theoretical catalytic motif into stable protein scaffolds, and after subsequent laboratory evolution, the enzyme achieved measurable activity [\[49\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0049). However, those efforts had very low success rates – tens of thousands of designs might yield one weakly active enzyme – underscoring the difficulty of the problem [\[50\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0050).

Recent advances in AI and computational modeling are dramatically improving the success of *de novo* enzyme design. One breakthrough has come from applying generative models, where AI models are trained to produce new protein sequences or structures with certain desired properties. Instead of manually specifying an active site geometry and painstakingly designing a scaffold (as in classical approaches), researchers can now leverage deep learning to “imagine” new proteins. A striking example is the “hallucination” approach developed by the Baker lab, in which a neural network is used to generate novel protein structures that satisfy certain design objectives [\[51\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0051). This method was used to create light-emitting enzymes (luciferases) that are unlike any natural protein [\[50\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0050). The team defined the chemical reaction they wanted (oxidation of a luciferin substrate to emit photons) and then used a deep-learning algorithm to hallucinate thousands of possible protein folds that could catalyze this reaction. Crucially, these hallucinated proteins were not modifications of known enzymes – they were built upon *de novo*\-designed scaffolds generated by AI. After incorporating a putative active site (for example, positioning an arginine in the model to stabilize the transition state's negative charge) and optimizing sequences, several designs were synthesized and tested. Remarkably, at least three designs showed luciferase activity, and one named “LuxSit” was highly efficient – emitting blue light with an intensity visible to the naked eye. LuxSit is only 117 amino acids in size (smaller than any known natural luciferase) and proved to be quite robust (partially folded even near boiling temperatures). This case opens the door to custom enzymes for almost any chemical reaction in principle.

Another revolutionary tool in *de novo* enzyme design is diffusion-based protein models. RFdiffusion adopted the principles of diffusion models (which have been used to generate images and text) to protein structures [\[23\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0023). RFdiffusion was used to design a complex serine hydrolase enzyme from scratch, achieving catalytic efficiency on par with a naturally occurring enzyme [\[52\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0052). The design pipeline began by specifying the desired reaction mechanism: in this case, ester hydrolysis via a classic serine-histidine-aspartate catalytic triad and an oxyanion hole for stabilizing intermediates. The 3D coordinates of the ideal active site (the arrangement of those key residues and the substrate binding geometry) were fed into RFdiffusion, which then generated entire protein structures that could hold that active site. The output of RFdiffusion is a novel protein backbone (a fold) that positions the catalytic residues correctly. Then, a second AI algorithm (such as a sequence design network like ProteinMPNN [\[24\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0024)) assigns amino acid identities to produce a viable sequence, and a third program evaluates how well each design might stabilize all steps of the reaction mechanism. Using this approach, the team generated about 1,000 *de novo* designs and screened them in wet lab, finding several that successfully catalyzed the full four-step hydrolysis mechanism with efficiencies comparable to natural enzymes. This level of catalytic performance was unprecedented for an enzyme designed *de novo*, underscoring the capacity of generative AI methods to capture intricate catalytic requirements associated with multistep reactions, which have historically challenged conventional design approaches. It is important to recognize that this achievement still required iterative experimental validation, where AI-generated candidates were synthesized, tested, and optimized. Nonetheless, the initial selection of enzyme designs was systematically guided by AI, representing a significant advancement over traditional random or trial-and-error strategies.

Beyond these specific techniques, a variety of generative models for protein design have flourished. These include variational autoencoders (VAEs) that learn a latent representation space of protein sequences [\[53\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0053), generative adversarial networks (GANs) like ProteinGAN [\[25\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0025) that are trained to produce plausible enzyme sequences, and large-scale language models such as ProGen [\[26\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0026) and ProtGPT2 [\[27\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0027) which can generate novel protein sequences character by character, having learned grammar from millions of natural proteins. These models can be used to generate proteins with specific properties. For example, ProGen has been used to create enzyme sequences based on a particular enzyme classification (EC number) or protein family, resulting in proteins that closely match the intended function or group. Such AI-generated enzymes still need experimental validation, but they expand the search beyond what evolution has sampled. In the context of retrosynthesis, one can imagine using generative models to propose an enzyme for a “missing reaction.” For example, designing an enzyme active site for a carbon–silicon bond formation (an unnatural reaction) and letting the model create a protein to catalyze it. While still an emerging area, there have been proof-of-concept successes where AI-designed enzymes enabled entirely new biocatalytic steps.

Despite these advances, *de novo* enzyme design remains challenging. Success often requires generating a huge number of candidates and depends on subtle factors that are not fully captured by current models (such as protein dynamics, solvent effects, and the need for cofactors or metal ions in some reactions). However, the rapid improvement in AI techniques is cause for optimism. The luciferase and hydrolase examples show that each year brings orders-of-magnitude improvements in success rate and enzyme performance. As generative models are further refined (for instance, incorporating physics-based feedback or training on enzyme mechanism data), we can expect bespoke enzymes for virtually any reaction to become achievable. For retrosynthetic planning, this means that even if a proposed biosynthetic pathway has “gaps” (steps with no known enzyme), one day it may be routine to fill those gaps by designing a new enzyme *in silico*, thus truly expanding biocatalysis to new frontiers of chemistry.

 

## 6.4 Perspectives

AI/ML is transforming retrosynthesis and biocatalysis, but there are still significant opportunities and challenges ahead. Examples include the integration of biocatalysis with traditional chemocatalysis in synthetic route design, the development of more powerful AI models (including foundation models and large language models) for synthesis planning, advances in predicting enzyme properties and designing enzymes for new-to-nature reactions, the standardization of data resources for model training, and improvements in the interpretability of deep learning models. Addressing these will push the boundaries of what's possible in computational retrosynthesis and accelerate the discovery of sustainable synthetic routes.

 

### 6.4.1 Integrating Biocatalysis with Chemocatalysis

In the future, we envision retrosynthetic planners that seamlessly combine biocatalysis and chemocatalysis, capitalizing on the strengths of each. For example, an early step in a synthetic route might be best done by a highly selective enzyme, while a later step might require a metal-catalyzed coupling that no enzyme can do. AI models should be developed to consider such trade-offs and propose hybrid pathways [\[54\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0054). Recent discussions highlight that current retrosynthesis algorithms seldom incorporate biocatalytic steps alongside traditional steps. To change this, more data on chemo-enzymatic sequences of reactions will be needed so that planners can learn patterns of when to insert an enzyme-catalyzed step for optimal results. There have been successful examples of chemoenzymatic synthesis, such as routes to certain pharmaceuticals where an enzyme step improved yield or selectivity compared to purely chemical routes [\[55\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0055).

In practical terms, a retrosynthesis AI may propose a multistep route where an engineered enzyme converts a cheap starting material into an intermediate, which is then coupled chemically to another fragment, followed by an enzymatic resolution step, etc. Such hybrid routes can yield shorter, more economical syntheses. Moving forward, the community will benefit from efforts to bridge the gap between organic chemistry and biochemistry datasets. Initiatives might include expanding retrosynthetic rule sets to cover enzymatic transformations, and teaching models to evaluate sequences of steps by combined metrics (e.g. overall yield considering both chemo and bio steps, compatibility of reaction conditions). Successfully combining biocatalysis and chemocatalysis *in silico* will mirror what synthetic chemists often do in the lab – using “the best tool for the job” at each step – but with the speed and breadth of exploration that AI offers. Ultimately, this integration is expected to produce more creative and greener synthetic routes for complex molecules, transcending the boundaries of traditional retrosynthesis.

 

### 6.4.2 Toward Next-Generation AI for Retrobiosynthesis Planning

While significant progress has been made in retrosynthetic route prediction, there is a clear need for more powerful AI models dedicated to biosynthetic planning. Many current retrosynthesis algorithms (whether template-based or template-free) were developed for organic synthesis and then adapted to include biotransformation in a limited way. Future models should be built from the ground up with biochemistry in mind. One promising direction is the development of foundation models for chemistry and biology – large AI models trained on massive amounts of reaction data or biochemical knowledge that can then be fine-tuned for specific tasks. In the chemistry domain, we already see large transformer models that have “learned” chemistry from millions of reaction examples. Analogous models could be trained on networks of metabolic pathways and enzymatic reactions [\[10\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0010). A foundation model could encode general principles of retrosynthetic logic (e.g. recognizing strategic bonds to break in molecules) while also understanding enzyme constraints (like recognizing which functional groups enzymes commonly act upon).

Additionally, the advent of large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT opens the door to interactive retrosynthesis planning. One can imagine a ChatBot for retrosynthesis that allows chemists to dialog with the AI: the user might ask for a synthetic plan for a target, the AI proposes a route (mixing chemical and enzymatic steps) and explains its reasoning, and the user can ask follow-up “what if” questions (such as swapping in an available enzyme or considering an alternative starting material). To achieve this, LLMs would need to be imbued with retrosynthetic knowledge – possibly by training on texts (papers, patents) about synthetic methods and pathways. Early experiments in this vein are appearing, where LLMs have been used to suggest chemical reactions or annotate pathways, but much development is needed for reliable performance.

 

### 6.4.3 Enhancing Enzyme Prediction and Design Capabilities

As retrosynthetic planning models become more advanced, a parallel need is for more powerful AI tools to predict enzyme properties and to design new enzymes. Having a pathway plan is only half the battle – one must ensure the chosen enzymes can actually carry out their steps efficiently. We discussed earlier how AI/ML can predict certain properties and how generative models can create new enzymes. Going forward, these capabilities need to be expanded and made more accurate to truly enable on-demand biocatalyst development for any reaction.

One critical challenge is accurately predicting enzyme-substrate pairs: given a candidate enzyme, can we predict if it will accept a proposed substrate and at what rate? Current approaches, like docking simulations or simple sequence similarity, have limited reliability, especially for novel substrates. Moreover, current AI models primarily rely on protein-level embeddings and are often unable to reliably predict catalytic efficiency across diverse enzyme families. Given that even single mutations can drastically alter catalytic properties, existing models frequently struggle with transferability and accuracy, severely limiting their trustworthiness. Improving existing models will likely require more training data – e.g. high-throughput screening results or kinetics data for various enzyme-substrate combinations and enzymes with single-mutation resolution – which calls for community efforts to share and standardize such data. If successful, such models would greatly aid retrosynthesis: whenever a model suggests a reaction, the enzyme-activity predictor could suggest a feasible enzyme or the need for engineering.

On the enzyme engineering front, better AI/ML models for mutation effects will make it easier to optimize enzymes *in silico*. We foresee more use of large pretrained protein models (like those that produce residue embeddings) to predict the effect of mutations on function. Currently, there are computational methods that leverage transformer models to predict beneficial mutations by analyzing patterns within multiple sequence alignments. However, current methods remain highly dependent on the initial diversity of mutation libraries and struggle significantly with capturing epistatic interactions between mutations, which are critical but often overlooked in current modeling approaches. Future tools might allow a scientist to engineer enzymes with a bulkier substrate, and the AI model outputs a set of mutations predicted to enlarge the binding pocket without disrupting the enzyme's fold or activity. More powerful AI/ML models, possibly incorporating physics-informed neural networks, could even estimate how a mutation affects the transition state stabilization – a key piece for catalysis that is currently almost impossible to know without experiments.

Importantly, to unlock truly new-to-nature reactions, *de novo* enzyme design using generative models will continue to advance. In the near future, generative models might design enzymes for reactions that are completely artificial (for instance, forming chemical bonds not found in any metabolic pathway). Some research groups are already working on training generative models conditioned on reaction chemistry descriptors, essentially asking the model to “hallucinate” an enzyme given a description of the reaction. We expect the quality of AI-designed enzymes to improve to the point that fewer design-build-test cycles are required. As generative models become more adept, enzyme design could become a standard step in retrosynthesis: whenever no natural enzyme is available for a desired transformation, the retrosynthesis program could invoke a generative model to propose a new enzyme, effectively adding a “virtual enzyme inventory” to the planner's toolkit.

 

### 6.4.4 Data Standardization and Model Interpretability

The progress of ML in retrobiosynthesis is tightly linked to the availability of high-quality data. One pressing need is to standardize and expand databases for enzymes, reactions, and pathways, in formats conducive to AI/ML model development. Currently, information is scattered across resources: enzyme sequences and basic functions in UniProt [\[40\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0040), detailed kinetic data in BRENDA [\[28\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0028) or SABIO-RK [\[31\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0031), metabolic pathways in KEGG [\[29\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0029) or MetaCyc [\[56\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0056), and experimental protein engineering data in literature or niche databases like ProtaBank [\[57\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0057). Many of these databases were not designed with ML in mind – they may lack negative examples, have inconsistent naming, or miss links between datasets (e.g. which sequence in UniProt [\[40\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0040) corresponds to which kinetics entry in BRENDA [\[28\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0028)). To build robust AI/ML models, we need comprehensive datasets with consistent annotations. For example, a model that predicts enzyme specificity would benefit from a dataset that, for each enzyme, lists substrates it acts on and does not act on, under standard conditions. Achieving this requires the community to agree on data schemas and share experimental results even when they are “failures” (to avoid biasing models). Going forward, concerted initiatives to link these databases (so that a model can easily fetch all relevant info about an enzyme: sequence, structure, reactions, kinetics, mutants, etc.) will greatly facilitate AI/ML development.

Finally, as AI models for retrobiosynthesis become more complex (deep neural networks with millions of parameters), there is a growing call for interpretable and explainable models. Currently, many deep learning models are “black boxes” – they might predict which enzyme to use or which mutation to make, but not why. Increasing interpretability can take several forms. One approach is to integrate mechanistic knowledge or constraints into the model, so that its outputs follow known rules of chemistry. For instance, a retrosynthesis model might be constrained by atom-mapping rules that ensure mass balance, or an enzyme activity predictor might highlight which amino acid positions in the active site contributed most to its decision (perhaps via an attention mechanism that can be visualized). Another approach is post-hoc interpretation: analyzing a trained model to extract human-comprehensible insights. For example, if a neural network predicts enzyme function from sequence, tools like saliency maps could identify motifs or residues that the network finds important – which might correspond to known catalytic motifs or suggest new ones. In one study, an AI/ML classifier for enzyme families was designed to be “biochemically interpretable,” meaning it associated certain learned features with known biochemical properties [\[58\]](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0058). Such interpretability not only builds trust but can lead to scientific discovery (e.g. uncovering new sequence patterns that correlate with specificity).

In conclusion, the future of AI/ML-enabled retrobiosynthesis is bright. We anticipate a positive feedback loop where better data leads to better models, and better models enable experiments that generate even more valuable data. In this synergy of computation and biotechnology, enzymes – nature's catalysts – will play a starring role, guided by algorithms that can learn from nature's examples and imagination that can go beyond them. With integrated chemoenzymatic planning, powerful AI-driven design tools, and a focus on interpretable and trustworthy AI, the vision of on-demand biosynthesis of any molecule is becoming increasingly tangible. The coming years will likely witness retrosynthesis AI evolving from a clever assistant to an indispensable creative partner in synthetic chemistry and biotechnology.

# 7  
Machine Learning to Accelerate the Discovery of Therapeutic Peptides

*Nicole Soto-Garcia^()*

*¹Universidad de Magallanes, Departamento de Ingeniería en Computación, 6210427, Avenida Bulnes 01855, Punta, Arenas, Chile*  
*²Leibniz Institute of Plant Biochemistry, Department of Bioorganic Chemistry, 06120, Weinberg 3, Halle, Germany*

 

## 7.1 Introduction

In this chapter, we present a comprehensive overview of current machine learning (ML)-based methods and strategies that are transforming and accelerating the discovery and design of therapeutic peptides. We begin by introducing key biological concepts related to peptides, including their therapeutic relevance, mechanisms of action, and the advantages they offer over traditional small-molecule drugs – such as higher specificity, lower toxicity, and the ability to target challenging biological interfaces. We also address their limitations, including stability, bioavailability, and susceptibility to degradation.

Next, we describe the main data sources available for extracting relevant information about peptides, covering aspects such as biological activity, molecular function, pharmacokinetics, and potential toxic effects. We then introduce traditional data-driven strategies used in developing ML models for peptide property prediction, focusing on supervised learning pipelines that incorporate sequence encoding, model training, and validation.

Following this foundation, we explore both classical and state-of-the-art ML approaches across various tasks, including bioactivity classification, prediction of toxic adverse effects (such as cytotoxicity, hemolysis, and immunogenicity), and estimation of key pharmacological properties such as half-life, *IC*[*50*], or stability in physiological environments. In addition, we examine recent advances in generative modeling and *de novo* peptide design, highlighting how approaches such as variational autoencoders (VAEs), generative adversarial networks (GANs), and diffusion models enable the creation of novel peptide sequences with optimized properties.

Finally, we discuss the emerging field of autonomous peptide design, driven by the integration of ML-based agents capable of iterative learning, optimization, and decision-making. We evaluate current frameworks that incorporate reinforcement learning, active learning, and closed-loop design pipelines, and we assess their potential to enable self-improving platforms for therapeutic peptide discovery. The chapter concludes with a critical analysis of the advantages, limitations, and open challenges in building fully autonomous systems, emphasizing how ML can drive the next generation of intelligent, data-guided peptide therapeutics.

 

## 7.2 Peptides: Definitions and Main Characteristics

In contrast to the full-length enzymes discussed in [Chapters 5](#c05.xhtml) and [6](#c06.xhtml), peptides are short chains of amino acids linked by peptide bonds, typically ranging from 2 to 100 amino acid residues, and with molecular weights between 0.5 and 10 kDa [\[1\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0001).

Structurally, peptides can adopt a variety of secondary conformations, including α-helices, β-sheets, and random coils [\[2\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0002). However, their stability can be compromised by enzymatic degradation and conformational flexibility, limiting their bioavailability and therapeutic efficacy [\[3\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0003).

Peptides are involved in a wide array of biological processes, including hormone regulation, immune response, cell signaling, and tissue repair, making them key molecular tools across both scientific and industrial domains [\[4\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0004).

Due to their structural and functional versatility, peptides play essential roles in biological systems and hold high value in biotechnology, medicine, and various industrial applications [\[5\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0005). [Figure 7.1](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0001) summarizes the most common applications of peptides.

In the food industry, peptides function as bio-active compounds with antioxidant [\[6\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0006) and food preservative properties [\[7\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0007).

In biotechnology, peptides are utilized in the development of biosensors, where they act as recognition elements for detecting specific molecules [\[8\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0008). They are also applied in plant protection, acting as biopesticides or disease resistance enhancers [\[9\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0009), in immune modulation [\[10\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0010) and in protein purification workflows through affinity-tag-based techniques [\[11\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0011).

Finally, in biomedical research and therapeutics applications, peptides play a central role in drug design and delivery. Their uses include the development of antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) with antifungal, antiviral, and antibacterial activity, as well as tumor-targeting agents and components in cell signaling pathways [\[4\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0004).

In industrial contexts, peptides play a vital role in the food industry, particularly as natural antioxidants and food preservative agents. Beyond their applications in food technology, peptides are widely utilized in biotechnology. Peptides serve important functions in plant protection, acting as bio-based insecticides and herbicides, as well as components in biosensors and the development of disease-resistant crops through genetic engineering. Moreover, peptides are crucial in the pharmaceutical and medical fields. They function as therapeutic agents with antimicrobial, antiviral, and anticancer properties, and are also employed in drug delivery systems due to their biocompatibility, specificity, and low toxicity. Their versatility and efficacy make them indispensable tools across multiple industrial sectors.

## 7.3 Benefits and Limitations of Therapeutic Peptides

The therapeutic potential of peptides stems from their ability to bind with high affinity and specificity to cell surface receptors, triggering precise intracellular signaling pathways [\[12\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0012). This selectivity makes them particularly effective against a variety of pathogens, including viruses, bacteria, fungi, and parasites [\[13\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0013). Therapeutic peptides exhibit enhanced tissue penetration, improved bioavailability, and increased potency—making them promising candidates for targeted therapies with reduced off-target effects and minimized side effects [\[14\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0014).

Compared to small-molecule drugs, therapeutic peptides offer several advantages. Their synthesis is often simpler and more cost-effective, particularly through solid-phase peptide synthesis or recombinant production methods [\[15\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0015). Their high target specificity not only boosts efficacy but also significantly reduces the likelihood of adverse effects [\[16\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0016). Furthermore, peptides generally exhibit lower immunogenicity, improving their clinical safety profile. Being biodegradable, they are less likely to accumulate in tissues, thus reducing systemic toxicity and aligning well with the principles of precision medicine [\[17\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0017).

Despite all described advantages, therapeutic peptides face several clinical and pharmacological challenges. Their short half-life, due to rapid enzymatic degradation and renal clearance, limits their therapeutic window [\[18\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0018). Oral administration is typically ineffective due to poor gastrointestinal stability and low permeability, often necessitating parenteral delivery routes (e.g. intravenous, subcutaneous, or intramuscular), which can reduce patient adherence and introduce risks such as discomfort and infection [\[19\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0019). Moreover, peptides are vulnerable to denaturation under extreme pH conditions and exhibit low membrane permeability, limiting intracellular access and bioefficacy [\[20\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0020).

To address these limitations, ongoing research focuses on improving peptide stability, bioavailability, and delivery strategies. Techniques such as peptide cyclization, PEGylation, lipidation, nanoparticle encapsulation, and the use of cell-penetrating peptides are being explored to enhance pharmacokinetics and therapeutic performance [\[21\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0021).

In parallel, drug discovery and drug repurposing strategies are accelerating therapeutic peptide development. Drug discovery efforts aim to identify novel bioactive peptides through high-throughput screening (HTS), computational modeling, and peptide libraries. In contrast, drug repurposing investigates new therapeutic indications for already approved peptides, significantly reducing development time and cost [\[22\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0022). These approaches have broadened the clinical landscape of peptide therapeutics, providing new treatment options for diseases that were previously challenging to manage with traditional small-molecule drugs [\[23\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0023).

As advances in peptide engineering, delivery technologies, and computational biology continue to evolve, therapeutic peptides are poised to become even more powerful tools in modern medicine—offering personalized, targeted, and safer alternatives for a wide array of conditions [\[24\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0024).

 

## 7.4 Computational Design of Therapeutic Peptides

The integration of computational strategies has revolutionized the discovery and design of therapeutic peptides, significantly accelerating the identification of candidates with high bioactivity, specificity, and stability [\[25\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0025). Techniques such as ML, peptide-protein docking, and bioinformatics enable the rapid screening of vast peptide libraries and the prediction of essential properties, including binding affinity, solubility, stability, and toxicity [\[26\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0026). By leveraging large-scale biological datasets and predictive modeling, these tools reduce reliance on time-consuming and costly wet-lab experiments, thereby streamlining and expediting drug development pipelines [\[27\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0027).

Among computational methodologies, deep learning models and sequence-based algorithms have proven particularly effective in predicting peptide bioactivities and interactions with biological targets [\[28\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0028). Trained on comprehensive datasets, these models uncover intricate sequence–function relationships, supporting the design of highly potent and selective therapeutic peptides [\[29\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0029). Additionally, molecular dynamics simulations provide atomic-level insights into peptide conformational stability and target binding, facilitating the optimization of physicochemical and pharmacological properties [\[30\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0030).

The advent of generative models, including transformers, GANs, and VAEs, has further advanced *de novo* peptide design. These models are capable of generating novel peptide sequences with tailored pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiles, expanding the chemical and functional space beyond naturally occurring sequences [\[5\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0005).

Moreover, structure-based drug design (SBDD) and computational docking refine peptide–target interactions by predicting binding affinities, conformational flexibility, and energetically favorable poses, thereby supporting the selection and optimization of lead candidates [\[31\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0031). AI-driven screening pipelines also integrate bioinformatics resources to identify natural peptides with therapeutic potential, analyzing protein–peptide interaction networks, sequence motifs, and 3D structural features [\[25\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0025).

To ensure the clinical viability of therapeutic peptide candidates, multi-objective optimization algorithms are employed to simultaneously balance key parameters such as stability, potency, bioavailability, and toxicity [\[32\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0032). The application of these strategies enables the rational prioritization of candidates for preclinical validation.

As computational methodologies continue to evolve, their synergy with experimental validation is critical for achieving effective and reliable peptide design [\[33\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0033). Hybrid approaches – which combine *in silico* predictions with HTS, structural biology, and biophysical characterization – enhance both the accuracy and efficiency of the discovery process [\[34\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0034). Furthermore, AI-driven peptide engineering platforms enable rational modifications aimed at improving enzymatic stability, membrane permeability, and systemic bioavailability [\[35\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0035).

By merging computational power with empirical validation, modern strategies are reshaping the landscape of therapeutic peptides, offering innovative solutions for complex and previously untreatable diseases, and unlocking new avenues for precision medicine [\[26\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0026).

 

## 7.5 Data Sources for Peptide Discovery

The advancement of drug design, driven by AI and the increasing availability of biological data, has led to the development of specialized databases and computational methodologies that are now fundamental to biomedical research [\[5\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0005). Core resources such as the Protein Data Bank [\[36\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0036) and UniProt [\[37\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0037) provide comprehensive structural and sequence data for proteins, supporting tasks such as molecular modeling, protein annotation, and SBDD. In parallel, dedicated peptide databases – such as Peptipedia v2.0 or DRAMP – provide specialized information on peptide sequences (see [Table 7.1](#c07.xhtml#c07-tbl-0001) for a list of the most relevant databases used to facilitate the study of therapeutic peptides). These platforms play a crucial role in the identification and optimization of therapeutic peptide candidates, centralizing large-scale datasets and integrating computational tools that accelerate peptide discovery, design, and refinement for clinical and industrial applications.

Peptide-related databases encompass a wide range of resources, from general repositories that catalog diverse peptide types to specialized databases focused on particular peptide families, biological functions, or pharmacological properties \[[25](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0025), [49](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0049), [57](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0057)\]. These repositories support therapeutic and biotechnological applications by providing access to peptide sequences, structural data, and functional annotations [\[58\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0058).

General-purpose peptide databases such as StraPep and PepBank compile extensive datasets to support research into structure–function relationships and biological activities. StraPep focuses on natural bioactive peptides, documenting their structural features, while PepBank uses text mining techniques to extract and curate peptide data relevant to therapeutic and diagnostic development \[[40](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0040), [47](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0047)\]. Within functional classifications, AMPs have attracted considerable interest due to the growing threat of antibiotic resistance [\[59\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0059). Several AMP-specific databases – including Peptipedia v2.0, dbAMP, DBAASP, LAMP, DRAMP, InverPep, and CAMPR – provide curated information on natural, synthetic, and patented peptides, covering their antimicrobial spectra, structural characteristics, and optimization tools for therapeutic development \[[4](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0004), [38](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0038), [39](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0039), [41](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0041)–[43](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0043), [51](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0043)\].
