Beyond AMPs, specialized databases focused on peptides with particular biomedical applications have been implemented. For example, AVPdb catalogs antiviral peptides (AVPs) targeting pathogens such as HIV, RSV, and SARS [\[45\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0045), while CancerPPD is dedicated to anticancer peptides (ACPs) [\[44\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0044). Other focused repositories include Hemolytik (hemolytic peptides) [\[46\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0046), B3Pdb (blood–brain barrier-penetrating peptides) [\[52\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0052), Quorumpeps (quorum-sensing peptides) [\[53\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0053), and AntiAngioPred (antiangiogenic peptides) [\[55\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0055). In addition, databases like PEPlife and PLifePred provide data on peptide half-life and *in vivo* stability, which are critical for pharmacokinetic optimization \[[49](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0049), [54](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0054), [60](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0060)\]. Other repositories track bioactivity metrics such as *IC*[*100*] values for AVPs [\[61\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0061) and *IC*[*50*] values for antihypertensive and antidiabetic peptides [\[48\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0048).

Understanding peptide–target interactions is essential for the rational design of bioactive peptides. Databases focusing on these interactions are typically categorized into large-scale general repositories, reference datasets, and specialized collections derived from specific experimental studies [\[25\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0025). In addition to research-oriented resources, databases documenting regulatory-approved peptides are vital for drug repurposing and clinical translation [\[62\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0062). For instance, THPdb provides curated information on therapeutic peptides and proteins, including sequences, physicochemical properties, mechanisms of action, and pharmacodynamics [\[50\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0050). Similarly, PepTherDia compiles detailed data on 105 FDA-approved peptide drugs, covering administration routes, pharmacokinetics, and therapeutic indications [\[56\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0056).

Collectively, these repositories not only support fundamental research but also accelerate drug discovery by enabling data-driven peptide optimization and expanding the therapeutic potential of peptides across various disease areas.

 

## 7.6 ML-Based Strategies to Accelerate the Discovery of Therapeutic Peptides

The design of ML-based predictive models has become a fundamental strategy for classifying bioactivities and estimating the physicochemical or pharmacological properties of therapeutic peptides. These data-driven approaches follow a systematic pipeline that includes the collection and curation of peptide datasets, numerical encoding of peptide sequences, model training using suitable ML algorithms, performance evaluation through established metrics, and application of the trained model to predict properties or activities of novel peptide sequences [\[63\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0063).

This section outlines the methodologies used to develop sequence-based predictive models, emphasizing data preprocessing, feature representation strategies, and model training workflows. Moreover, the applicability of ML-based strategies for classifying bioactive functions, predicting toxicological risks, and estimating relevant pharmacological properties of therapeutic peptides is highlighted.

 

### 7.6.1 Data-Driven Approaches

The application of data-driven approaches for developing sequence-based predictive models aimed at estimating peptide properties or bioactivities is illustrated in [Figure 7.2](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0002). This process generally involves two main stages: the preparation of data for model training and the training and evaluation of the predictive model itself.

The first stage begins with the collection and preprocessing of peptide sequences, which must be carefully aligned with the specific objective of the model – whether it is to classify AMPs, predict half-life values, or estimate solubility. These sequences are typically obtained from curated datasets and public peptide databases, as described in [Section 7.5](#c07.xhtml#c07-sec-0006). Once collected, the dataset undergoes a cleaning process to remove redundant entries, correct inconsistencies, and filter out sequences that contain noncanonical amino acids or incomplete annotations. This step ensures the quality and reliability of the data used for training.

After curation, the peptide sequences must be transformed into numerical representations to make them compatible with ML algorithms. Several encoding strategies can be employed for this purpose, ranging from classical approaches such as one-hot encoding and physicochemical property descriptors to frequency-based methods like *k*\-mers and signal transformations. In recent years, more advanced techniques based on pretrained protein language models – such as ESM, Mistral, and ProT5 – have gained popularity, as they generate embeddings that capture the contextual and functional features of peptide sequences with remarkable accuracy [\[1\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0001).

Once the numerical representations are ready, the dataset is typically divided into training, validation, and testing subsets, often using a 70:20:10 ratio. In cases where datasets are relatively small, an 80:20 split between training and testing is preferred, supplemented with cross-validation techniques to minimize overfitting and enhance the model's generalization capabilities.

With the data partitioned, the training phase begins. During this stage, ML models are constructed using the training subset. A variety of algorithms can be applied depending on the problem and the nature of the data, including distance-based, rule-based, regression-based, kernel-based, and ensemble-based methods. In some cases, particularly when working with large datasets or rich sequence embeddings, deep learning architectures such as convolutional or recurrent neural networks (RNNs) may be used to capture complex, high-dimensional patterns in the data.

Following training, the performance of the model is evaluated using the validation and test datasets. Classification tasks are typically assessed using metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score, while regression tasks are evaluated through correlation-based metrics like Pearson and Spearman correlation coefficients, as well as error-based metrics such as mean absolute error (MAE) and root mean squared error (RMSE). The validation dataset is also essential for tuning hyperparameters, which is commonly done using optimization strategies such as grid search, genetic algorithms, or Bayesian optimization to identify the most effective configuration for the model.

![Figure 7.2 Overview of the workflow for developing sequence-based predictive models.](images/c07f002.png)

Figure 7.2 Overview of the workflow for developing sequence-based predictive models.

Finally, the independent test dataset is used to evaluate the model's generalization ability and to report final performance metrics. This dataset also serves as a benchmark for comparison with alternative methods or previously published results. Once validated, the trained model can be exported and is ready for deployment in practical applications, including peptide screening, drug discovery, and the rational design of therapeutic candidates.

The process begins with the construction of a dataset by gathering peptide or protein sequences from public databases or repositories. Preprocessing steps are then applied to remove redundancy, correct inconsistencies, and ensure data quality. The curated sequences are transformed into numerical representations using encoding techniques, making them suitable for ML algorithms. These encoded datasets are used to train predictive models through supervised learning. Finally, the model's performance is evaluated using validation and testing datasets to ensure accuracy, reliability, and generalization.

 

### 7.6.2 ML Strategies for Peptide Bioactivity Classification

The growing number of experimentally characterized peptides has accelerated the adoption of computational biology and data-driven techniques for sequence analysis, functional prediction, and design optimization. In particular, ML approaches have emerged as powerful tools for developing predictive models capable of classifying and characterizing peptide bioactivities, including antimicrobial, antifungal, antiviral, and anticancer properties, among others [\[64\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0064). These models not only facilitate the identification of promising therapeutic candidates but also reduce experimental costs and time by enabling *in silico* screening prior to synthesis and validation.

In this section, we present an overview of the current state of the art in ML-based predictive modeling for therapeutic peptides. We describe the main components of the modeling pipeline, including data collection, sequence encoding strategies, model training, and performance evaluation, and discuss recent advancements leveraging deep learning and protein language models. Special attention is given to tools and frameworks designed to support the discovery and development of peptides with specific bioactivities.

 

#### 7.6.2.1 Classification Models for Antimicrobial Peptides

Recent advances in AMP classification models have been driven by the integration of cutting-edge ML and deep learning techniques. These models have become increasingly sophisticated, leveraging diverse architectures and learning strategies to improve the accuracy and generalizability of AMP prediction and design.

One notable example is Diff-AMP, a generative framework that integrates attention mechanisms, diffusion models, and reinforcement learning to automate AMP generation, activity prediction, and sequence optimization. By incorporating pretraining and transfer learning, Diff-AMP achieves enhanced performance and adaptability across diverse peptide datasets [\[65\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0065). In parallel, the representation of peptide sequences has become more varied and nuanced. For instance, AMPActiPred relies on traditional feature engineering approaches, extracting a comprehensive set of compositional and physicochemical descriptors to construct predictive features [\[66\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0066).

Other models take hybrid approaches. AntiBP3 combines binary profiles of terminal residues with distributed representations (embeddings), achieving outstanding performance with an AUC of 0.98 in predicting Gram-negative antibacterial peptides [\[67\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0067). Meanwhile, Deep-ABPpred utilizes bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM) networks in combination with word2vec embeddings to capture sequential and contextual information from peptide sequences, demonstrating over 94% accuracy on independent test datasets [\[68\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0068).

More recently, large-scale models have embraced the power of pretrained protein language models. AMP-Detector, for example, integrates representations from protein language models with ML classifiers to screen large peptide libraries. This framework successfully identified over 190,000 putative AMPs and facilitated the design of more than 500 novel candidate peptides with predicted antimicrobial activity [\[1\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0001).

 

#### 7.6.2.2 Classification Models for Antiviral Peptides

AVP prediction has evolved considerably over the past decade, progressing from early ML classifiers to more complex deep learning architectures and virus-specific frameworks. AVPpred was the first predictive model specifically designed for AVPs. It employed a support vector machine (SVM) classifier and achieved an accuracy of 86% with a Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) of 0.71, laying the groundwork for subsequent computational methods in the field [\[69\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0069).

Later models introduced ensemble learning techniques, such as Random Forests and AdaBoost, which improved predictive performance, reaching accuracies as high as 93.26% [\[70\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0070). Ensemble-based meta-predictors like Meta-iAVP and PePred-Suite further enhanced classification performance by integrating multiple base classifiers and feature types, demonstrating the value of combining diverse model outputs for robust AVP prediction \[[71](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0071), [72](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0072)\].

With the rise of deep learning, architectures incorporating bidirectional RNNs (BiRNNs) and convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have been developed to automatically extract high-level sequence patterns, improving the generalization and scalability of AVP predictors [\[73\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0073). One innovative example is AI4AVP, which combines CNNs with GANs to synthetically augment training datasets, addressing the limited availability of labeled AVP sequences and improving model robustness [\[74\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0074).

More recent models have extended their scope beyond binary classification to include multi-label prediction of target viral families, as seen in FFM-AVP [\[75\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0075). In parallel, virus-specific predictors have been developed to identify AVPs active against particular pathogens, including coronaviruses [\[76\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0076), dengue virus [\[77\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0077), hepatitis C virus [\[78\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0078), and HIV [\[79\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0079). For instance, iDVIP focuses on peptides that inhibit HIV integrase, while the DBAASP platform includes predictive tools for linear peptides that block viral entry into host cells \[[80](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0080), [81](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0081)\].

 

#### 7.6.2.3 Classification Models for Antifungal Peptides

Computational models for antifungal peptide (AFP) classification have evolved rapidly, integrating increasingly sophisticated ML and deep learning techniques to enhance predictive performance and model interpretability. Early models like AntiFP employed a support vector machine classifier using simple amino acid composition features, representing one of the first attempts at *in silico* AFP prediction [\[82\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0082).

As the field progressed, models began to incorporate more informative descriptors. Deep-AntiFP, for example, combined physicochemical and quasi-sequential features with deep neural networks, enabling improved discrimination between AFPs and non-AFPs [\[83\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0083). Further advancement came with Deep-AFPpred, which introduced a hybrid deep learning framework based on one-dimensional CNNs (1D-CNNs) and BiLSTM networks, enhanced by transfer learning. This architecture demonstrated strong generalization capabilities on independent test datasets [\[84\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0084).

Building on these architectures, DeepAFP achieved even higher predictive accuracy (93.29%) by integrating evolutionary information – such as position-specific scoring matrices (PSSMs) – alongside physicochemical features within a CNN-BiLSTM hybrid model, showcasing the benefits of combining sequence conservation with structural properties [\[85\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0085).

More recently, cutting-edge models have adopted transformer-based encodings and attention mechanisms. iAFPs-Mv-BiTCN represents a state-of-the-art model that fuses skip-gram and transformer-derived sequence embeddings, SHAP-based feature selection, and a bidirectional temporal convolutional network (BiTCN), offering enhanced sequence modeling capabilities and interpretability [\[86\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0086). Similarly, MLAFP-XN employed eight different feature extraction and selection strategies in conjunction with XGBoost, achieving a remarkable accuracy of 99.48%. Notably, it incorporates SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) to interpret model predictions and identify key features driving classification decisions [\[87\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0087).

These advances reflect the growing complexity and refinement of AFP prediction frameworks. From traditional handcrafted features to embedding-based and explainable models, the field continues to push the boundaries of what is possible in peptide-based antifungal drug discovery. Continued integration of evolutionary, structural, and contextual sequence information promises to further improve the reliability and applicability of these tools in therapeutic design.

 

#### 7.6.2.4 Additional Classification Models for Therapeutic Peptides

In addition to antimicrobial, antiviral, and AFPs, a variety of ML-based predictive models have been developed to classify other therapeutic peptide categories with significant clinical relevance. These include antiparasitic, anticancer, tumor-homing, wound-healing, and antiaging peptides, among others. This section highlights representative computational approaches used for the classification of these specialized peptides, underscoring the diversity of techniques and applications in the field.

For antiparasitic peptides (APPs), models such as i2APP adopt a two-stage approach that integrates LightGBM and SVM classifiers, achieving an accuracy of 91.3% and an AUC of 0.935, showcasing the benefit of hybrid ensemble strategies [\[88\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0088). Similarly, PredAPP employs a combination of feature selection techniques and ensemble classifiers to improve predictive robustness and generalization performance [\[89\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0089).

In the domain of ACP prediction, recent models have embraced deep learning and dimensionality reduction for enhanced performance. ACPPfel, for instance, combines multiple feature selection and embedding techniques with deep learning models, reaching an impressive accuracy of 98.53% and an AUC of 0.997 [\[90\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0090). Likewise, cACP-DeepGram integrates FastText-based skip-gram embeddings with deep neural networks, effectively capturing local sequence patterns relevant to anticancer activity [\[91\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0091). MLACP 2.0 takes a meta-learning approach, combining CNNs with diverse encoding schemes to support multi-view learning and further improve ACP classification accuracy [\[92\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0092).

For tumor-homing peptides (THPs), THPep uses a Random Forest classifier trained on compositional and physicochemical descriptors to distinguish peptides with tumor-targeting potential, offering a useful tool for peptide-based drug delivery research [\[93\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0093).

In other therapeutic categories, models continue to expand the scope of peptide discovery. WHP-Pred leverages XGBoost to predict wound-healing peptides (WHPs) based on a curated feature set derived from sequence and biochemical properties [\[94\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0094). Meanwhile, Antiaging-FL focuses on identifying antiaging peptides by incorporating feature-level fusion and ML classifiers, enabling the exploration of peptides with potential regenerative or protective effects in age-related biological processes [\[95\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0095).

These models illustrate the growing application of ML in peptide therapeutics beyond conventional categories. As curated datasets grow and representation methods improve, predictive tools tailored to specific therapeutic contexts will become increasingly valuable for accelerating *in silico* peptide discovery.

 

### 7.6.3 Strategies for Building Toxicity Classification Models

ML techniques have greatly facilitated the development of predictive models aimed at the early detection of adverse toxic effects in therapeutic peptides. These toxic responses can severely limit the clinical applicability of peptide-based drugs and typically include cytotoxicity, hemolysis, and allergenicity. Cytotoxicity refers to a peptide's potential to damage or destroy host cells, leading to tissue injury or compromised organ function. Hemolysis involves the rupture of red blood cell membranes, which can result in the release of hemoglobin into the bloodstream and cause serious complications such as anemia or renal failure. Allergenicity denotes the ability of a peptide to provoke immune hypersensitivity reactions, ranging from mild inflammatory responses to severe and potentially life-threatening allergic reactions.

Given the complexity and variability of these toxicological outcomes, computational models have emerged as valuable tools for systematically assessing safety risks during the early stages of peptide development. In particular, ML-based approaches can learn intricate sequence–function relationships from experimental data, enabling them to identify peptides likely to cause adverse effects with high accuracy.

This section highlights a variety of ML frameworks designed to predict toxicity in therapeutic peptides. These include traditional classification models based on physicochemical descriptors, as well as more advanced deep learning architectures that leverage sequence embeddings and transfer learning to enhance predictive performance. By integrating these tools into the peptide discovery pipeline, researchers can effectively filter out unsafe candidates prior to synthesis and biological testing, thereby improving both the safety profile and the efficiency of therapeutic peptide development.

 

#### 7.6.3.1 Toxicity Prediction

ToxinPred was one of the pioneering tools developed for predicting peptide toxicity, employing SVMs trained on sequence-derived features to classify toxic and nontoxic peptides with reasonable accuracy [\[96\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0096). Since then, the field has evolved significantly, incorporating more powerful ML and deep learning techniques to capture the complex relationships underlying toxic effects.

Recent models have leveraged deep neural networks to improve generalization and predictive accuracy. For instance, extensions of ToxinPred now incorporate deep learning frameworks that can automatically extract hierarchical features from peptide sequences, providing more robust toxicity assessments [\[97\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0097). Other approaches, such as ToxDL, utilize CNNs to model local residue-level patterns associated with toxicity, enabling the detection of subtle sequence motifs that traditional models may overlook [\[98\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0098).

Hybrid architectures have also shown strong performance in toxicity prediction tasks. Models like ToxIBTL combine CNNs with BiLSTM networks, capturing both spatial and sequential dependencies within peptide sequences [\[99\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0099). Furthermore, the integration of protein language models, such as CSM-Toxin, has marked a significant advancement by using large-scale unsupervised pretraining to generate contextualized embeddings, which are then fine-tuned for toxicity prediction [\[100\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0100).

More recently, the incorporation of structural information into toxicity models has opened new avenues for enhancing prediction accuracy. Tools such as ToxGIN integrate both sequence and structural data using Graph Isomorphism Networks (GINs), enabling the model to capture complex topological and physicochemical interactions at the molecular level [\[101\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0101). This sequence-structure fusion represents a promising direction for developing more biologically informed and explainable toxicity predictors.

 

#### 7.6.3.2 Immunogenicity Identification

The prediction of peptide immunogenicity – an essential step in therapeutic peptide design – has advanced considerably with the integration of ML and deep learning techniques. POPI was the first computational model developed specifically to predict immunogenic peptides. It utilized SVMs trained on physicochemical properties of amino acids to distinguish peptides capable of eliciting immune responses from those that do not [\[102\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0102). Building on this foundation, PAAQD introduced a more refined feature space by incorporating amino acid pairwise contact parameters and quantum topological molecular similarity descriptors, allowing the model to better capture structural and spatial characteristics relevant to immunogenicity [\[103\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0103).

Subsequent models have embraced ensemble learning and advanced neural network architectures to enhance prediction performance. INeo-Epp, for example, employed Random Forest classifiers and demonstrated improved accuracy in predicting T-cell epitope immunogenicity, benefiting from both feature diversity and ensemble robustness [\[104\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0104). Meanwhile, deep learning approaches such as DeepHLApan integrated RNNs to model peptide–MHC binding affinities and immunogenic potential, effectively capturing sequential dependencies in the amino acid chains [\[105\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0105).

Other models, like DeepImmuno, utilized CNNs to learn local residue patterns associated with immunogenicity, offering a powerful approach for epitope identification and neoantigen prediction [\[106\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0106). More recently, the incorporation of transfer learning strategies has further advanced the field. For example, TLImmuno2 combines pretrained embeddings from protein language models with downstream classifiers to improve learning efficiency and predictive performance, particularly in data-scarce scenarios [\[107\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0107).

 

#### 7.6.3.3 Hemolysis Evaluation

The prediction of hemolytic activity – a critical safety concern in peptide therapeutics – has been the focus of several computational models aimed at identifying peptides with potential hemotoxic effects. Early tools such as HemoPI, HemoPred, and HemoNet laid the groundwork for *in silico* hemotoxicity assessment. These models primarily relied on sequence-derived features, physicochemical descriptors, and structural properties to classify peptides based on their likelihood of causing red blood cell lysis \[[108](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0108)–[110](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0110)\]. Such tools have been instrumental in filtering out hemolytic peptides during the early stages of drug discovery, improving safety profiles prior to experimental validation.

Building upon these foundations, more recent approaches have introduced advanced learning paradigms to further improve prediction accuracy and model interpretability. Quantum ML (QML) has emerged as a novel strategy for identifying nonhemolytic peptides, leveraging the principles of quantum computing to capture complex sequence relationships that traditional models may overlook [\[111\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0111). Additionally, transfer learning has been employed to enhance hemotoxicity prediction in the context of AMPs. For example, models like AMPDeep use pretrained representations and domain-specific fine-tuning to more accurately distinguish between hemolytic and nonhemolytic variants, even when training data is limited [\[112\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0112).

A particularly promising advancement involves the combination of QML with protein language models, enabling simultaneous prediction of binary hemolytic activity and continuous toxicity metrics such as *HC*[*50*] concentration, a quantitative measure of hemolytic potency. These integrative approaches not only improve the granularity of toxicity assessments but also support the rational design of safer therapeutic peptides by providing both classification and regression outputs for hemolytic risk evaluation [\[113\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0113).

 

#### 7.6.3.4 Other Toxic Adverse Effect Predictions

In addition to models developed for general toxicity, immunogenicity, and hemolytic activity, specialized predictive frameworks have been created to address other biologically relevant adverse effects associated with therapeutic peptides. These include neurotoxicity, allergenicity, and autoimmune responses, each of which presents unique challenges in peptide-based drug development.

Deep learning techniques have recently been applied to predict neurotoxin-related adverse effects, particularly in the context of peptide toxins such as conotoxins. These neurotoxic peptides, often derived from marine organisms, can interfere with neuronal signaling and ion channel function. Emerging models trained on conotoxin datasets use deep neural architectures to classify neurotoxic peptides and evaluate their potential neurological risks, supporting safer design of peptide therapeutics targeting the nervous system [\[114\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0114).

Allergenicity prediction has also received considerable attention, especially due to its relevance in peptide-based vaccines, food-derived peptides, and biologics. Tools like AllerTOP v.2 and AllerCatPro 2.0 apply ML to analyze amino acid sequences and physicochemical features, enabling the identification of peptides with high allergenic potential \[[115](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0115), [116](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0116)\]. These models have been validated using curated allergen databases and offer user-friendly platforms for allergen screening during peptide design.

Furthermore, the prediction of autoimmune responses to specific peptide epitopes – such as those associated with gluten intolerance – has led to the development of more specialized models. In the context of celiac disease, tools like CDpred and CICERON predict T-cell epitopes that trigger immune responses in genetically predisposed individuals. These models analyze sequence motifs associated with HLA-DQ2/DQ8 binding and immune activation, facilitating the identification and exclusion of immunopathogenic peptides in therapeutic or nutritional applications \[[117](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0117), [118](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0118)\].

 

### 7.6.4 Data-Driven Strategies for Modeling Pharmacological Profiles

The computational prediction of peptide properties – such as half-life, stability, and pharmacological activityhas become increasingly important due to its direct impact on therapeutic efficacy and safety profiles [\[49\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0049). Accurate *in silico* models allow researchers to assess and optimize peptide candidates before experimental validation, saving both time and resources in the drug development pipeline.

A variety of computational approaches have been developed to estimate peptide half-life, each leveraging different types of input data and modeling strategies. ProtParam, for example, predicts peptide half-life based on the N-terminal rule, which relates the stability of a peptide to its N-terminal amino acid residue [\[119\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0119). Other models utilize multivariable regression frameworks to incorporate additional sequence features and biochemical properties into half-life prediction algorithms [\[120\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0120).

Some tools are designed for specific peptide classes. PyAMPA, for instance, focuses on predicting half-life for AMPs using tailored descriptors and modeling strategies suited to their structural features [\[121\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0121). Other models account for specific physiological conditions; HLP, for example, uses SVMs to predict peptide half-life in a digestive-tract-like environment, reflecting the challenges of oral peptide delivery [\[122\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0122).

Advanced models like PepMSND integrate a wide array of features – including molecular descriptors, physicochemical properties, SMILES strings, and 3D structural data – to improve predictions of blood stability [\[123\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0123). Similarly, Plifepred combines SVMs, linear regression, and Gaussian process models, using molecular descriptors and binary residue profiles to predict half-life in both natural and chemically modified peptides [\[54\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0054). More comprehensive tools such as PepAnalyzer go beyond half-life estimation by predicting multiple peptide attributes, including *in vitro* stability, net charge, and isoelectric point, providing a versatile platform for early-stage peptide characterization [\[124\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0124).

In parallel with stability modeling, there has been substantial progress in the prediction of pharmacological properties, particularly regarding peptide potency and toxicity. AVP-IC50Pred estimates the *IC*[*50*] values of AVPs, achieving a correlation coefficient of up to 0.74 [\[125\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0125). Nath's meta-classifier employs a stacking-based ensemble approach to predict both *IC*[*50*] and *pIC*[*50*] values with improved accuracy [\[126\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0126). For AVPs targeting the Flaviviridae family, a proteochemometric modeling (PCM) approach achieved a correlation coefficient of 0.85 in *pIC*[*50*] prediction, highlighting the utility of integrating chemical and biological descriptors [\[127\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0127).

In the antimicrobial domain, CNNs have been used for simultaneous classification and regression to estimate the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC), offering insight into both potency and spectrum of activity [\[128\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0128). Finally, tools like xDeep-AcPEP incorporate structural and compositional features to predict a wide range of pharmacological endpoints – including *EC*[*50*], *LC*[*50*], *IC*[*50*], and *LD*[*50*] – for ACPs, supporting both efficacy and toxicity assessment in a single framework [\[129\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0129).

 

### 7.6.5 *De novo* Design of Therapeutic Peptides

Generative models are a class of ML algorithms that learn to model the underlying distribution of data to generate new, previously unseen samples with similar characteristics. In the context of therapeutic peptides, generative models can propose novel sequences with optimized bioactivity, reduced toxicity, enhanced stability, or target specificity – thus accelerating rational peptide design [\[5\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0005).

Several types of generative architectures have been adapted for peptide discovery, including VAEs, GANs, transformer-based language models, and, more recently, diffusion models. Each strategy offers unique advantages in capturing peptide sequence representations and guiding the generation process based on biological, chemical, or structural constraints.

These models differ not only in architecture but also in the type of control they offer over the design process. For instance, VAEs are well-suited for navigating continuous latent spaces and enabling conditional generation, GANs excel at producing highly realistic sequences through adversarial learning, transformers provide context-aware generation informed by global sequence dependencies, and diffusion models offer a powerful framework for generating peptides while incorporating multimodal biological constraints.

In the following section, we focus specifically on the application of ML strategies for *de novo* design of therapeutic peptides, detailing the algorithms, architectures, and design principles that underpin these next-generation generative frameworks.

 

#### 7.6.5.1 Variational Autoencoder-Based Approaches

VAEs are probabilistic generative models that encode input data into a latent space and then decode it to reconstruct or generate new samples. They are particularly effective at learning smooth, continuous representations of peptide sequences, which can be manipulated to generate novel variants with desired properties.

Different VAE-based strategies have been developed for peptide discovery. For AMPs, models such as PepVAE [\[130\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0130), PepCVAE [\[131\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0131), and GM-Pep [\[132\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0132) have shown strong potential in generating active peptide sequences. [\[133\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0133) proposed a deep autoencoder model for AMP design, which achieved a 10% hit rate within 48 days of generation and experimental validation.

A notable development in this area is HydrAMP, a conditional VAE (cVAE) that learns a continuous latent representation of peptide space, enabling guided and controllable generation of sequences. This approach led to the creation of Hydraganan-1, a novel and highly active AMP derived from the parent peptide Pexiganan, with confirmed efficacy against *E. coli* strains [\[134\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0134).

Beyond AMPs, VAE-based models have been used to generate target-specific inhibitors [\[135\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0135), peptides with membrane permeability and bioactivity optimization [\[136\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0136), inhibitors of β-catenin [\[137\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0137), and peptides with high-affinity MHC binding potential [\[138\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0138).

 

#### 7.6.5.2 Generative Adversarial Networks

GANs represent another widely used generative architecture. They consist of two neural networks – a generator and a discriminator – trained in competition. GANs are particularly useful in generating biologically plausible sequences due to their ability to model complex, high-dimensional distributions.

One of the most well-known peptide design tools based on GANs is GANDALF (Generative Adversarial Network Drug-tArget Ligand Fructifier), a deep convolutional GAN that incorporates drug-target interaction data, 3D protein structures from PDB, and protein pocket information from CASTp. Instead of relying on protein–protein interaction datasets, GANDALF is trained on FDA-approved peptides from the THP database and has been used to generate peptides targeting cancer-related proteins such as PD-1, PDL-1, and CTLA-4 \[[50](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0050), [139](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0139)–[141](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0141)\].

Another GAN-based approach, PandoraGAN, focuses on generating bioactive AVPs. It uses LeakGAN, a modified GAN architecture originally developed for text generation, to produce sequences that are then validated using physicochemical filters like net charge, instability index, and motif patterns [\[142\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0142).

Other notable GAN implementations include AMPGAN v2 [\[143\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0143), which supports controlled generation of AMP sequences, AI4AVP for AVP design [\[74\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0074), and HelixGAN, which focuses on generating peptides with helical conformations often associated with membrane activity [\[144\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0144).

 

#### 7.6.5.3 Transformer-Based Language Models

Inspired by advances in natural language processing (NLP), transformer-based language models have also been applied to peptide generation. These models treat peptides as sequences of tokens (amino acids) and learn contextual representations that preserve structural and functional motifs.

AMPTrans-LSTM is a hybrid language model that combines a long short-term memory sampler with a transformer-based converter to generate AMPs. This dual architecture enables the preservation of essential AMP features while enhancing generative creativity. The model reports success rates ranging from 30% to 50% for generating active peptides [\[145\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0145).

 

#### 7.6.5.4 Diffusion Models

Diffusion models have emerged as a powerful alternative to traditional generative architectures, especially in molecular and structural biology. These models work by iteratively denoising random noise to generate samples that resemble the training data distribution.

In peptide design, diffusion-based methods such as AMP-Diffusion combine latent diffusion models with protein language embeddings, allowing for high-quality generation of AMPs with tunable properties [\[146\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0146). Watson et al. [\[147\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0147) demonstrated that the combination of structure prediction networks and diffusion generative frameworks can facilitate the rational design of therapeutic peptides with broad-spectrum antiviral activity.

Other innovative methods include Geometric Latent Diffusion, which incorporates 3D geometric constraints into the generation process [\[148\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0148), and multimodal contrastive diffusion models, which align peptide generation with both structural and functional modalities for improved biological relevance [\[149\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0149).

 

## 7.7 Next-Generation Peptide Design Through Multi-Agent Systems

In recent years, peptide and protein designs have undergone a significant transformation, driven by data-driven methods and ML, which have emerged as fundamental tools in the discovery of novel proteins with specific properties [\[150\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0150). These strategies have greatly improved our ability to predict protein structure, properties, and functions directly from amino acid sequences. A landmark achievement in this area is AlphaFold, a DL model that revolutionized protein structure prediction and set a new standard in the field [\[151\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0151).

Despite these advances, several challenges and open questions remain – particularly regarding how to develop intelligent systems capable of addressing complex tasks by integrating diverse sources of knowledge and methodologies. One promising solution lies in the implementation of multi-agent systems powered by large language models (LLMs) [\[152\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0152). LLMs have been pivotal in enabling conversational AI agents and have facilitated a shift from human–AI interaction to AI–AI and AI–tool collaboration, allowing greater autonomy in task execution [\[153\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0153).

At present, there is no single, universally accepted definition of an agent. However, some authors describe an agent as a system capable of perceiving its environment, making decisions, and acting in response to external stimuli [\[154\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0154). Others define it as an autonomous system that continuously receives environmental input and performs actions to accomplish a specific task [\[155\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0155).

Autonomous agent models are an emerging topic in scientific research and have found applications across multiple domains [\[155\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0155). Initially, their development focused on automating tasks such as literature reading and article analysis. Examples include PaperQA, an agent that retrieves articles from databases, analyzes their content, and answers queries about them [\[156\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0156); and WikiCrow, an extension of PaperQA that additionally generates summaries of scientific publications [\[157\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0157).

In parallel, new agents have been developed to assist researchers in experimental design and data analysis within laboratory environments. These include Context-Aware Language Models for Science (CALMS) [\[158\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0158), BioPlanner [\[159\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0159), CRISPR-GPT [\[160\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0160), LLM-RDF [\[161\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0161), and Organa, which provides feedback to researchers and generates comprehensive reports based on experimental results [\[162\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0162).

From a chemical perspective, specialized models such as Chemist-X, ChemCrow, AtomAgents, and LIDDIA have been developed to serve as virtual assistants in various tasks, including organic synthesis, drug discovery, materials design, and reaction planning \[[163](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0163)–[166](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0166)\].

While the application of autonomous agents in peptide and protein design remains relatively underexplored, the development of ProtAgent represents a significant step forward. ProtAgent is a multi-agent system capable of handling a wide range of protein design tasks – from sequence retrieval and functional analysis to *de novo* protein generation. Its structured workflow is composed of multiple specialized agents: the Planner defines strategies tailored to each task; the Assistant executes those plans using various computational tools; the Critic monitors performance, provides feedback, and refines the outputs; and the Chat Manager coordinates communication and task synchronization across the system [\[153\]](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0153).

Looking ahead, the implementation of multi-agent systems such as ProtAgent has the potential to revolutionize protein design by minimizing the need for manual intervention and accelerating the discovery process. This approach could significantly facilitate the generation of peptides and proteins with customized properties for biomedical, biotechnological, and pharmaceutical applications.

 

## 7.8 Developing AI-Agent for Autonomous Therapeutic Peptide Design

The discovery of therapeutic peptides is a multifaceted challenge that requires the integration of biological, chemical, and computational knowledge. To streamline and accelerate this complex process, we propose a modular and adaptive agent-based methodology designed to manage the complete peptide design pipeline – from user-defined prompts to *in silico* validation and experimental refinement (see [Figure 7.3](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0003)). This system harnesses the power of transformer-based deep learning models for both sequence generation and predictive evaluation, while reinforcement learning serves as a mechanism to optimize the entire design process based on experimental feedback.

The workflow begins with a user inputting a structured or natural language prompt that defines the desired characteristics of the target peptide. For example, a prompt might specify antiviral activity against a protein target like GP41, a half-life range between three and five hours, and the absence of antimicrobial activity or known toxic effects such as immunogenicity or hemolysis. This prompt is processed by an interpretation agent, which translates it into a formalized set of computational objectives and constraints. This step ensures that all downstream processes – generation, evaluation, and validation – are driven by clear, quantifiable design goals.

Next, a generative agent invokes a transformer-based model pretrained on large-scale peptide or protein datasets to produce novel sequences. Depending on the available domain-specific data, this model may be fine-tuned or conditioned through the input prompt to increase specificity. The generated peptides are designed to exhibit high internal diversity, minimizing redundancy and increasing the likelihood of identifying functionally novel candidates.

The candidate peptides are then assessed by a suite of predictive agents, which oversee two key types of models: classifiers and regressors. The classification agents evaluate discrete properties such as antiviral, antimicrobial, and antifungal activities, as well as safety-related attributes like hemolysis, allergenicity, and immunogenicity. These models are primarily transformer-based, benefiting from transfer learning and fine-tuning on high-quality, curated datasets. In parallel, regression agents use deep learning models to predict quantitative pharmacokinetic parameters such as half-life, *IC*[*50*], and *pIC*[*50*]. Together, these predictive agents provide a comprehensive assessment of each peptide, with results synthesized into a ranked list based on overall fit to the initial design criteria.

Peptides that meet the evaluation thresholds are passed to a validation agent, which performs *in silico* analyses using a range of bioinformatic tools. This includes molecular docking to estimate binding affinities, structural modeling to assess conformational stability, and physicochemical profiling to evaluate solubility, charge, and other essential characteristics. The integration of these validations helps ensure that only biologically viable and computationally promising candidates are selected for experimental testing.

An agent-controlled generative model produces diverse peptide sequences, which are evaluated by classification models for activity (e.g. antiviral), safety (e.g. nonhemolytic, non-immunogenic), and specificity. Additional agents oversee regression models predicting pharmacokinetic properties such as half-life and binding affinity. Candidate sequences undergo in silico validation using bioinformatic tools. Figure 7.3 Agent-based framework for therapeutic peptide design and discovery. The system receives a user-defined prompt specifying desired biological and pharmacological properties. An agent-controlled generative model produces diverse peptide sequences, which are evaluated by classification models for activity (e.g. antiviral), safety (e.g. nonhemolytic, non-immunogenic), and specificity. Additional agents oversee regression models predicting pharmacokinetic properties such as half-life and binding affinity. Candidate sequences undergo *in silico* validation using bioinformatic tools. Throughout the process, agent coordination enables task distribution and information flow. A reinforcement learning mechanism integrates experimental feedback to iteratively improve the system's performance and guide future generations toward optimal candidates.

To continuously improve the quality of generated peptides, the system incorporates a reinforcement learning agent that implements a feedback loop. Experimentally tested peptides serve as the foundation for reward signals that are fed back into the generative and predictive models. Successful candidates reinforce generation and prediction strategies, while poor outcomes penalize ineffective patterns. Importantly, this adaptive learning process not only updates the generative model but also refines the classification and regression models, ensuring that the entire predictive framework evolves in response to empirical data and converges toward increasingly accurate and functional outputs.

The entire system operates through a modular, agent-based architecture, where each agent is responsible for a specific task – ranging from prompt interpretation, sequence generation, classification, regression, and structural validation to learning from experimental feedback. These agents interact within a shared environment using standardized communication protocols, enabling seamless data flow and coordinated decision-making.

One of the core strengths of this approach is its modularity. Individual components can be independently improved or replaced as new models, algorithms, or datasets become available, without disrupting the integrity of the pipeline. This flexibility allows the system to adapt to novel therapeutic targets, new evaluation metrics, or evolving biological constraints. The incorporation of reinforcement learning adds another layer of adaptability, allowing the platform to refine its performance over time based on real-world outcomes.

Despite its many strengths, the methodology is not without limitations. Running multiple transformer-based models and conducting large-scale simulations in parallel demands significant computational resources. Moreover, coordinating heterogeneous models – each potentially trained on different input features and objectives – requires careful integration to maintain consistency and interpretability. Additionally, the reinforcement learning component is dependent on high-quality experimental data, which can be costly and time-intensive to obtain. Finally, building and maintaining a multi-agent architecture introduces initial complexity, requiring robust orchestration logic and well-defined interfaces to ensure effective collaboration among agents.

 

## 7.9 Conclusion and Perspectives

The study and application of therapeutic peptides have rapidly evolved, supported by their biochemical versatility, high specificity, and broad therapeutic relevance. From their foundational roles in natural biological systems to their tailored synthesis for biomedical use, peptides have demonstrated exceptional utility in domains ranging from diagnostics and biosensing to antimicrobial and anticancer therapies. Nevertheless, their inherent limitations – such as low stability, enzymatic degradation, and delivery challenges – continue to pose significant hurdles for clinical translation. To address these limitations, recent research has turned toward computational approaches, including the use of artificial intelligence and ML, which offer promising avenues to rationally design, optimize, and predict peptide functionality with greater efficiency and precision.

The integration of ML techniques has marked a paradigm shift in peptide science. By leveraging curated datasets, numerical representations, and advanced learning algorithms, researchers can now build highly accurate classification and regression models that predict biological activity, toxicity profiles, and pharmacokinetic properties. Pretrained protein language models and deep learning architectures have proven particularly effective in capturing the subtle sequence–function relationships that govern peptide behavior. Furthermore, the use of generative learning has enabled the exploration of entirely new regions of peptide chemical space, allowing the *de novo* design of sequences with desirable and custom-tailored properties.

Looking toward the future, the implementation of intelligent agent-based systems is expected to further transform the field by enabling autonomous peptide discovery pipelines. These multi-agent systems, composed of specialized modules that oversee generation, classification, validation, and feedback integration, allow for flexible and scalable design workflows. By coordinating predictive and generative models through shared communication protocols and reinforcement learning, these platforms minimize the need for manual intervention while continuously learning from experimental feedback. Such frameworks are particularly suited for addressing the complexity of therapeutic peptide development, as they can rapidly respond to new design constraints and integrate heterogeneous sources of biological knowledge.

Therapeutic peptide research stands at the intersection of molecular biology, computational science, and artificial intelligence. The integration of ML-driven methodologies, supported by accessible databases and experimental feedback loops, is not only accelerating discovery but also expanding the functional and therapeutic landscape of peptides. As this chapter has outlined, the adoption of data-driven and autonomous systems holds great promise for next-generation peptide engineering. These approaches are likely to play a central role in the development of personalized and precision-based therapeutics, ultimately transforming how peptide-based drugs are discovered, optimized, and brought to the clinic.

Machine Learning Approaches for High-Throughput Microbial Identification/Culturing
