The eVOLVER platform is a scalable, HTP growth experiment DIY platform applicable for use in microbiology, molecular evolution, and systems biology. The system achieves controlled microbial cell growth conditions such that it's possible to observe subtle phenotypic differences. The eVOLVER platform has been applied to determine the adaptive niches in yeast as well as to detect temperature-sensitivity-altered strains, indicating applicability of the platform to optimizing processes [\[98\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0098). Miniature bioreactors (MBRs) are also turning out to be extremely significant in the bioprocessing acceleration through enabling HTP parallel cell cultivations. MBRs find applications in media development, strain optimization, and process optimization. With automated robotic systems and other miniature process modules, MBRs can offer highly integrated, HTP cell cultivation process development solutions [\[99\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0099).

 

### 8.5.3 Synthetic Biology and AI-Driven Strain Engineering

Synthetic biology and AI-guided strain engineering have revolutionized the field of metabolic engineering, enabling precise genetic modifications and optimized strain design. ML plays a key role in predicting gene knockouts for enhanced growth and productivity, and AI-based programs have significantly improved CRISPR/Cas9 target prediction.

ML algorithms have been instrumental in predicting gene knockouts that can enhance microbial growth and metabolite production. ML algorithms take complex genomic and metabolic data to search for potential targets for genetic engineering. With the utilization of large datasets and complex computational models, ML can predict the effect of gene deletions or alterations on cellular metabolism and growth rates. This approach has been particularly valuable for the optimization of microbial strains for industrial applications, e.g. biofuel production or high-value chemicals. AI-powered CRISPR/Cas9 target prediction has greatly improved the efficiency and accuracy of genome editing.

Computational methods like AcRanker, an ML-based method, have been developed to predict putative anti-CRISPR proteins from just protein sequence information [\[100\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0100). This has led to the discovery of new anti-CRISPRs, AcrIIA20 and AcrIIA21, which can inhibit various Cas9 proteins. These discoveries have important implications for the control of gene editing technologies and our understanding of CRISPR-Cas systems.

The CASPER (CRISPR Associated Software for Pathway Engineering and Research) tool demonstrates the ability of AI to do CRISPR target prediction. CASPER reports higher accuracy for prediction of on- and off-target activity compared to conventional methods, a 2.4% boost for on-target, and a stunning boost by 30.2% for off-target prediction [\[101\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0101). This tool also enables novel applications such as multitargeting analysis and multispecies population analysis, which are critical for advanced genome editing projects and consortium-based engineering. ML has been applied in numerous aspects of strain engineering in microbial synthetic biology. For instance, in the well-known microbial cell factory *Pichia pastoris*, CRISPR-based instruments for gene editing and transcriptional regulation have been set up [\[102\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0102). These tools include mechanisms for efficient gene knockout, repression, and activation. The CRISPR-ARE (Activation, Repression, and Editing) system demonstrated in *P. pastoris* allows for the simultaneous activation, repression, and editing of a gene, mirroring the versatility of CRISPR-based approaches in synthetic biology. Similarly, CRISPR/Cas9 systems have been extensively employed in *Saccharomyces cerevisiae* for various forms of genetic manipulation, including single-nucleotide resolution editing, multigene editing, transcriptional regulation, and genome-scale remodeling.

These advances have opened the door to accelerating microbial engineering, reducing labor and time requirements while maximizing our understanding of cellular genetics and physiology. The synergy between AI and synthetic biology has also led to the development of genome-scale engineering technology. Tools such as CRISPR-based control, synthetic small regulatory RNA (sRNA)-based knockdown, promoter design, and multiplex automated genome engineering (MAGE) are now very effective microbial genome-scale engineering tools. The technologies allow fine-level control of gene expression and genome editing, which makes it feasible for scientists to optimize microbial metabolism for application. Overall, the synergy of synthetic biology and AI-strain engineering opened new avenues in metabolic engineering.

 

## 8.6 Challenges and Limitations of Machine Learning in HTP Microbial Research

Several challenges and limitations still exist in its application to this area. Data quality and data standardization are among the significant challenges of HTP microbial research. The accuracy and reliability of ML models depend significantly on the quality of data input. Data collection procedures, storage, and processing strategies in microbiology can be extremely heterogeneous, adding inconsistencies and potential biases to datasets [\[103\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0103). This lack of standardization can result in models that fail to generalize across laboratories or experimental systems. Furthermore, the diversity and complexity of microbial systems also make it challenging to determine shared data collection protocols, again contributing to the issue of data quality.

Bias and interpretability of ML models are another challenge. ML algorithms, particularly DL models, are “black boxes” in which it is difficult for researchers to understand the reasons behind the predictions [\[104\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0104). Interpretability is an issue in microbiology because knowing the biological pathways involved in predictions is important. In addition, training dataset biases can lead to biased results, potentially reinforcing existing prejudices or overlooking important but underrepresented microbial species or phenomena [\[105\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0105). To mitigate these issues, researchers are exploring XAI techniques to enhance model interpretability and transparency, as evidenced in the meibomian gland dysfunction classification study.

Computational complexity and high processing cost are significant challenges to the widespread application of ML in HTP microbiological studies. Massive genomic and metagenomic data analysis requires large computational power, which may not be accessible to every research facility [\[104\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0104). The need for specialized hardware, such as high-performance computing clusters or GPU arrays, may limit accessibility and increase the cost of research. Moreover, the complexity of some ML algorithms, particularly in DL, demands significant expertise in both computer science and microbiology, leading to a shortage of skills that is not straightforward to rectify. The lack of comprehensive training datasets for some microbial species is a significant limitation to the implementation of ML on HTP microbial studies. While well-studied model organisms have abundant data, many microbial species are poorly represented in existing datasets. This lack of data can lead to poor or biased models when extrapolated to less-studied microorganisms. To overcome this shortcoming, scientists need to prioritize the generation and dissemination of data on a wider range of microbial species, as well as the development of transfer learning and domain adaptation methods that can lend knowledge from data-abundant species to make better predictions for data-scarce ones.

Ethical and regulatory concerns of AI-based microbiology are arising as ML applications in this area grow. Issues such as data confidentiality, consent to use data, and the potential for misuse of AI-derived insights within microbial research need to be carefully addressed [\[106\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0106). There also has to be a set of precise rules and regulations for applying ML in microbiology, particularly where there is a direct concern with human health, e.g. the prediction of antibiotic resistance or the detection of pathogens. Having ethical standards and regulatory procedures in place that balance innovation with proper use of AI in microbiology is crucial to the long-term health and public trust of the profession. To address these problems, there are several conceivable solutions and topics for future study that can be entertained. Data quality and standardization must be addressed, prioritizing the development and implementation of standardized protocols of data acquisition, processing, and storage in microbial research [\[107\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0107).

 

## 8.7 Future Perspectives and Emerging Trends

The integration of ML with multi-omics technologies is revolutionizing microbial studies and their applications in numerous fields. The use of multiple technologies is resulting in a more advanced and detailed understanding of complex biological processes. In multi-omics integration, ML software is evolving essential tools to interpret and analyze the vast amount of data generated by genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics studies. These approaches are particularly powerful in uncovering intricate interactions among different biological layers and identifying novel biomarkers and therapeutic targets. For instance, in the field of oncology, multi-omics technologies combined with ML enable a deeper understanding of the tumor microbiome and its role in carcinogenesis, metastasis, and treatment response. Similarly, in osteoarthritis research, multi-omics techniques are facilitating the identification of molecular signatures and cellular subpopulations, allowing for more precise diagnosis and personalized therapeutic strategies [\[108\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0108). Application of ML to combine multi-omics data is not without challenges. The complexity and volume of data from heterogeneous omics platforms require sophisticated computational tools and algorithms. However, developments in ML and DL algorithms are increasingly improving our ability to process and interpret such complex datasets. With the advancement of technologies, we can expect even more accurate predictions and insights into microbial behavior and interactions. For personalized medicine applications, the integration of multi-omics data with ML is opening new avenues for targeted therapeutic interventions. This approach allows for a more precise characterization of personalized health profiles and may lead to more effective treatments with fewer side effects [\[109\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0109). Pharmacometrics is also being revolutionized by these technologies, with ML techniques being integrated into model-informed drug development and discovery strategies [\[110\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0110). Stepping ahead toward the future, future applications of microbial ML include possible implementation using quantum computing. Not being specifically mentioned in the provided papers, quantum computing can possibly better handle complex computations that go into the analysis of multi-omics data at a large scale using normal computers. This could lead to faster speed and accuracy in the predictions that are made in microbial research. Federated learning and decentralized AI approaches, though not directly referred to in the context presented, could be of utmost significance in microbiome studies. These approaches could facilitate collaborative research with data privacy, a critical factor in personalized medicine and clinical research. Practical applications of ML and multi-omics integration are already observed in numerous fields. In microbiology and environmental microbiology, these approaches are expanding our understanding of microbial community function and function in biogeochemical cycles [\[111\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0111). In agriculture and horticulture, the integration of multi-omics information and AI is transforming plant phenotyping toward precision horticulture, predictive breeding, and improved crop management [\[112\]](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0112). The role of XAI in microbial science, while not directly discussed in the papers presented, will become even more prominent. As ML models become more sophisticated, it will be crucial to provide transparency and interpretability of results to build confidence in AI-driven microbial science and its applications. The future of AI in microbial sciences, in general, looks bright and revolutionary. Leveraging ML with multi-omics approaches is going to speed up progress in personalized medicine, drug discovery, and environmental microbiology. As progress is made with technologies and computational power, we are likely to see better predictions, deeper insight into microbial systems, and new uses across multiple disciplines.

 

## 8.8 Conclusion

The intersection of ML with HTP microbial techniques is a paradigm shift in microbiological diagnostics and research. As traditional culture-based and molecular methods are being depleted, ML offers quick, scalable, and extremely accurate solutions for microbial identification, AMR prediction, and cultivation optimization. Given access to different data sources from metagenomic sequences and MS spectra to imaging and FCM profiles, ML models can recognize hidden patterns and make predictions with unparalleled accuracy.

This chapter illustrates how supervised, unsupervised, and RL techniques are being successfully applied across various fields of microbial science, including strain classification, growth prediction, and synthetic biology. The combination of ML with cutting-edge platforms such as MALDI-TOF MS, microfluidics, LOC devices, and CRISPR-based genome editing accelerates innovation in diagnostics, drug discovery, and personalized medicine. There are still challenges in data standardization, model interpretability, computational requirements, and regulatory approval. Resolving these issues will be crucial to making ML-based microbiology reproducible and trustworthy. Future breakthroughs, such as XAI, federated learning, and quantum computing, have the potential to continue revolutionizing the field, enabling the performance of robust, ethical, and globally collaborative microbial science. As ML expands, its role in shaping the next generation of microbiological tools will be critical to propelling progress in science and medicine.

# 9  
Generative AI for Knowledge Mining of Synthetic Biology and Bioprocess Engineering Literature

*Zhengyang Xiao and Yinjie J. Tang*

*Washington University in St. Louis, Department of Energy, Environmental, and Chemical Engineering, St. Louis 63130, MO, USA*

 

## 9.1 Introduction

Synthetic biology (SynBio) and bioprocess engineering are historically constrained by the stochastic nature of biological systems \[[1](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0001), [2](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0002)\] and the sheer volume of multidisciplinary data \[[3](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0003), [4](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0004)\]. Over the past decade, synthetic biology has moved from a proof-of-concept field to industrial applications, producing natural products \[[5](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0005), [6](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0006)\], RNA vaccine [\[7\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0007), antibody drugs [\[8\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0008), etc. Yet, designing efficient microbial strains and optimizing bioreactor conditions remain iterative and labor-intensive processes. Researchers rely on fragmented datasets – scattered across lab notebooks, proprietary databases, and journal publications – often requiring manual curation to form actionable insights. Prior chapters often highlight the importance of curated data, but it is crucial to understand the challenges and methods involved in this curation process, which is a key focus of this chapter. GenAI and LLMs revolutionize this field by understanding relevant knowledge to perform human-like planning and tasks. LLMs have been evolving from earlier instruction-tuned model GPT-4 [\[9\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0009), Llama [\[10\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0010), and Qwen [\[11\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0011), to recent chain-of-thought reasoning models like OpenAI o1 and DeepSeek-R1 [\[12\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0012). LLMs support applications like SynBio Q&A chatbot \[[13](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0013), [14](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0014)\], DNA sequence model [\[15\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0015), and autonomous protein engineering [\[16\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0016). LLMs also show potential to integrate multimodal data (e.g. genetics, pathways, and bioreactor operations) into actionable insights [\[17\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0017).

Bioprocess development must integrate legacy biotechnologies with modern SynBio advancements – such as genetic circuits, heterologous pathways, and CRISPR-enabled strain engineering – to optimize cell performance. These multifaceted challenges highlight the need for GenAI tools to drive the next generation of biomanufacturing. The chapter begins by examining knowledge mining tools like NEKO and GraphRAG, which convert fragmented and heterogeneous literature into knowledge graphs. These tools enable researchers to pose SynBio-related questions and receive answers and SynBio information supported by cited, up-to-date evidence. Next, a protocol for using LLMs to automate the extraction of structured bioprocess data, such as strain engineering parameters and reactor conditions, from scientific publications is introduced. This approach accelerates dataset construction for ML applications, providing valuable insights to guide future SynBio experiments and bioprocess development ([Figure 9.1](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0001)).

![Figure 9.1 Integrating experiment data and AI-driven knowledge mining to form a multilevel bioprocess machine learning (ML) database.](images/c09f001.png)

Figure 9.1 Integrating experiment data and AI-driven knowledge mining to form a multilevel bioprocess machine learning (ML) database.

 

## 9.2 Text Mining Using Knowledge Graph Tools

LLMs excel at answering general scientific questions but are limited by their pretraining cut-off dates and cannot provide citations without RAG. Additionally, current LLMs face scaling law limitations, where exponential increases in computational resources and model parameters yield only marginal, linear improvements in performance. This reflects an inherent conflict between the vastness of available information and the finite capacity of LLM parameters. To address these challenges, protocols for augmenting LLMs with knowledge graphs are proposed, enabling more effective knowledge extraction from extensive text sources. This approach is implemented by using Ollama, an all-in-one local LLM deployment package, to run Qwen2.5-instruct-14B (Alibaba Cloud, China). Hardware constraints influence deployment choices: a 14-billion-parameter model requires approximately 12 GB of GPU/CPU memory, making cloud APIs a more viable option for users with limited computational resources. To run LLM package locally, the user could begin by installing Ollama and Python 3.11. All codes used in this chapter are available on Github [https://github.com/xiao-zhengyang/Advanced-Biotechnology-Series](https://github.com/xiao-zhengyang/Advanced-Biotechnology-Series). User gets better results with larger parameters LLM provided by cloud computing. An example code using the OpenAI API is also provided on GitHub.

 

### 9.2.1 NEKO: A Lightweight Knowledge Graph Tool

NEKO allows researchers to extract relationships between biological entities (genes, species, bioreactor parameters) from PubMed abstracts or full-text articles [\[18\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0018). This system addresses two challenges: the manual effort to correlate findings from hundreds of papers, and the inability of general-purpose LLMs to provide responses with citations. Here, this section demonstrates how NEKO generates interactive knowledge graphs that map causal interactions (e.g. enzyme-substrate relationships) based on user-defined keywords (e.g. “*Yarrowia lipolytica*”) ([Figure 9.2](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0002)). The implementation code is available on GitHub and users can run the workflow within one Jupyter notebook ([https://github.com/xiao-zhengyang/Advanced-Biotechnology-Series/tree/main/NEKO](https://github.com/xiao-zhengyang/Advanced-Biotechnology-Series/tree/main/NEKO)).

![Figure 9.2 A schematic overview of the NEKO workflow for searching a publication database, identifying causal relationships, and visualizing and summarizing findings in a knowledge graph.](images/c09f002.png)

Figure 9.2 A schematic overview of the NEKO workflow for searching a publication database, identifying causal relationships, and visualizing and summarizing findings in a knowledge graph.

*   **Step 1: Literature Search and Text Collection** NEKO initiates the process by retrieving relevant texts through PubMed's API. Users specify a keyword, such as “*Yarrowia lipolytica carotene production*”. The `search_pubmed` function retrieves articles matching the search. The `fetch_details` function extracts article titles, journal names, and abstracts, compiling them into a structured Excel file. As in our example, the workflow fetches 500 abstracts, though this can be adjusted using the `retmax` parameter (up to ∼9,000 abstracts per search). This step ensures that the input text incorporates the most recent publications, overcoming the pretraining cut-off limitations of LLMs.
*   **Step 2: Entity and Relationship Extraction with LLM** Abstracts are analyzed by the locally deployed LLM: Qwen2.5-14B via `Ollama` – to identify biological entities and their relationships. The LLM has a prompt tailored to SynBio tasks, instructing it to output entity pairs in a strict (Entity A, Entity B) format. Here, this section demonstrates an example of extracting entities from *Yarrowia* β-carotene production studies.
*   **Step 3: Combine Entities with Similar Meanings** Biological terminology varies across studies. Phrases like “C:N ratio” and “carbon-to-nitrogen ratio” refer to the same parameter. NEKO mitigates this ambiguity using an embedding to combine semantically similar terms. Entity pairs are converted into vector representations, and near-identical terms (cosine similarity >0.8) are mapped to a standardized vocabulary. For instance, “C/N ratio” and “C:N ratio” are unified under the latter term to ensure consistency. The cleaned datasets are saved for graph construction.
*   **Step 4: Knowledge Graph, RAG, and Summarization Report** This step assembles entities and relationships into a knowledge graph using `Pyvis`. Nodes represent unique biological entities (e.g. genes, bioreactor parameters), while edges denote the sources (the titles of journal articles). Each relationship is traceable to its source article in the Excel file dataset. Users can query the graph to identify connections between specific nodes, for example, what are the entities related to β-carotene-producing *Yarrowia lipolytica*, and generate summaries via RAG and LLM interpretation of linked relationships ([Figure 9.3](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0003)a). Under best practices with a more capable 72B LLM, NEKO workflow can produce a summary report more specific and reliable than GPT-4 zero-shot question and answer ([Figure 9.3](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0003)b).

![Figure 9.3 (a) A sample knowledge graph from NEKO workflow. The nodes are biological entities and the edges are labeled as citations. (b) Compared with GPT-4 zero-shot Q&A, NEKO can find β-carotene-specific titer, production genes, strain engineering methods, and cultivation conditions in the knowledge graph \[18\] / Elsevier / CC BY 4.0.](images/c09f003.png)

Figure 9.3 (a) A sample knowledge graph from NEKO workflow. The nodes are biological entities and the edges are labeled as citations. (b) Compared with GPT-4 zero-shot Q&A, NEKO can find β-carotene-specific titer, production genes, strain engineering methods, and cultivation conditions in the knowledge graph [\[18\]](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0018) / Elsevier / CC BY 4.0.

 

### 9.2.2 GraphRAG

GraphRAG is an advanced but computationally expensive framework to enhance LLMs in generating domain-specific outputs. In contrast to NEKO, GraphRAG integrates three distinct query modes – global, local, and DRIFT search – enabling comprehensive questioning-answering capabilities through natural language input. This section demonstrates steps for using LLM and GraphRAG to study β-carotene production in *Yarrowia lipolytica* ([Figure 9.4](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0004)). Codes are in GitHub repository [https://github.com/xiao-zhengyang/Advanced-Biotechnology-Series/tree/main/GraphRAG](https://github.com/xiao-zhengyang/Advanced-Biotechnology-Series/tree/main/GraphRAG).

*   **Step 1: Configure Ollama LLM** Ollama's default LLM context length (e.g. 2 k tokens) truncates long texts. To avoid this, a customized LLM with longer context is needed. Create an 8 k context length `qwen2.5:14b` LLM by running this in the terminal.
    
    `ollama show qwen2.5:14b --modelfile > settings.txt`
    
    ![Figure 9.4 A sample knowledge graph from GraphRAG.](images/c09f004.png)
    
    Figure 9.4 A sample knowledge graph from GraphRAG.
    
    This command generates a `settings.txt` file in the terminal's current directory. Modify the model's `settings.txt` file by adding one line specifying the context length.
    
    `PARAMETER num_ctx 8196`
    
    Then run this command below to create a custom `qwen2.5:14b_8k model`.
    
    `ollama create qwen2.5:14b_8k -f settings.txt`
    
*   **Step 2: Initialize GraphRAG and Prompt Tuning** The GraphRAG version used in this section was 1.2.0. The user can install it by pip.
    
    `pip install graphrag==1.2.0`
    
    The user can initialize a new GraphRAG project by typing the following in the terminal:
    
    `graphrag init --root. /[Yarrowia_local]`
    
    For illustration purposes, a preconfigured GraphRAG project, including preloaded input text, is available in the GitHub repository for user convenience. For systems without GPU, increase the `request_timeout` value to `≥10 000` seconds in the `settings.yaml` to prevent interruptions. Prompt engineering is important, as entity-relationship extraction relies on domain-specific instructions. The user should use the autotune command to generate context-aware prompts with examples.
    
    `python -m graphrag prompt-tune --root. /[Yarrowia_local] --config. / [Yarrowia_local]/settings_prompt_tune.yaml`
    
    Note that large-parameter LLMs (>70B) should be used for prompt generation to minimize manual corrections, as smaller LLMs may yield suboptimal prompts. In this example, GPT-4o is used for prompt tuning. The user should substitute their own OpenAI API key in the `settings_prompt_tune.yaml` file. After automatic prompt tuning, move the generated prompts to the project's prompt folder.
    
*   **Step 3: Indexing the Input Text** Execute GraphRAG indexing command to initiate structured knowledge graph generation from input text. `Graphrag index --root. /[Yarrowia_local]`
    
    Processing times vary with the user's hardware. CPU-based systems typically require more than 10 hours, while utilizing GPU acceleration reduces processing time to under 30 minutes.
    
*   **Step 4: Querying and Visualization** GraphRAG's three query modes enable targeted interrogation of the knowledge graph by using LLM and RAG. Global search provides high-level summaries of broad topics. Local search retrieves details. The generated knowledge graph is saved in the output folder and can be exported to visualization tools like Gephi or Cytoscape, allowing users to interactively explore its connections.

 

## 9.3 LLM-Automated Data Extraction for Machine Learning

The efficacy of ML highly depends on a large, structured database. Traditional data collection in synthetic biology relied on the manual extraction of experimental results from journal articles. This process is time-consuming, error-prone, and prone to inconsistencies due to subjective interpretations. Generative AI now offers automated extraction of data at scale. This paradigm shift not only accelerates dataset creation but also enhances reproducibility and unlocks data-driven insights. This section presents a scalable protocol for converting unstructured text into ML-ready datasets ([Figure 9.5](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0005)). An example code with both input text and output CSV is provided on GitHub [https://github.com/xiao-zhengyang/Advanced-Biotechnology-Series/tree/main/Extract\_data\_by\_LLM](https://github.com/xiao-zhengyang/Advanced-Biotechnology-Series/tree/main/Extract_data_by_LLM).

![Figure 9.5 Scientific articles are converted into structured features by LLM, and then used in ML to predict production metrics under complex conditions.](images/c09f005.png)

Figure 9.5 Scientific articles are converted into structured features by LLM, and then used in ML to predict production metrics under complex conditions.

*   **Step 1: Gathering Text and Preprocessing** Peer-reviewed articles are downloaded as PDFs and converted to individual.txt files. One python code reads files and handles encoding errors common in parsed PDFs, for example, special characters or line breaks. Invalid files are flagged to prevent downstream problems.
*   **Step 2: Structured Data Extraction via LLM** The processed text files are processed by LLM in bulk (using OpenAI API). The prompt example used is:
    
    > “*Extract a multicolumn spreadsheet from the given text | article doi | product | product concentration | Carbon source | Carbon source concentration | yield | media | time | mode of bioreactor operation | strain name | parent strain | knocked out genes | overexpressed native genes | heterologous genes| Promotor | genome integration Y/N | codon optimized | culture volume | culture vessel: Shake flask, Batch, fedbatch, chemostat, microplates | nitrogen condition: sufficient, limited |oxygen condition: sufficient, limited, anaerobic | pH | temperature | Direct evolution Y/N |When outputting the daughter strain, you need to include the expressed and knockout genes in the parent strain. Always provide full table if data is not provided, just leave as NA. Do not provide explanations and notes*.”
    
    This prompt minimizes hallucinations by restricting responses to tabular formats and explicitly requiring null values for missing data. Here, OpenAI o1-mini is used for a balance of performance and cost.
    
*   **Step 3: Automated CSV Generation and Human Validation** Extracted tables are split into rows using delimiters and saved as individual.csv files. A domain expert user could review outputs to verify accuracy.

 

## 9.4 Current Limitations

While GenAI and LLMs, empowered by knowledge graph and RAG, offer significant potential for SynBio applications, their integration into real-world workflows faces several challenges. *First*, infrastructure limitations persist. The performance and accuracy of LLMs are heavily dependent on their parameter size, and models larger than 70 billion parameters typically require cloud-based deployment. This raises data security concerns for proprietary research or sensitive data, which may deter academic and industrial adoption. Transmitting sensitive information to third-party cloud services introduces risks, even with encryption. Applications governed by strict regulations (e.g. healthcare) face compliance challenges, while models trained on sensitive datasets may inadvertently memorize and expose proprietary information. Securing local deployment of LLMs requires high-end GPUs, which remain cost-prohibitive for many laboratories. Until hardware companies prioritize local AI workflows, balancing performance and privacy will continue to be a challenge. *Second*, there are scalability limits to knowledge graphs. As the input text grows beyond approximately 5,000 articles, information retrieval and query efficiency decline. Additionally, LLMs struggle to reconcile conflicting information or non-mainstream viewpoints, which can propagate errors in reasoning. *Third*, LLM-driven data extraction is constrained by predefined features, creating a “feature bias” that limits the scope of ML explanations to only those predefined inputs. Overcoming these limitations will require collaboration across the SynBio and bioprocess engineering communities to establish standardized data reporting practices that enhance ML explainability.

 

## 9.5 Conclusion

The integration of generative AI into synthetic biology and bioprocess engineering represents a new direction toward data-driven biological design and manufacturing. Tools such as NEKO and GraphRAG exemplify how knowledge mining can combine fragmented scientific literature into actionable insights, bridging gaps between experimental data, strain engineering, and bioreactor optimization. Meanwhile, LLM-driven protocols for dataset generation address the longstanding bottleneck of manual data curation, enabling predictive ML studies, self-driving labs and digital twins. Ultimately, the synergy of generative AI with synthetic biology gives a future biomanufacturing foundation model.

## 10.1 Introduction

Metabolomics is a powerful analytical approach that comprehensively analyzes small-molecule metabolites within biological systems to elucidate cellular metabolic states. Recent advancements in analytical technologies and big data processing have enabled the utilization of large-scale metabolomics datasets. However, metabolomics encompasses a diverse range of techniques, and selecting the appropriate method tailored to the specific research objective is essential for obtaining reliable data. Compared to other omics approaches, such as transcriptomics and proteomics, metabolomics deals with physicochemically diverse compounds, and metabolites generally have a much faster turnover rate than DNA or proteins. Unlike the sequence-derived function of enzymes, peptides, and DNA parts as described in prior chapter, the metabolome is more responsive and dynamic. As a result, selecting – and sometimes even developing – appropriate sample preparation and analytical methods tailored to the target metabolites is crucial [\[1\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0001). [Section 10.2](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-0002) provides guidance on selecting suitable metabolome analytical techniques for specific research objectives.

Metabolomics has driven technological innovations across a wide range of fields, including medical science \[[2](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0002)–[7](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0007)\], environmental analysis [\[8\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0008), food evaluation [\[9\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0009), microbiome research [\[10\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0010), and synthetic biology \[[11](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0011), [12](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0012)\]. In particular, the field of synthetic biology has been rapidly advancing, allowing for the rational engineering of cells to enhance the production of target compounds. This progress has led to the development of sustainable biomanufacturing processes with reduced environmental impact. The analysis and applications of metabolomics data in synthetic biology will be discussed in [Section 10.3](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-0005). Furthermore, the use of artificial intelligence (AI)-driven metabolomics will be described in [Section 10.4](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-0009), followed by a discussion on future perspectives of metabolomics applications in [Section 10.5](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-0010). These methods of measuring metabolomes are critical for developing the models of flux analysis that are described in [Chapters 11](#c11.xhtml) and [12](#c12.xhtml).

 

## 10.2 Methods for Metabolomics

The utilization of metabolomics can be broadly categorized into two main approaches: obtaining quantitative information and obtaining qualitative information [\[13\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0013). The former involves cases where specific compounds have been predetermined for quantification, and their intracellular levels need to be measured. In such cases, standard reference compounds are analyzed in advance to confirm peak positions and establish calibration curves. The sample analysis results are then compared against these references to obtain quantitative values. This type of metabolomics analysis is referred to as targeted metabolomics. On the other hand, the latter approach is used for identifying nmetabolic differences between strains or extracting characteristic features from samples. In such cases, non-targeted analysis is employed. This method identifies compounds by mass spectrometry (MS) and database matching, eliminating the need for pre-prepared reference standards [\[14\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0014).

The sample preparation and analytical methods for metabolome analysis must be carefully selected based on the group of compounds being analyzed [\[15\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0015). For instance, metabolic intermediates in central metabolic pathways such as glycolysis and the tricarboxylic acid cycle (TCA) cycle exhibit rapid turnover, making them highly susceptible to artificial variations caused by environmental changes during cell sampling. Conversely, metabolites with relatively slow turnover, such as lipids, are less affected by such changes. Additionally, sample preparation methods vary depending on the analytical instrument used. For example, when measuring hydrophilic compounds via GC-MS, trimethylsilylation (TMS) derivatization is often required to convert target analytes into volatile compounds [\[16\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0016).

 

### 10.2.1 Preparation of Samples

Metabolomics samples are generally prepared through multiple steps ([Figure 10.1](#c10.xhtml#c10-fig-0001)). The first step is quenching, where the metabolic state of the cells is rapidly halted, followed by cell collection. Next, the cells are disrupted to extract metabolites. This may be followed by protein removal or concentration through drying. The cold methanol method is the most commonly used approach for quenching [\[1\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0001). In this method, cells are rapidly cooled by mixing cold methanol solution, effectively stopping metabolic reactions. The cells are then collected via low-temperature centrifugation. However, it is important to note that methanol can disrupt cell membranes, leading to leakage of intracellular metabolites before the extraction step. In *Chlamydomonas reinhardtii*, it has been reported that using 60% methanol containing 70 mM 2-(4-\[2-hydroxyethyl\]piperazin-1-yl)ethanesulfonic acid (HEPES) as the quenching solution, mixed with the sample at a 1 : 1 ratio at −40 °C, reduces metabolite leakage [\[17\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0017). For cyanobacteria, enzymatic activity can be sufficiently halted using 30% methanol at −24 °C [\[18\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0018). Furthermore, cold glycerol saline (GS) solution has been evaluated for intracellular metabolite recovery in various microbial models, including *Pseudomonas fluorescens*, *Streptomyces coelicolor*, and *Saccharomyces cerevisiae*. The results suggested that using GS solution led to significantly higher intracellular metabolite levels with less leakage compared to cold methanol-water solutions [\[19\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0019). For plants and photosynthetic microorganisms, changes in light conditions during sampling can significantly alter metabolite intermediate concentrations. In plants, an *in situ* sampling device has been used to instantaneously switch between labeled and unlabeled ^(13)CO[2] gas, enabling the measurement of metabolite labeling dynamics and the identification of rate-limiting steps in metabolic pathways [\[20\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0020). In cyanobacteria, a phenol extraction-based rapid quenching and sampling method has been employed to preserve the *in vivo* state while measuring the metabolic state, thereby elucidating the activation dynamics of CO[2] fixation metabolism [\[21\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0021).

![Figure 10.1 A schematic overview of a metabolomics workflow. The process begins with culturing cells, followed by quenching (e.g. cold methanol or cold glycerol) to halt metabolic activity. Harvesting is typically performed via centrifugation or quick filtration, and the extracted metabolites can be obtained using methods such as boiling ethanol or methanol–water–chloroform. Depending on the physicochemical properties of the compounds, gas chromatography (GC), liquid chromatography (LC), or capillary electrophoresis (CE) is used for separation. Finally, detection and quantification are conducted using various mass spectrometers (e.g. triple quadrupole, time-of-flight, Fourier transform ion cyclotron resonance).](images/c10f001.png)

Figure 10.1 A schematic overview of a metabolomics workflow. The process begins with culturing cells, followed by quenching (e.g. cold methanol or cold glycerol) to halt metabolic activity. Harvesting is typically performed via centrifugation or quick filtration, and the extracted metabolites can be obtained using methods such as boiling ethanol or methanol–water–chloroform. Depending on the physicochemical properties of the compounds, gas chromatography (GC), liquid chromatography (LC), or capillary electrophoresis (CE) is used for separation. Finally, detection and quantification are conducted using various mass spectrometers (e.g. triple quadrupole, time-of-flight, Fourier transform ion cyclotron resonance).

During the extraction step, intracellular metabolites are recovered via chemical lysis and/or mechanical disruption of cell walls. In microbial metabolomics, chemical lysis is the most commonly employed method. For extracting water-soluble compounds, approaches such as boiling ethanol and the buffered methanol-water-chloroform method are frequently used. However, variations in organic solvents, temperature, and pH are known to influence measurement results, and thus, employing multiple extraction methods is recommended [\[1\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0001). For *Escherichia coli*, acidic acetonitrile has been suggested as the most suitable solvent for metabolite extraction [\[22\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0022). For lipid extraction, traditional methods such as the Bligh and Dyer method and the Folch method, which use methanol and chloroform, have been widely used. However, alternative approaches utilizing green solvents such as ethanol and isopropanol, as well as supercritical CO[2] extraction, have been developed to reduce toxicity concerns [\[23\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0023).

 

### 10.2.2 Detection and Quantification

Chromatography combined with MS is widely used for metabolite analysis in metabolomics [\[24\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0024). Gas chromatography (GC) and liquid chromatography (LC) are selected based on the target compounds. GC is primarily used for volatile compounds and sugars, while LC enables the analysis of organic acids, amino acids, and fatty acids. In LC, C18 columns, which utilize hydrophobic interactions, are commonly used. However, these columns are not well-suited for separating hydrophilic compounds, particularly those containing phosphate groups, such as sugar phosphates and nucleotides. The use of hydrophilic interaction LC (HILC) columns or ion-pair reagents can facilitate the analysis of hydrophilic compounds \[[25](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0025), [26](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0026)\]. Additionally, a comprehensive analytical method called unified-hydrophilic-interaction/anion-exchange LC has been developed to simultaneously analyze a wide range of compounds with diverse physicochemical properties [\[27\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0027). Furthermore, capillary electrophoresis (CE) is particularly suited for separating ionic and highly polar compounds, such as phosphorylated metabolites, amino acids, and organic acids. The combination of CE with MS (CE-MS) serves as a complementary technique to GC-MS and LC-MS [\[28\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0028). Recent advancements in sheathless CE-MS and improvements in sample injection techniques have enhanced sensitivity and stability [\[29\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0029). These developments highlight the importance of selecting appropriate separation techniques based on the physicochemical properties of the target compounds.

The choice of MS detector connected to GC, LC, or CE also depends on the analytical objectives. Single-stage MS commonly employs quadrupole (Q) or time-of-flight (TOF-MS), where quantification is achieved by measuring molecular ion intensities. However, these methods provide limited structural information, making it challenging to distinguish between isomers or multiple molecular species. For improved structural elucidation, tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) techniques, such as triple quadrupole (QqQ), quadrupole-TOF (Q-TOF), and quadrupole-Fourier transform MS (Q-FTMS), are frequently used. Triple quadrupole MS (QqQ) is highly sensitive and well-suited for targeted quantification. In contrast, Q-TOF and Q-FTMS offer higher mass resolution and superior compound identification capabilities, making them ideal for non-targeted analysis. Thus, the selection of MS techniques should align with the objectives of the metabolomics study. Integrating multiple analytical techniques, including nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), enables more comprehensive metabolite profiling and enhances the depth of metabolomic analysis [\[30\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0030).

 

## 10.3 Analysis and Application of Metabolomics Data for Biotechnology

Microbial production of valuable compounds using *Escherichia coli*, *Saccharomyces cerevisiae*, cyanobacteria, and other microorganisms has gained attention due to its environmentally friendly nature, operating under ambient temperature and pressure while utilizing various carbon sources such as plant biomass and CO[2] [\[31\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0031). The target products range from food additives, pharmaceuticals, and pigments to commodity chemicals such as plastics and fuels. However, achieving high-yield and high-efficiency production requires microbial strain modification, screening, and optimization of cultivation conditions. These processes are typically carried out through the Design-Build-Test-Learn (DBTL) cycle, a workflow used in synthetic biology and metabolic engineering [\[11\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0011). In the design phase, genome-scale metabolic models and omics data are used to design metabolic pathways, promoters, and enzymes. During the build phase, synthetic biology techniques, including DNA synthesis, CRISPR-based genome editing, and robotics, are employed to construct the desired microbial strains. In the test phase, the engineered strains are evaluated in high-throughput, not only for production levels, but also for transcriptome, proteome, and metabolome profiles. Finally, in the learn phase, the acquired data are analyzed to guide the next cycle of strain design [\[12\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0012). The DBTL cycle is applied not only to strain engineering but also to microbiome engineering, where omics technologies, including metabolomics, play a crucial role in elucidating complex metabolic networks within microbiomes [\[32\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0032). The following section will provide a more detailed discussion on the role of metabolomics in strain engineering.

 

### 10.3.1 Metabolomics for Identification of Pathway Bottlenecks

In metabolic pathways converting glucose or other substrates into target compounds, enzymes with low conversion rates can limit overall productivity. Enhancing the expression or activity of such enzymes can lead to increased production yields. These bottleneck reactions often result in the accumulation of their substrate intermediates. Metabolomics enables the identification of such accumulated metabolites, providing a rational approach to metabolic engineering \[[12](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0012), [33](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0033), [34](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0034)\]. This strategy is universal across various microbial strains, including *Escherichia coli*, *Saccharomyces cerevisiae*, *Corynebacterium glutamicum*, cyanobacteria, and *Streptomyces*. It is also applicable to a wide range of production targets, such as organic acids, terpenoids, aromatic compounds, and lipids, with demonstrated effectiveness ([Table 10.1](#c10.xhtml#c10-tbl-0001)). For example, in an *E. coli* strain engineered for 1-propanol production, metabolomics analysis revealed the accumulation of 2-ketobutyrate, a key precursor ([Figure 10.2](#c10.xhtml#c10-fig-0002)). This suggested that the downstream enzymes, alpha-ketoisovalerate decarboxylase (KivD) or alcohol dehydrogenase (YqhD), constituted pathway bottlenecks. Enhancing YqhD activity led to a 1.38-fold increase in 1-propanol production [\[35\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0035). Acetyl-coenzyme A (acetyl-CoA) is a crucial precursor for various valuable compounds, but in cyanobacteria, its accumulation is typically low, limiting the productivity of acetyl-CoA-derived chemicals. In a xylose-utilizing *Synechococcus elongatus* UTEX2973 strain, metabolomics analysis showed high accumulation of sugar phosphates in the presence of xylose, indicating insufficient metabolic flux toward acetyl-CoA. To address this, a heterologous phosphoketolase (Pkt) was introduced to convert sugar phosphates into acetyl phosphate, a direct precursor of acetyl-CoA. Additionally, to enhance the supply of fructose-6-phosphate (F6P), a phosphofructokinase (Pfk) knockout was combined with fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase (Fbp) overexpression. These modifications successfully increased acetyl-CoA accumulation, and when a 3-hydroxypropionic acid (3-HP) biosynthetic pathway was introduced, 3-HP production was enhanced 4.1-fold compared to the original strain [\[36\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0036).

Metabolomics not only aids in the direct identification of pathway bottlenecks but also helps discover byproduct formation and key metabolic pathways that contribute to production improvement in mutant strains. For instance, in a *Corynebacterium glutamicum* strain engineered for 3-amino-4-hydroxybenzoic acid (3,4-AHBA) production, metabolomics revealed significant accumulation of lactate. To suppress lactate formation, lactate dehydrogenase gene (*ldh*) knockout was performed, leading to a 1.33-fold increase in 3,4-AHBA production [\[37\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0037). Similarly, in an *E. coli* strain engineered for succinic acid production, metabolomics identified excessive accumulation of mannitol, a byproduct. Deleting mannitol dehydrogenase gene (*mtlD*) successfully reduced mannitol synthesis and resulted in a 1.2-fold increase in succinic acid production [\[38\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0038). Metabolomics-guided engineering is also effective for the production of secondary metabolites. The metabolic pathway for the opioid precursor benzylisoquinoline alkaloids contains several potential bottlenecks. A phylogenetically distinct *Bombyx mori* 3,4-dihydroxyphenylacetaldehyde synthase (DHPAAS) was identified as a bypass enzyme, enabling the direct conversion of L-3,4-dihydroxyphenylalanine (L-DOPA) to 3,4-dihydroxyphenylacetaldehyde (DHPAA), effectively skipping an enzymatic step [\[39\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0039). In this study, metabolomics analysis revealed that depletion of S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) limited the methylation of downstream DHPAA-derived benzylisoquinline alkaloids to produce reticuline. To address this, a two-step cell production system was developed, separating SAM-dependent methylation reactions, which successfully increased the levels of downstream products, including reticuline. Additionally, in antifungal antibiotic amphotericin B (AmB) production by *Streptomyces nodosus*, a high-production mutant strain (ZJB2016050) was obtained through random mutagenesis using UV irradiation and addition of N-methyl-N-nitroso-N-nitroguanidine. To further improve productivity, metabolomics analysis was conducted on ZJB2016050 strain, revealing significant accumulation of tetrahydrofolic acid (THF) and other one-carbon metabolism-related metabolites compared to the wild-type strain. Based on this finding, folate metabolism was hypothesized as a key metabolic pathway in the mutant strain, and overexpression of methionine synthase gene (*metH*) led to a 1.26-fold increase in AmB production [\[40\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0040).

### 10.3.2 Absolute Metabolomics and Thermodynamic Analyses

The quantification accuracy of targeted metabolomics is not always precise due to factors such as compound degradation, oxidation during sample preparation, and ion suppression effects in MS [\[41\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0041). To address these issues, the stable isotope dilution internal standard method has been developed \[[42](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0042), [43](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0043)\]. This method involves adding a known concentration of stable isotope-labeled internal standards (^(13)C, ²H, ^(15)N-labeled compounds), which have the same chemical structure but a different mass from the target metabolites, into the sample. By comparing the signal intensity ratio of labeled (internal standard) and unlabeled (endogenous metabolite) compounds during measurement, this approach corrects for variability in ionization efficiency and metabolite loss during sample preparation, enabling more accurate absolute concentration calculations.

Furthermore, by precisely measuring intracellular metabolite concentrations, this method allows for a detailed evaluation of relative concentration ratios and energy balances within metabolic pathways. Specifically, analyzing the ATP/ADP/AMP ratio, which reflects cellular energy status, and tracking intermediate metabolite concentration changes in the TCA cycle can help identify thermodynamically constrained reactions \[[44](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0044), [45](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0045)\]. By integrating this approach with flux balance analysis (FBA) and thermodynamic flux analysis (TFA), it is possible to clearly define rate-limiting steps in metabolic pathways and optimize pathway designs for targeted compound synthesis. For example, Gibbs free energy can be calculated from measured absolute concentrations to identify reactions with high thermodynamic barriers. This information can then be incorporated into thermodynamically constrained models to predict optimal biosynthetic pathways, such as those for polyhydroxybutyrate (PHB) production [\[46\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0046).

 

### 10.3.3 Evaluation and Optimization of Metabolic Flux

Thus far, we have discussed methods for quantifying and evaluating metabolite pool sizes. However, analyzing metabolite concentrations alone is insufficient to assess intracellular metabolic fluxes. Metabolic flux analysis (MFA) is performed by measuring the incorporation of stable isotopes using MS. By comparing isotopic labeling patterns and positional atom data with flux distributions within a metabolic model, intracellular flux distributions can be estimated. MFA can be classified based on whether intracellular metabolite concentrations and isotopic labeling reach a steady state [\[47\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0047). For instance, when cells are supplied with \[1−^(13)C\] glucose, the isotopic distribution of intracellular metabolites at steady state can be used to determine flux distributions. However, for autotrophic organisms such as cyanobacteria and plants, where CO[2] is the sole carbon source, steady-state labeling with ^(13)CO[2] results in complete labeling of all metabolites, making this method ineffective. Instead, time-course measurements of ^(13)C incorporation are performed under conditions where metabolite concentrations are assumed to be constant. This approach enables flux distribution calculations in autotrophic systems [\[48\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0048). Furthermore, in non-steady-state conditions where metabolite concentrations fluctuate dynamically, metabolic flux changes can be estimated by detailed time-series analysis of all intracellular metabolite concentrations within the metabolic model [\[21\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0021). Additionally, flux variations over the entire cultivation period can be inferred from measurements of selected metabolite concentrations at different time points [\[49\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0049).

 

## 10.4 Artificial Intelligence (AI)-Based Metabolomics Data Processing and Analysis

AI has emerged as an indispensable tool to process and interpret metabolomics data \[[50](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0050), [51](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0051)\]. One major application is metabolite identification and annotation. Untargeted metabolomics via MS often produces many features (mass peaks) that must be assigned to actual metabolites, a process fraught with uncertainty and considered a major bottleneck in metabolomics data processing. Bayesian modeling can rigorously handle this uncertainty. For example, Integrated Probabilistic Annotation (IPA) is a Bayesian-based method developed to annotate metabolomic features by integrating various evidence sources [\[52\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0052). In IPA, information such as isotope patterns, adduct formations, chromatographic retention time, and known biochemical connections is used as input to a probabilistic model. The method computes the posterior probability that a given set of spectral features corresponds to a particular metabolite. IPA not only assigns metabolite identities automatically but also quantifies the confidence in each annotation. By starting with prior probabilities (e.g. likelihood of certain metabolites based on biochemical pathways) and updating these beliefs with observed data (*m/z* matches, isotope ratios, etc.), the algorithm refines metabolite identities in a principled way. This provides a confidence score for each putative metabolite identification, which is lacking in traditional deterministic matching methods. IPA demonstrated that incorporating multiple evidence streams can markedly reduce false annotations and improve consistency in metabolomic analyses. In practical terms, Bayesian annotation helps researchers focus on the most probable metabolite identifications and flag ambiguous cases for further validation, thereby streamlining one of the most challenging tasks in metabolomics. Furthermore, recent advancements in machine learning-based metabolomics data processing are exemplified by the development of MS-DIAL 5 [\[53\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0053). MS-DIAL 5 is an advanced multimodal MS data analysis environment that utilizes electron-activated dissociation (EAD)-based tandem MS for in-depth lipid structural elucidation. By incorporating machine learning algorithms to analyze spectral patterns and predict collision-cross section values, MS-DIAL 5 achieves a 96.4% accuracy in annotating lipid structures, including the assignment of *sn*\-, OH-, and C=C positions. This platform not only facilitates detailed structural characterization of lipids but also integrates MS imaging (MSI) data to map lipid localizations. Thus, MS-DIAL 5 provides a complementary strategy to Bayesian methods like IPA by enhancing the resolution and reliability of metabolite annotations, ultimately contributing to the effective management of uncertainty and the streamlining of metabolite identification in complex biological samples.

Another key application of AI in metabolomics and synthetic biology is optimizing metabolic pathways for improved production or efficiency. For example, data-driven models can perform MFA in a novel way: instead of relying solely on predefined kinetic equations, machine learning can learn the mapping from enzyme levels and metabolite concentrations to pathway fluxes. Costello and Martin demonstrated that combining ML with abundant time-series multiomics data (proteomics and metabolomics) enabled accurate prediction of metabolic pathway dynamics, outperforming a traditional kinetic model [\[54\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0054). Their ML model can integrate proteome and metabolite data to forecast how a pathway's flux changes over time or under perturbations without the need for manually deriving rate laws. AI has also been used to recommend genetic modifications for pathway optimization. By learning from prior engineering data, AI systems can suggest which genes to overexpress, knock out, or mutate to achieve a target output. A notable example is an Automated Recommendation Tool (ART) developed for multi-gene pathway engineering [\[55\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0055). This tool used an ensemble of probabilistic models and Bayesian optimization to iteratively design and evaluate strain modifications. In a case study on *S. cerevisiae* tryptophan production, ART evaluated over 250 engineered strains with different promoter and gene combinations [\[56\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0056). Another exciting use of AI is in discovering or engineering new pathway steps. Vavricka and coworkers sought to enhance production of benzylisoquinoline alkaloids (plant-derived compounds) in microbes. In this case, some bottleneck steps of the plant pathway are catalyzed by no known counterparts in microbes. Therefore, the team trained ML models (support vector machines, SVMs) trained with enzyme sequence data to predict “missing link” enzymes and were able to rank candidate genes from plants [\[57\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0057). The candidate genes were then expressed in a microbial host and metabolomic analysis was applied to verify if the pathway was completed. Metabolomics indicated that two predicted enzymes (an aromatic acetaldehyde synthase and a phenylpyruvate decarboxylase) were functional, leading to the production of key intermediates that had been absent before. By integrating the new enzymatic steps, the engineered pathway output (a specific alkaloid) could be increased significantly. This case illustrates how AI-driven insights (predicting an enzyme from sequence space) coupled with metabolomics verification can expand biosynthetic pathways beyond their natural limits – effectively pathway engineering by AI discovery. In summary, AI methodologies empower metabolic pathway optimization by predicting pathway behavior, guiding genetic interventions, and even inventing new pathway routes, all informed and validated by comprehensive metabolomic data.

 

## 10.5 Future Direction of Metabolomics and Its Analysis

Publicly available datasets from genomics, transcriptomics, and proteomics have facilitated large-scale meta-analyses, leading to new insights. However, metabolomics data are more challenging to compare and integrate across different laboratories and experimental batches due to variations in sample preparation protocols, differences in experimental handling, and quantification inconsistencies caused by ion suppression effects. To overcome these challenges, advancements in automation of sample processing, adoption of absolute quantification methods, and enhancement of database platforms are crucial. For instance, studies have demonstrated that automation of sample preprocessing significantly improves reproducibility, as indicated by relative standard deviation values that ensure sufficient consistency [\[58\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0058). Autonomous laboratory systems may be applicable to metabolomics-based strain engineering in the future [\[59\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0059). Additionally, high-quality ^(13)C-labeled internal standards for metabolomics are being developed to enhance quantitative accuracy [\[60\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0060). Further technological advancements and widespread adoption of these methods are expected to improve the overall quality of metabolomics data ([Figure 10.3](#c10.xhtml#c10-fig-0003)).

![Figure 10.3 A conceptual overview of future directions in metabolomics and its analysis. Automation of sample preparation, the use of 13C-labeled internal standards for improved quantification, and the expansion of public repositories are central to enhancing data quality and reproducibility. Integrating these advances with robust analytical and “learning” platforms will enable more comprehensive, cross-laboratory comparisons and large-scale meta-analyses.](images/c10f003.png)

Figure 10.3 A conceptual overview of future directions in metabolomics and its analysis. Automation of sample preparation, the use of ^(13)C-labeled internal standards for improved quantification, and the expansion of public repositories are central to enhancing data quality and reproducibility. Integrating these advances with robust analytical and “learning” platforms will enable more comprehensive, cross-laboratory comparisons and large-scale meta-analyses.

Moreover, recent innovations in MS-based fingerprinting offer promising future directions for metabolomics analysis. For example, a study on genome-scale prediction of gene ontology from MALDI-TOF mass fingerprints demonstrated that machine learning models, such as SVM and random forest algorithms, can rapidly and accurately predict gene functions from high-throughput mass spectral data [\[61\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0061). This approach, applied to a comprehensive yeast knockout library, not only enabled functional annotation of genes but also highlighted the potential for optimizing bioproduction chassis selection. By integrating rapid mass spectrometric fingerprinting with machine learning algorithms, such predictive methods pave the way for more comprehensive, automated, and standardized workflows. As more high-quality metabolomics datasets are deposited into public repositories \[[62](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0062)–[77](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0077)\] ([Table 10.2](#c10.xhtml#c10-tbl-0002)), cross-laboratory and large-scale comparative analyses will become increasingly feasible, further advancing our understanding of cellular metabolism.

# 11  
Strain Engineering, Flux Design, and Metabolic Production Using Big Data: Ongoing Advances and Opportunities

*Rafael S. Costa^()*

*²Associate Laboratory i4HB – Institute for Health and Bioeconomy, School of Science and Technology, Universidade NOVA de Lisboa, 2829-516 Caparica, Portugal*

## 11.1 Introduction

The biotech industry is being transformed by the Big Data advent, made possible by the unprecedented capacity to massively profile and process data, resulting in an explosion of usable information on individual biosystems. Representative sources of biotech Big Data include (bio)process data and various types of omics data (e.g. genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics) that are systematically stored and managed at several publicly available repositories for a wide range of healthcare, agriculture, industrial, and environmental endpoints \[[1](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0001)–[4](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0004)\]. Although the production of data in the most diverse biotechnology areas is increasing at a high rate, nevertheless, computational techniques are necessary to process such data and subsequently tap into their full potential. The power of machines to transform and learn from biodata is reshaping the current outlook [\[5\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0005). However, the structural complexity, heterogeneity, high-dimensionality, and increasingly massive volumes of bioprocess and omics data, coupled with the context-sensitive and stochastic nature of living systems, challenge the capacity to reach the desired phenotypes.

Complementarily, recent advancements in molecular engineering have revolutionized strain engineering and flux design, enabling the redirection of metabolic flux toward desired products \[[5](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0005), [6](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0006)\] (for further details about metabolic flux analysis, see [Chapter 12](#c12.xhtml)). The metabolic engineering field relies on genetic modifications (activation, underexpression, knockout, and/or modulation of regulatory elements) to reprogram native metabolic pathways for producing a wide variety of valuable compounds. This process has been further streamlined by the Design-Build-Test-Learn (DBTL) cycle framework for strain engineering, leveraging on high-throughput profiling to accelerate and optimize the development of strains [\[7\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0007). In this pipeline, the Design aq ?component outlines the strategic approach, while the Build step involves the techniques used to introduce sequence diversity. The Test phase includes the workflows for phenotyping, and the Learn component involves the application of computational tools to analyze the data collected during the testing. While computational tools are integrated throughout the cycle (from statistical analyses to complex simulations) to guide the process (analyze experimental results and identify new modification targets), the Learn stage remains an area with significant room for improvement [\[8\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0008).

A combination of multi-experiment data and data-driven analytical approaches (machine learning (ML) techniques) offers a compelling solution to address the introduced challenges while complying with the DBTL cycle. Currently, many biomanufacturing companies are investing in the digitalization of biotechnological systems and processes, recurring on various computational modeling formalisms, including mechanistic constraint-based modeling (CBM), ML, and hybrid modeling approaches. CBM approaches are based on fundamental principles such as mass and energy conservation, knowledge of the stoichiometry of metabolic networks that describe the range of steady-state flux distributions, using, for instance, the popular flux balance analysis (FBA) approach [\[9\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0009), and require relatively less experimental data. On the other hand, ML explores the capability of computers to perform tasks without explicit programming and no necessity to integrate background knowledge on metabolic processes. To carry out these tasks, ML algorithms can identify patterns, derive predictions, and continuously improve their performance through adaptive mechanisms \[[10](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0010), [11](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0011)\]. Moreover, the adaptive mechanisms present in ML allow computers to learn from datasets. These learning mechanisms, including ongoing deep learning (DL) breakthroughs, enable computers to progressively improve performance in diverse biotechnological applications, such as enzyme optimization, discover relevant genes in biosynthetic pathways, and propose new designs for the next DBTL cycle \[[12](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0012)–[14](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0014)\]. In this regard, sharing large-scale, high-quality data from bioreactor experiments and monitored organisms is crucial for learning purposes. ML techniques able to represent, integrate, and process high-dimensional data are an invaluable asset in any future biotechnology area to achieve a deep understanding of biosystems [\[15\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0015). In parallel to the emergence of pure ML models, integrative approaches that combine mechanistic CBM with ML (e.g. hybrid ML/FBA models) are gaining traction in computational strain design \[[16](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0016), [17](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0017)\].

This chapter is structured as follows. The first part reviews critical ML-based approaches for the descriptive and predictive modeling of Big Data in the biotech domain. An overview of hybrid ML/CBM approaches is also provided. The second part of the chapter presents several successful case studies and associated methodologies in the context of metabolic engineering research for the principled illustration of the introduced methods. Lastly, open challenges and future perspectives are outlined.

 

## 11.2 Big Data in Biotechnology: Prerequisites for ML-Based Approaches

The design of experimental studies in the biotechnological domain should abide by fundamental principles for the optimal application of subsequent learning tasks, including devising standardized protocols across experiments to ensure comparability between samples and reproducibility, recording all relevant endogenous and exogenous features that can impact the study (e.g. bioreactor cultivation conditions, strain backgrounds), guaranteeing a good coverage of diverse experimental parameterizations (e.g. unbiased sampling techniques for gene knockouts, media composition, environmental conditions) to promote the learning capacity, selecting control groups whenever applicable, isolating causes of noise and artifacts, calibrating instruments regularly and validating measurements to ensure data quality and accuracy, collecting replicates to assess/reduce variability and improve reliability, ensuring sufficient sample size to enable robust statistical analysis and generalization capacity, collecting data across various scales (e.g. multiple omics layers) for holistic learning, and monitoring longitudinal experiments at fine and consistent sampling rates. Complementarily to design considerations, the following sections devise subsequent data preprocessing principles to handle the multimodal, high-dimensional, longitudinal, and noisy nature of bioprocess and omics data.

 

### 11.2.1 Data Multimodality and Heterogeneity

In metabolic engineering experiments, data can be collected from a wide variety of biological and physicochemical modalities. First, multiple modalities can be identified at each omic layer, including genomics (genotyping, methylation), transcriptomics (RNAseq, chromatin accessibility), proteomics (abundance, post-translational modifications), and metabolomics (see [Chapter 10](#c10.xhtml)). Complementarily, molecular interactions (interactomics) between metabolites and other molecules, such as proteins, whether binding or regulatory, can be profiled. Second, metabolic flux analysis (fluxomics) allows the estimation of intracellular fluxes. Third, accompanying biophysical and biochemical measurements are generally relevant to assessing enzyme activity, kinetics, binding affinities, and reaction energetics. Fourth, imaging data, including fluorescence, electron, or confocal microscopy for structural and functional analysis, as well as cellular imaging, may also be available for specific ends. Fifth, phenotype profiling (phenomics) can encompass growth rate measurements (e.g. biomass accumulation), metabolite yield and productivity (production rates of desired compounds), stress response, and morphological analyses (e.g. characterization of cell size, shape, and structure). Finally, and most central, physiological measurements of environmental parameters, nutrient availability (e.g. concentrations of substrates, cofactors) and byproduct accumulation (e.g. toxic or inhibitory compounds) are generally critical.

Complementarity, data heterogeneity can arise due to variations in the monitoring protocols, instrumentation, environmental setups (e.g. temperature, pH, media composition, oxygen availability, and other conditions), (epi)genotypic and phenotypic diversity of strains and organisms, data annotation process sampling rates on longitudinal studies, and feature coverage (e.g. specific omics and fluxes only profiled on a subset of all samples leading to blockwise missing data). Such sources of heterogeneity – whether caused by collection methods, populations, or environments – can introduce several types of biases that hinder the subsequent learning goals, including sampling biases toward specific conditions that lead to generalization difficulties, measurement biases associated with systematic differences that can be assigned to the protocol and not the measured phenomenon, confounding biases due to spurious associations between variables or temporal patterns, and batch effects capturing systematic nonbiological forms of variation [\[18\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0018). Differences in the extent of recorded features or denormalized protocol variations can lead to feature spaces where large segments of missing entries will occur in blocks, generally claiming for dedicated handling principles, ranging from manifold alignment and domain-aware imputation to multi-source ensemble learning (models learned from subsamples and subspaces without block-wise missings) [\[19\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0019).

To guarantee the capacity to learn from multimodal and heterogeneous sources of data, several principles should be considered (e.g. [\[20\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0020)), including data integration principles to consolidate datasets from different modalities using mapping tables and ontologies for cross-referencing or more advanced principles (e.g. kernel-based fusion, hierarchical integration); standardization principles to handle heterogeneity such as scaling methods, batch effect correction (e.g. ComBat, RUV), and quantile normalization; adding protocol variations as covariates for ensuring sensitivity to protocol-specific biases; integrative learning principles such as graph-based approaches (e.g. heterogeneous networks) matrix factorization techniques (e.g. NMF) to find common patterns; quality assessment principles to quantify signal-to-noise ratios and subsequently apply filtering criteria to retain high-quality data; sampling principles to guarantee an uniform penetration of heterogeneity sources across training, validation, and testing observations; and harmonization principles such as cross-dataset alignment using canonical correlation analysis (CCA), Procrustes analysis, and embedding techniques; representation learning and multi-view learning principles can be used to learn from experimental data combining two or more distinct data structures (e.g. time series data, imaging data).

 

### 11.2.2 Stratification and Data Transformations

Complementarily, data sampling challenges pertaining to strata representativity, as well as the presence of categorical targets exhibiting class imbalance and numerical targets displaying skewed distributions, are common and stem from distinct underlying causes, including biases of experimental setups toward certain outcomes (e.g. neglection of certain conditions or emphasis on specific outputs of interest), experimental design choices, annotation inconsistencies, as well as natural biological constraints that make specific outcomes typically rare (e.g. successful strain designs, high-yield production), a common case with targeted modifications where successful interventions are relatively few compared to the vast number of possible perturbations.

Strategies to mitigate these challenges include resampling to reduce imbalances and skewness, incorporating domain-specific knowledge to transform and engineer input and/or output features with more adequate statistical distributions, optimizing the subsequent learning approaches (e.g. adjust decision thresholds, penalize misprediction of minority classes and numeric ranges via dedicated losses) and opt for their pretraining on related data, and acquiring new experimental data from underrepresented strata. Complementarily, data augmentation strategies recurring to variational autoencoders, metabolic models, perturbations to the existing data samples, or generative adversarial networks can be applied to generate synthetic data to handle limits pertaining to data availability, sampling biases, and imbalance of targets. Finally, pairwise learning principles under contrastive loss functions [\[21\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0021) can be used to counteract generalization difficulties.
