## 13.4 Challenges for Implementing Fully Automated Biofoundries

The long-term vision for biofoundries is to develop fully automated bioengineering pipelines that can execute the DBTL cycles seamlessly. However, several practical limitations currently hinder the realization of this goal. These challenges can be grouped into distinct categories based on their underlying causes ([Figure 13.2](#c13.xhtml#c13-fig-0002)).

One of the most significant hurdles in biofoundry automation is the lack of standardization across different platforms, equipment, and protocols. Unlike traditional engineering disciplines, biology inherently exhibits high variability due to differences in host organisms, genetic constructs, and environmental conditions. Most laboratory instruments still operate using proprietary software and non-standardized data formats, complicating integration efforts. Ensuring compatibility between robotic liquid handlers, analytical instruments, and computational design tools remains a substantial challenge. Without universally accepted standards, reproducibility is hindered, and cross-institutional collaboration becomes more difficult. Addressing these limitations is essential to unlocking the full potential of biofoundries.

Another major challenge lies in the ability of biofoundries to support scaling-up efforts. While small-scale automated workflows have demonstrated success in high-throughput strain engineering, scaling up strain performance to industrial levels remains complex. Many automated workflows require customization for specific applications, making it difficult to establish universally applicable automation pipelines. Additionally, large-scale fermentations present different gradients in nutrient availability as well as gas-liquid transfer dynamics, exposing strains to environments that differ significantly from benchtop reactors. The transition from benchtop automation to large-scale biofoundries necessitates significant investment in infrastructure and process refinement. Furthermore, biofoundries should be flexible enough to accommodate a wide range of biological systems, from microbial strains to mammalian cells. Recent efforts in this direction have been directed to implement “versatile” biofoundries, which can be adapted depending on specific requirements (e.g. anoxic conditions). However, this adaptability is hindered by the limitations of current robotic systems, which are often designed for specific workflows and cannot easily transition between different experimental setups. Overcoming these scalability and flexibility constraints requires innovations in modular automation systems that can be readily reconfigured based on experimental demands.

Biological systems are inherently complex, exhibiting dynamic behaviors, stochasticity as well as intricate regulatory networks. This complexity challenges the predictability and control required for biofoundry automation. Unlike mechanical or electronic systems, biological parts interact in nonlinear ways, making it difficult to design predictable, scalable workflows. Engineering biology at scale necessitates robust modeling and simulation tools capable of accurately capturing cellular behaviors under diverse conditions. Current computational models often oversimplify biological interactions, limiting their predictive power. Furthermore, emergent properties such as genetic instability, metabolic burden, and unintended interactions can introduce unexpected variability, complicating system optimization. Advancements in computational biology and HTS methods will be essential to overcoming these challenges.

![Figure 13.2 Key challenges for implementing a fully automated biofoundry. Created with BioRender.com.](images/c13f002.png)

Figure 13.2 Key challenges for implementing a fully automated biofoundry. Created with [BioRender.com](http://biorender.com).

AI and ML are poised to revolutionize biofoundries by optimizing experimental design, predicting biological behaviors and accelerating data analysis. However, the effective integration of AI-driven decision-making into fully automated workflows remains a formidable challenge. One key limitation is the availability of high-quality, structured datasets required for training AI models. Biological data often exhibits significant noise, variability, and inconsistencies, making it difficult to derive reliable predictive models. Furthermore, implementing AI in biofoundries requires real-time data acquisition, processing, and feedback loops. Developing robust AI frameworks that can dynamically adjust experimental parameters based on real-time results is an ongoing challenge. Additionally, ensuring that AI-driven decisions align with biological constraints and experimental feasibility is critical for successful implementation.

Another major bottleneck is the throughput variability across the DBTL cycle steps. Differences in the efficiency and duration of each phase can create imbalances, leading to bottlenecks and delays in workflow completion. For instance, while design and build phases may proceed rapidly with automated DNA synthesis and assembly, testing and learning steps often require complex biological assays that take days or weeks to yield meaningful data. Variability in cell growth rates, gene expression levels, and assay reproducibility can further complicate standardization across different DBTL iterations. Addressing these disparities requires improved automation of phenotypic characterization and data integration to ensure smooth progression through all phases.

The massive datasets generated by automated biofoundries present significant challenges in data management, storage, and analysis. High-throughput experiments produce vast amounts of sequencing data, metabolomic profiles, and imaging datasets that require efficient processing and interpretation. Data heterogeneity further complicates integration efforts, as different experiments generate diverse data types that must be harmonized for meaningful insights. Standardized ontologies, metadata frameworks, and cloud-based storage solutions are essential for managing large-scale biological datasets. Additionally, developing AI-driven data analytics pipelines will be key to extracting actionable insights, optimizing workflows, and improving system predictability. Also, high capital costs make it challenging for emerging economies to develop biofoundry infrastructures. Developing and maintaining automated biofoundries require substantial financial investment. High costs associated with robotic instrumentation, protocol implementation, AI-driven software development, and continuous system upgrades pose significant barriers to widespread adoption. While large-scale research institutions and companies can afford these investments, smaller laboratories and startups struggle to access automated biofoundry resources. Infrastructure constraints, including space requirements, power consumption, and maintenance demands, further complicate implementation. Traditional laboratories cannot support large-scale automation, necessitating extensive retrofitting or construction of dedicated facilities. Reducing automation costs and developing compact, modular biofoundries is key to enabling broader accessibility.

The automation of synthetic biology workflows raises concerns regarding biosecurity and ethical implications. Fully automated biofoundries possess the capability to rapidly design and construct genetically modified organisms (GMOs), which could potentially be misused. Establishing biosecurity measures, e.g. access control, screening mechanisms, and regulatory compliance, is essential to mitigate potential risks. Ethical considerations also arise in the context of intellectual property and equitable access to biofoundry technologies. The increasing privatization of synthetic biology tools and automation technologies may create barriers for smaller research institutions and developing nations. Addressing these concerns requires international regulatory frameworks that promote responsible innovation and ensure equitable distribution of biofoundry capabilities.

 

## 13.5 Perspectives and Outlook

We have seen how biofoundries can increase the throughput of the DBTLc and assist in iterating through the four phases using automated setups. The challenges mentioned in the previous section can serve as a foundation for developing trajectories that the field may adopt to maximize the impact of these infrastructures, which is the focus of this section.

Regarding the issue of standardization, it is desirable to establish standardized procedures and data management strategies as early as possible within the biofoundry framework – ideally through a pilot campaign before the first official one begins. Standardization should involve all team members across the DBTLc to ensure that generated data is correctly stored and promptly processed by the team responsible for the next phase. Implementing this strategy will help maintain high standards and ensure compliance throughout the entire cycle. Additionally, if the biofoundry's purpose is to serve customers, it should ensure that generated and transferred data is discussed and clearly understood by the customer. The further development of universally accepted standards will enhance reproducibility, streamline automation, and facilitate seamless collaboration between different biofoundries. We believe that associations such as the GBA might favor while developing technical roadmaps for implementing these universally accepted standards.

Optimizing and streamlining procedures within a biofoundry will inevitably emphasize certain types of processes or applications. This trend is already partially evident in [Table 13.2](#c13.xhtml#c13-tbl-0002), where some biofoundries specialize in specific DBTL cycles. We believe that a well-functioning biofoundry should have a clear mission and focus on refining procedures that align with its objectives – rather than serving as a generalized high-throughput platform for a wide range of scopes and applications. That said, biofoundries are also highly flexible in adapting to new workflows. This adaptability was demonstrated by the temporary repurposing of London's biofoundry for SARS-CoV-2 test screening, showcasing how these facilities can rapidly pivot to address urgent scientific and societal needs [\[135\]](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0135).

One example of such applications could be biofoundries that specialize in improving the scalability of microbial cultures for large-scale cultivation. There is an inherent limitation in simulating such cultivations in small-scale setups as a biofoundry would offer. However, adopting batteries of miniaturized stirred bioreactors for scale-down experimentation can offer a solution for simulating large-scale fermentation [\[136\]](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0136), including the investigation of multiple parameters that can hinder the transition from bench-top to cubic-meter fermenters.

When dealing with the unpredictability of biological systems, we believe that by focusing on a specific purpose for the biofoundry (e.g. mammalian cells), it will be possible to learn how the biological samples running through the DBTLc behave. This approach will allow us to understand which variables most affect standardization, thereby reducing variability. In the case of using different species of microorganisms, one potential solution to reduce cross-contamination is to introduce kill-switch mechanisms, e.g. temperature-sensitive mechanisms and CRISPR-based strategies [\[44\]](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0044), in the strains. This would help prevent their persistence in machinery when those systems are used for other species.

ML can aid in managing the unpredictability of biological systems by employing neural networks to predict biological features. For instance, in protein engineering evolution, models are now capable of creating artificial proteins with desired functions by training the network against millions of sequences available in databases [\[137\]](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0137). Moreover, AI is expected to contribute to coordinating dry lab and wet lab activities across the different phases of the DBTLc. Although we are not there yet, we are getting closer and closer [\[3\]](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0003).

When dealing with different throughput sizes across the DBTL modules, one option could be to simplify (as much as possible) the amount of data to process during the data-heavy test phase. For example, using growth-coupled designs and associated screening campaigns for modules linked to growth fitness can be a useful ally for testing metabolic activities \[[77](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0077)[138](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0138)–[142](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0142)\] or evolving enzymatic functions of interest \[[92](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0092), [143](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0143)–[146](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0146)\]. Additionally, biosensors that provide fluorescence signals in the presence of a molecule could become useful tools to reduce the burden of the test phase \[[83](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0083), [147](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0147)–[149](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0149)\].

Establishing biofoundries requires high investments in capital and operational costs. To promote the emergence of biofoundries beyond Europe, North America, Asia, and Oceania, early-stage biofoundries could benefit from adopting cheaper and simpler apparatuses for their operational units. For example, small-scale (<20 mL volume) mini-bioreactors that are open source allow customers to interact and program them as needed [\[150\]](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0150). We believe that this type of solution offers a good trade-off between throughput, controlled conditions, and lower capital expenses.

We foresee that the implementation of one or more of these perspectives will likely be adopted when developing new biofoundries or improving pipelines in existing ones. These approaches will enable biofoundries to optimize their workflows, reduce costs, and enhance scalability, ultimately fostering the growth and success of synthetic biology across various industries.

## 14.1 Bioprocess Modeling and Optimization

 

### 14.1.1 Challenges in Bioprocess Modeling

The fourth industrial revolution, often referred to as “Industry 4.0,” requires the integration of smart technologies into manufacturing and industrial processes, playing a key role in the improvement of bioprocess efficiency, sustainability, and profitability \[[1](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0001), [2](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0002)\]. Due to the desire to further explore the potential of bioprocess automation, digitalization is currently at the forefront of bioprocess development [\[3\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0003). Digitalization itself relies on the development of digital twins, a concept first proposed in 2002, in which bidirectional information transfer between the physical and digital domains occurs automatically. An effective digital twin facilitates real-time decision-making to maximize productivity, efficiency, and sustainability [\[4\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0004). Modeling plays a key role in the development of a digital twin by simulating the physical domain in real-time, as well as potentially being used to predict unobservable states using soft sensors \[[5](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0005)–[7](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0007)\]. The main challenge associated with the development of a bioprocess digital twin is having a sufficiently accurate and validated mathematical model of the desired bioprocess to make rapid predictions and process adjustments [\[6\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0006), which is why official records show the first implementation of a digital twin within an industrial-scale bioprocess to be as recent as 2019 [\[8\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0008).

Developing models for fermentation bioprocesses is immensely appealing due to their various potential applications in frameworks such as process control and optimization, design of experiments (DoEs), and robust Quality by Design (QbD) for the ever-expanding production of biofuels, biochemicals, and biopharmaceuticals. In an ideal world, a fully descriptive mechanistic model could be constructed and applied to a bioprocess. However, designing such models and identifying their parameters to an adequate degree is highly challenging in bioprocessing; a fully descriptive bioprocess model would need to include various considerations such as self-inhibitory and self-catalytic feedback interactions, nonhomogeneous cell populations and phases, pH andaq ? temperature dependence, and even mass transfer limitations. As a result, simple models, such as first-order kinetics (which are commonly seen in chemical reaction systems [\[9\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0009)), are generally only applicable in narrow operating spaces. Therefore, when constructing a predictive bioprocess dynamic model, a balance must be found between the incorporation of sufficient complexity and the identifiability of the model parameters.

Bioprocess models found in literature can generally be categorized somewhere on the spectrum between machine learning (“data-driven” or “black box”) and mechanistic (“kinetic” or “white box”) [\[10\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0010). Due to the aforementioned challenges associated with constructing a detailed mechanistic model, similar to those described in [Chapters 1](#c01.xhtml)–[2](#c02.xhtml), [9](#c09.xhtml), and [11](#c11.xhtml)–[12](#c12.xhtml), a sensible approach can be to build a simplified mechanistic model based on fundamental assumptions, often referred to as “first principles” [\[11\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0011). Such models contain physically interpretable parameters for the system at hand, providing a degree of process insight. However, when assumptions are made for model derivation, the model itself will only be valid within the operating space where the assumptions hold true, meaning that its generalizability is lost. An example of a relatively simple kinetic model is the Monod model, which can fit some batch processes well; however, it ignores the potential inhibitory effects of high cell density (HCD) and high substrate concentrations [\[12\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0012). Improving generalizability can be achieved by constructing a more detailed mechanistic model by introducing further process understanding; however, this will require more data, especially if additional state and control variables are introduced [\[10\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0010). Moreover, adding further detail to a kinetic model without adequate hypothesis testing introduces inductive bias, which can actually reduce predictive capabilities of the model if the additional “knowledge” is not reflective of the system. In addition, increasing the intricacy of a kinetic model can increase the number of model parameters, thus reducing parameter identifiability and increasing model uncertainty [\[13\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0013).

On the other end of the spectrum, machine learning models have no prerequisite assumptions and can have strong generalization capabilities. For example, artificial neural networks (ANNs) are known to be able to approximate any function [\[14\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0014). Employing pure machine learning models may sound appealing; however, large quantities of data are required to sufficiently capture the potentially nonlinear relationships, such as the relationships between substrates and cell growth, that are known to exist in biosystems. In addition, experiments are expensive to run, with some states being challenging to measure, leading to bioprocess data typically being multisource, multi-scale, noisy, and heterogeneous (a mixture of online and offline, and binary and continuous) [\[15\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0015). Therefore, it is uncommon to have access to an adequate availability of data to train particularly nonlinear machine learning models for biosystems while avoiding overfitting. Moreover, machine learning models provide limited insight since the model structure itself is not physically interpretable, which is reflected by the poor extrapolative capabilities of machine learning models [\[10\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0010).

Irrespective of the model built, challenges such as batch-to-batch variation can also lead to issues with model training and validation. In addition, models can fall short during upscaling due to various phenomena, including differing flow regimes and more prevalent localized nutrient and cell population heterogeneity. As a result, upscaling often observes different process dynamics that result in lower yields and productivity or even total failure of the culture. Therefore, it is important to develop bioprocess models with the strongest possible extrapolative capabilities and generalizability to maximize both the accuracy of predictions and the ability to incorporate new information. As such, navigating the hurdles of developing a state-of-the-art bioprocess model is no simple task.

In this chapter, we will explore the use of machine learning to enhance our understanding of bioprocesses for modeling and optimization of fermentation processes, while making the most of the limited available experimental data and fundamental process knowledge.

 

### 14.1.2 Machine Learning for Bioprocess Modeling

Machine learning is a powerful tool for tackling a lack of process knowledge and high system complexity, which is often the case when assessing biosystems. The ability to handle intricate and poorly understood systems has encouraged the application of machine learning to a multitude of bioprocesses using a variety of techniques. In this section, we will explore a brief overview of different machine learning applications, both recent and not, in biosystems.

 

#### 14.1.2.1 Principal Component Analysis and Partial Least Squares

Principal component analysis (PCA) is a linear dimensionality reduction technique that generates latent variables, called principal components, to explain the most variance in the original variables as possible [\[16\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0016). PCA has been applied to several biochemical applications, including the identification of patterns between operating factors for biogas and biofuel production \[[17](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0017), [18](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0018)\], cell phenotype discrimination [\[19\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0019), process abnormality detection [\[20\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0020), and determining statistical similarities and differences between product distributions [\[21\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0021). Due to the innate complexity of biosystems, dimensionality reduction can be particularly useful for problem simplification; a study combining PCA with an ANN for the productive capacity of *Eucalyptus* forest sites in Brazil showed that using the latent variables improved the ANN predictive capabilities [\[22\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0022). Naturally, the biggest limitation of applying PCA to model bioprocesses is the inability to capture nonlinear relationships that can be observed within some biosystems due to the linear nature of PCA.

Partial Least Squares (PLS) is similar in many ways to PCA; however, instead of only using latent variables, it directly relates inputs to outputs in a linear fashion. For Multiple Input Multiple Output (MIMO) models, PLS can be directly used; however, in some cases, multiple models are used in parallel for each individual output in a Multiple Input Single Output (MISO) format [\[23\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0023). In terms of biosystem applications, PLS has seen multiple applications, including classification and authentication of operating conditions in a yeast fermentation bioreactor [\[24\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0024), bioprocess monitoring [\[25\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0025), bioreactor state estimation and control \[[26](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0026), [27](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0027)\], mapping amino acid sequences with protein functions [\[28\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0028), and identifying flux relationships [\[29\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0029). Similar to PCA, PLS is limited to applications where nonlinear relationships do not need to be fully captured.

 

#### 14.1.2.2 Artificial Neural Networks

ANNs can capture complex nonlinear relationships and generally come in the form of an MIMO or MISO model. The inspiration for ANNs came from mimicking the human brain, where a network of neurons can be “activated” to pass on information [\[14\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0014). Due to the ability of an ANN to capture nonlinear relationships, ANNs have seen a variety of applications in biosystems. For example, previous studies have utilized the potential of ANNs for predicting methane content and biogas production [\[30\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0030), predicting fermentation dynamics online [\[31\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0031), recognizing appropriate kinetic model structures for batch processing [\[32\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0032), optimizing the production of algal biofuel [\[33\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0033), predicting protein structures [\[34\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0034), and classifying the three-dimensional (3D) structures of enzymes [\[35\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0035). ANNs are a powerful tool; however, the most prominent limitation in the application of ANNs to biosystems is the large amount of data that is required to capture complex nonlinear relationships. Such quantities of data are, at best, time-consuming or expensive to obtain and can be, at worst, infeasible to practically obtain.

However, in certain cases, the fundamental ANN structure can be expanded to enhance its ability to capture different relationships. For example, deep neural networks (DNNs) are a subcategory of ANNs that possess multiple hidden layers of nodes, allowing the approximation of more complex relationships. Successful incorporation of DNNs to biosystems in literature includes the construction of a hybrid model using a DNN for industry-scale fermentation [\[36\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0036), as well as the detection of “optimum tea fermentation,” where the tea has fermented enough to reach a desired quality but is yet to degrade due to over-fermentation [\[37\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0037). However, since DNNs have multiple layers, they tend to have a higher number of parameters, which means they need even more training data than a shallow ANN to avoid overfitting. Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are another type of ANN that have been applied to biochemical processes. What makes them “recurrent” compared to a feed-forward neural network is the addition of an internal cycle; possessing this internal memory facilitates the learning of sequential data, such as time-series [\[38\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0038). The capability of RNNs to identify sequential relationships has been harnessed in various biosystem applications, such as statistically summarizing amino acid sequences [\[39\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0039), and recognizing promoter sequences in genetic engineering [\[40\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0040). In addition, an RNN demonstrated improved fitting and predictive capabilities when compared to a feed-forward neural network in monitoring simultaneous saccharification and fermentation of ethanol [\[41\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0041). As with most ANNs, RNNs are not always applicable due to a lack of data availability for biosystems.

 

#### 14.1.2.3 Gaussian Processes

Gaussian processes (GPs) return a probabilistic function, instead of a scalar, for each output variable from a given multivariate input. If no noise is assumed, a GP will fit exactly to the dataset [\[42\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0042). GPs are particularly useful for uncertainty analysis as they can directly estimate the mean and variance of the output, unlike other machine learning methods. Several applications of GPs to biosystems have been presented in literature, including dynamic modeling and optimization of microalgal lutein production under uncertainty [\[43\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0043), ensuring the meeting of probabilistic constraints in bioreactor control [\[44\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0044), and estimating the cell density distribution in *δ*\-endotoxins batch production from *Bacillus thuringiensis* [\[45\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0045). A notable limitation of GPs is the high computational expense of calculating the inverse of the posterior, which scales poorly with higher-dimensional problems [\[46\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0046). However, studies are being conducted on approximating symmetric positive definite matrix inversions under reduced computational cost, which extends the applicability of GPs [\[47\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0047).

 

#### 14.1.2.4 Ensemble Learning

Ensemble learning (EL) combines several inducers (machine learning models that relate an input to an output) to generate a single output based on the outputs of each individual inducer. EL structures usually involve either a series structure, such as gradient boosting (GB), where the first inducer provides an initial prediction that is corrected by subsequent inducers, or a parallel structure, such as Random Forest (RF), where inducers in parallel have their predictions averaged or weighted to give a single output [\[48\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0048). With RFs being the more widely applied EL approach to biosystem modeling [\[23\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0023), application examples include the optimization of fermentation for Rifamycin B production [\[49\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0049), building soft-sensors for industrial-scale fed-batch fermentation [\[50\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0050), and estimating the cetane number of fatty acid methyl esters (FAMEs) for biodiesel synthesis [\[51\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0051). Although less utilized, GB has still been applied to cases such as liquid–liquid bioseparations [\[52\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0052) and predicting biohydrogen production [\[53\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0053). Despite being a powerful modeling tool, EL can suffer from overfitting due to the large number of parameters involved and can be computationally expensive to run if the system has an excessive number of inducers.

 

#### 14.1.2.5 Reinforcement Learning

Reinforcement Learning (RL) is a trial-and-error approach to learning optimal input sequences through the provision of rewards and penalties [\[54\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0054). RL has proven to be highly effective in the gaming world, with chess engines such as the free-to-access “Stockfish Engine” outperforming the best human players in the world in a fraction of the thinking time [\[55\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0055). With the ability to identify optimal input sequences, there exists a broad range of potential applications to biosystems, with previous studies exploring topics such as identifying an optimal control strategy for fed-batch biopharmaceutical processes [\[56\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0056), bioprocess kinetics identification \[[57](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0057), [58](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0058)\], and policy optimization subject to chance constraints for a stochastic dynamic bioreactor system [\[59\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0059). Despite having the potential to be utilized in model-free applications [\[23\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0023), RL can also be limited by large data requirements; a trial-and-error approach can require a large number of experiments that, in certain cases, are too expensive and time-consuming to conduct.

 

#### 14.1.2.6 Future Prospects for Machine Learning

As the push toward digitalization continues, new applications of machine learning are continually being explored. For example, studies have been conducted on automatic model generation through symbolic regression, which allows the automated generation of interpretable mathematical models for chemical and biochemical systems \[[60](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0060)–[62](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0062)\]. Automatic model generation has the potential to save large amounts of time by accelerating iterative model design, particularly when coupled with DoE for optimal gain of knowledge [\[62\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0062).

Alternatively, the concept of hybrid modeling, which will be explored in more detail in [Section 14.1.3](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-0010), has seen a recent surge in applications to bioprocesses \[[63](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0063), [64](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0064)\], despite hybrid modeling being first proposed as early as 1992 [\[8\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0008). [Section 14.1.3](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-0010) will explore the flexibility and applicability of hybrid modeling to infer why this methodology is increasing in popularity over 30 years after its conception.

 

### 14.1.3 Introduction to Hybrid Modeling

 

#### 14.1.3.1 Literature Review

The term “hybrid modeling” falls under the umbrella term “grey box” modeling as it lies on the spectrum between pure mechanistic “white box” and empirical “black box” modeling, as depicted in [Figure 14.1](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0001). But why build a hybrid model? Combining the two approaches to make a hybrid model allows improvement upon the accuracy of a mechanistic model by integrating a machine learning component that avoids the introduction of extra inductive bias from additional mechanistic terms developed using further assumptions. In addition, less data is required to train a hybrid model than a pure machine learning model because the mechanistic backbone of the model can capture some nonlinear relationships within the system, therefore leaving fewer nonlinear relationships that need to be approximated by the machine learning model.

There are two common structures for hybrid models: parallel and series. In a series hybrid model structure, either the mechanistic or machine learning component feeds into the other, which subsequently yields the output, as shown in [Figure 14.2](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0002)a, meaning the mechanistic and machine learning models do not act independently, though the first model may be independent from the second. Alternatively, in a parallel hybrid model structure, the mechanistic and machine learning components lie independently of one another; their respective outputs combine to give a single output, as shown in [Figure 14.2](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0002)b. The decision on whether a series or parallel structure should be used depends on the problem at hand. [Table 14.1](#c14.xhtml#c14-tbl-0001) highlights various examples of the applications of hybrid models in biosystems seen in literature, as well as the respective structures of the hybrid models built. The most common motivation for constructing a hybrid model appears to be improving model predictive capabilities for subsequent monitoring, optimization, and control applications. As can be seen in [Table 14.1](#c14.xhtml#c14-tbl-0001), a common hybrid model structure is that where a data-driven model feeds reaction rates (or time-varying kinetic parameters), in series, to a form of mechanistic model. However, it should be noted that such a hybrid model configuration is not a generic series or parallel structure since, for dynamic systems, the hybrid model updates the state variables, which will in turn update the data-driven model and subsequently the mechanistic component; it is more of a cyclical series structure as illustrated in [Figure 14.2](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0002)c.

![Figure 14.2 Illustrations of hybrid model structures for sequential series structures (a), where the white and black box come one-after-the-other in any order, parallel structure (b), where the white and black box models operate independently and combine to yield a single solution, and a dynamic hybrid structure (c), where a black box model updates time-varying parameters as a function of state variables to be used within a dynamic mechanistic white box model.](images/c14f002.png)

Figure 14.2 Illustrations of hybrid model structures for sequential series structures (a), where the white and black box come one-after-the-other in any order, parallel structure (b), where the white and black box models operate independently and combine to yield a single solution, and a dynamic hybrid structure (c), where a black box model updates time-varying parameters as a function of state variables to be used within a dynamic mechanistic white box model.

 

#### 14.1.3.2 Hybrid Modeling for Biosystem Optimization

As mentioned in [Section 14.1.3](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-0010), improving model predictive capabilities using hybrid modeling is particularly beneficial for optimization applications. For example, the machine learning component can be easily retrained upon running a new experiment. A potential approach for training and validating a hybrid model is to run an experiment from DoE, whether it be a predicted optimum or an area of poor knowledge, and use the new data to update the machine learning component; repeating this process iteratively can be an efficient way to identify a suitable “optimal” solution while simultaneously generating a well-trained model.

*C*[*S*],0 = Initial substrate concentration, *C*[*X*],0 = Initial cell density, *T* = Temperature, *T* (*t*) = Dynamic temperature profile, *t*[f] = Final time, *t*[ind] = Induction time, *N* = Rotor speed, *pH*(*t*) = Dynamic pH profile, *F*[*i*](*t*) = Dynamic feed *i* profile, *C*ind = Inducer concentration, KM = Kinetic Model, ANN = Artificial Neural Network.

Some examples of biosystem optimization studies using hybrid modeling are presented in [Table 14.2](#c14.xhtml#c14-tbl-0002). As one may expect, [Table 14.2](#c14.xhtml#c14-tbl-0002) highlights that objectives are often based on maximizing growth, yield, product titer, productivity, or profitability of the biosystem. [Table 14.2](#c14.xhtml#c14-tbl-0002) also shows that optimization from hybrid modeling is applicable over a variety of domains, whether it be mammalian cell lines, microalgal cultures, or fungi.

Overall, ANNs and hybrid modeling were first proposed in 1943 and 1992, respectively [\[8\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0008). However, despite being a modeling technique that is now over 30 years old, hybrid modeling is still proving to be a capable approach for advancing biosystem development at an increasing rate. The relevance of hybrid modeling is thanks to a multitude of factors, including improved computational power, as well as access to new tools and techniques for data collection, such as free-floating wireless sensors, soft-sensors, and chemometrics [\[81\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0081). Since hybrid modeling possesses a machine learning component, new data does not need to be incorporated directly into the mechanistic model if process knowledge is limited, thus keeping hybrid modeling relevant even as techniques for data collection advance.

 

## 14.2 Methodology for Hybrid Modeling

In this section, we explore the construction of a hybrid model for making predictions of a fermentation process. We start with the development of a preliminary mechanistic model before employing a machine learning component to improve model accuracy. Hereafter, uncertainty analysis is incorporated, and process optimization for a fed-batch fermentation system is illustrated. As a running example to show how the described methods are implemented, we imagine a batch process with homogeneous cell culture with a single substrate and a single product.

 

### 14.2.1 Mechanistic Model Construction

Preliminary mechanistic modeling aims to incorporate mechanistic information into the mathematical model. Implementing any mechanistic model structures introduces some inductive bias as all mechanistic models rely upon at least one assumption. As a result, it is important to stick to first principles and not venture into overly elaborate mechanistic structures, as they will introduce inductive bias and hinder the accuracy of a hybrid model. An example of an appropriate mechanistic relationship would be the assumption that each cell has the same specific uptake rate of substrate *q*[*S*], the same specific production rate of product *q*[*P*], and the same specific growth rate *μ*, irrespective of cell density, resulting in the system of ODEs shown in [Eqs. 14.1a](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0001)–[14.1c](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0003):

In this instance, we know that a model is needed to describe specific rates because, otherwise, the model structure implies that the cell culture will infinitely grow and excrete product while continuing to consume substrate even after substrate depletion, phenomena which we know to be incorrect. Although this may be sufficient mechanistic information for cases with more data, it can be beneficial to include further assumptions to prevent phenomena we know to be unrealistic. Since introducing further assumptions introduces inductive bias, the assumptions should be simple in nature. For example, introducing Monod kinetics for growth and substrate ensures that non-negative substrate concentrations will be maintained while allowing kinetic relationships between zero-order and first-order with respect to the substrate concentration [\[82\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0082). In order to prevent infinite growth of cells, we can also assume a first-order decay rate with respect to cell density. The resulting mechanistic model is described in [Eqs. 14.2a](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0004)–[14.2c](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0006):

where *μ*[max] is the maximum specific growth rate, *μ*[*d*] is the specific death rate, ![v Subscript max Underscript upper S Endscripts](images/c14-i0003.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>v</mi><msub><mi>max</mi><mi>S</mi></msub></msub></math> is the maximum specific substrate consumption rate, and *K*[*S*] is the saturation constant (the substrate concentration at which half the maximum specific consumption rate is achieved [\[82\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0082)). It should be noted that although the specific death rate and specific product production rate are likely to be some function of state variables (since products can be self-inhibitory or lead to cell death), we may not have enough knowledge of the system to make valid assumptions. Therefore, it is better to leave unknown relationships to the machine learning component that commences construction in [Section 14.2.2](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-0015).

The next step for the mechanistic component construction is parameter estimation of the mechanistic model, which involves solving the optimization framework described in Framework 14.3:

where the objective function in [Eq. 14.3a](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0007) minimizes the difference between the simulated state variables *C*[*i*](*t, β*) and their corresponding experimental measurements ![upper C Subscript i comma t Superscript italic meas](images/c14-i0004.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mtext mathvariant="italic">meas</mtext></msubsup></math>and measurement standard deviation ![alpha Subscript i comma t Superscript italic meas](images/c14-i0005.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msubsup><mi>&#945;</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mtext mathvariant="italic">meas</mtext></msubsup></math>for state *i* at time point *t* up until the final measurement time *t*[f].

Optimization Framework 14.3 can be carried out using a variety of tools. Gradient descent algorithms such as interior point optimization (IPOPT) are appropriate and can be freely accessed using the *fmincon* function in MATLAB or the Pyomo and SciPy packages in Python \[[83](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0083)–[85](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0085)\]. Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) can also be used to generate good initial guesses in cases where gradient descent algorithms converge to poor solutions as a result of sensitivity to the initial guess. However, its gradient-free nature prevents it from guaranteeing convergence to any local optima if used on its own.

Uncertainty analysis of the mechanistic model should also be conducted to assess the model's fitting performance. This can be addressed by calculating the uncertainty of each parameter from the Hessian of the objective function in [Eq. 14.3a](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0007) (referred to here as *Z* for simplicity) with respect to the estimated parameters *β*\*. The Hessian matrix of the parameter estimation objective function with respect to the estimated parameters ***H***(*Z, **β***\*) is inverted to generate the corresponding covariance matrix ***Cov***(*Z, **β***\*) of the model, as in [Eq. 14.4](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0009):

(14.4)![bold-italic upper C o v left-parenthesis upper Z comma bold-italic beta Superscript bold asterisk Baseline right-parenthesis equals bold-italic upper H left-parenthesis upper Z comma bold-italic beta Superscript asterisk Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript negative 1 Baseline comma](images/c14-math-0009.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Cov</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo mathvariant="bold">&#42;</mo></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#946;</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo></math> 

where the diagonal of the covariance matrix represents the individual parameter variances [\[86\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0086). Monte Carlo sampling can be used to generate parameter confidence intervals (in this chapter, we recommend the use of 95% confidence intervals, which corresponds to two standard deviations from the mean) and subsequently model trajectory confidence intervals. Confidence intervals are important for gauging the predictive capabilities of the model; a model may appear to capture data well using the nominal parameter values, but if confidence intervals are large, it will be less likely to make predictions with high precision. It should be noted that, at this point, if the mechanistic model predicts well within the desired operating range with adequately sized confidence intervals, the model is unlikely to require the further addition of a machine learning component. However, if predictive capabilities are poor and/or confidence intervals are inappropriately large, introducing a machine learning component could be greatly beneficial, the first step of which is described in [Section 14.2.2](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-0015).

 

### 14.2.2 Time-Varying Parameter Estimation

A mechanistic modeling does not always yield the predetermined desired predictive capabilities with sufficiently low uncertainty, making them inadequate for their applications. Under the assumption that further alterations to the mechanistic model cannot *confidently* be made, the introduction of a machine learning component could be advantageous as it can increase model accuracy while maintaining good generalizability.

Since we have a mechanistic backbone, it can be assumed that poor model performance is due to missing information from the model structure, meaning some of the constant parameters within the model are not constant parameters but time-varying functions of state variables and operating conditions. Henceforth, we will refer to such hidden functions embedded within parameters as *time-varying parameters*. The most appropriate parameters to dedicate to be time-varying are parameters that have the highest uncertainty, which are identified using the covariance matrix calculated in [Eq. 14.4](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0009); parameters with the highest standard deviation to nominal value ratio are deemed “most uncertain.” Normalizing standard deviation with respect to the parameter nominal value avoids potential bias introduced from the units chosen to describe the parameter. Sensitivity analysis must subsequently be conducted to ensure the chosen parameter has an appropriate effect on the mechanistic model trajectories; if not, the parameter should be removed altogether as it has a negligible impact on the model's accuracy.

Once the time-varying parameters have been identified, the end goal is to simulate them as a function of state variables and operating conditions using a machine learning model. Training the machine learning model is conducted in two stages: (1) identifying appropriate time-varying parameter profiles over the entire time course, and (2) training a machine learning model to estimate time-varying parameter profiles using corresponding state variable profiles and process conditions. Assuming that the most uncertain parameters in [Eqs. 14.2a](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0004)–[14.2c](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0006) are found to be *μ*[d], *K[S]*, and *q[P]*, identifying their respective time-varying profiles is achieved with a simple adjustment to [Eqs. 14.2a](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0004)–[14.2c](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0006) and parameter estimation Framework 14.3. The resulting parameter estimation framework is presented in Framework 14.5:

stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#183;</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>X</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></math> 

where ![lamda Subscript theta Sub Subscript k](images/c14-i0006.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mrow><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></msub></math> is a weight for the regularization term that penalizes dramatic deviations time-varying parameter *k*, and *θ[k]*(*t[θ]*) is the time-varying parameter of the nominal parameter *k* from time *t[θ]* to time *t[θ]* + Δ*t[θ]*. We recommend that each time-varying parameter discretization step Δ*t[θ]* to be no less than the time difference between consecutive measurements in order to minimize overfitting. Increasing the value of ![lamda Subscript theta Sub Subscript k](images/c14-i0007.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mrow><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></msub></math> results in stronger penalization of time-varying parameter deviations, thus reducing the overfitting of noisy data. However, this will also reduce the fitting accuracy as the data-fitting term in [Eq. 14.5a](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0010) is prioritized less.

Once time-varying parameter profiles have been identified, the simulation of state variables should have increased in accuracy. Therefore, the time-varying parameter profiles can be assigned to corresponding state variables and necessary operating conditions for training of the machine learning component, which is discussed in [Section 14.2.3](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-0016).

 

### 14.2.3 Machine Learning Model Construction

Regardless of the machine learning component chosen, the overall training aim is the same: generate a data-driven model that takes state variables and key process operating conditions as inputs to predict corresponding time-varying parameter values as outputs. For the simple batch example, we have multiple inputs, *C*[*X*](*t*), *C*[*S*](*t*), and *C*[*P*] (*t*), and multiple outputs *θμ*[d](*t*), ![theta Subscript upper K Sub Subscript upper S Baseline left-parenthesis t right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0008.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>S</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, and *θq*[*P*](*t*), at each time-point *t* from solving Framework 5. The inputs and outputs can then be related in the form of an MIMO machine learning model that is not directly dependent on time. In order to train the machine learning component, a loss function that minimizes the difference between the data-driven models predicted time-varying parameters and [Section 14.2.2](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-0015) estimated time-varying parameters is required. A general form of the loss function is shown in [Eq. 14.6](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0014):

[Section 14.2.3](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-0016) will consistently refer to the machine learning model as a single MIMO model. However, it should be noted that using several MISO models (one for each time-varying parameter) is theoretically sound, but it may require a larger number of parameters. In this section, we will use an ANN as the machine learning model as an example. As highlighted in [Section 14.1.3](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-0010), ANNs are commonly implemented within hybrid models as the machine learning component due to their ability to capture highly nonlinear relationships. Smaller networks (networks with fewer hidden layers and fewer nodes within each layer) are preferred where possible, as they contain fewer weights and biases, thus reducing overfitting of the training data. However, the size of the network will vary case-by-case and a variety of different architectures should be trialed to gauge the best performance on both training and validation.

In order to mitigate overfitting, the dataset should be split into three independent datasets; a training dataset that is used to train the ANN; a separate dataset for validation of the ANN that is not used during training, where hyperparameter retuning can take place, and a third dataset for testing the final model \[[89](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0089), [90](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0090)\]. The partitioning of a dataset into training, validation, and testing subsets depends on the quantity and diversity of data available; however, multiple permutations of data partitioning should be tested in order to assess the sensitivity of training to the data partitioning. Once the dataset has been partitioned, each variable should be individually standardized or normalized. In this chapter, we follow the commonly used standardization approach where each variable is linearly transformed to have a mean of zero and a standard deviation of unity [\[91\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0091), which has been known to improve the training speed and accuracy of neural networks \[[92](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0092), [93](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0093)\].

Once the ANNs of varying structures are set up and the data has been appropriately partitioned, training can commence. There are several choices to be made when training an ANN that change case-by-case, examples of which include incorporating regularization terms, the number of epochs, batch size, and finally, the optimization algorithm used to train the ANN.

Regularization terms can be added to the training objective function to reduce or remove unnecessary parameters and avoid overfitting [\[94\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0094). Several variations of regularization terms exist, including L1 and L2 regularization that penalize the absolute ANN parameter values and squared ANN parameter values, respectively [\[95\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0095). For example, introducing the L1 regularization term to the MAE loss function results in the objective function illustrated in [Eq. 14.9](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0019):

where *λ*[L1] is the penalty weight that can be increased to penalize weight magnitude more at the cost of ANN fitting. Similarly, adding an L2 regularization term to the MAE loss function yields the objective function shown in [Eq. 14.10](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0020):

Epoch number and batch size refer to the way in which data is fed to the training algorithm. Batch size dictates how many datapoints per batch to process before updating the ANN parameters [\[96\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0096). Batch size can be reduced from the size of the full training dataset in cases where the training dataset is too large to process in a single iteration [\[97\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0097). Epochs are simply how many times the entire dataset is seen by the optimization algorithm [\[96\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0096). So, increasing the number of epochs can improve the fitting of the ANN to the training data at the cost of longer computation time and an increased risk of overfitting. Early stopping is a form of regularization that assesses the trained ANN performance on validation data and terminates training if a stopping criterion is met [\[98\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0098), thus avoiding overfitting from using an excessive number of epochs.

Training an ANN generally involves back-propagation [\[99\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0099), which uses the chain rule to calculate the gradient of the loss function with respect to the ANN weights and biases. Several tools exist for ANN training, one of which is the Python package PyTorch [\[100\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0100), in which different loss functions, regularization terms (and weights), batch sizes, and epochs can be chosen.

 

### 14.2.4 Hybrid Model Uncertainty Estimation

Quantifying uncertainty is an important step in process model development, offering valuable insight into prediction confidence by assessing its expected precision. This effectively means that uncertainty analysis can be viewed as a form of model validation [\[101\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0101), despite often being overlooked as such, as excessive model uncertainty on a validation dataset can be a sign of overfitting of the training dataset [\[102\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0102). Although some level of uncertainty is inevitable, especially in biosystems, minimizing model uncertainty supports the development of optimal control strategies, such as strategies used in QbD methodologies.

In the context of hybrid modeling where the most uncertain and influential parameters have been regressed by the machine learning model, it can subsequently be assumed that hybrid model uncertainty will mostly stem from the data-driven model. One such methodology for uncertainty estimation is bootstrapping, a method widely applied in machine learning for quantifying uncertainty and improvising model stability and robustness \[[103](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0103), [104](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0104)\]. Bootstrapping involves using different random samples of the training dataset to train multiple independent machine learning models. Each model is then combined with the mechanistic component to make its own hybrid model. Having several hybrid models instead of one means multiple state variable trajectories are generated; sampling the different trajectories facilitates the calculation of confidence intervals that quantify the model uncertainty.

Data sampling for bootstrapping can be completely random, or they can follow a strategy; a previous study conducted bootstrapping such that all data over predetermined periods of time within the experimental time horizon were eliminated for the training of each model [\[105\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0105). Simulating scenarios where the system experiences missing information over a given duration helps assess how well a model generalizes to periods of incomplete data, an example of which is when sensors in an industrial bioprocess fail and require a fixed time horizon to be repaired. It should be noted that using GPs to simulate the machine learning component, instead of an ANN, can be beneficial for uncertainty analysis as they automatically generate the confidence interval of time-varying parameters and, therefore, the overall hybrid model. However, GPs are not always simple to implement due to their lack of an explicit model structure and are not suitable for systems with high-dimensional inputs, as discussed in [Section 14.1.2.3](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-0006).

 

### 14.2.5 Considerations for Hybrid Model Construction

There are multiple options when constructing a hybrid model. This section provides a brief overview of some key considerations that can be made during the construction of a hybrid model, particularly when using an ANN as the machine learning component.

 

#### 14.2.5.1 Hybrid Model Greyness

Hybrid model “greyness” refers to the ratio of white box to black box modeling within the hybrid model. No metric exists for the quantification of “greyness;” however, we know when “greyness” is being increased or decreased relative to an initial model design. For example, implementing more mechanistic knowledge would be moving toward the “white” end of the “greyness” scale. Although the hybrid model “greyness” will vary case-by-case, a study investigating the effects of differing hybrid model “greyness” found that incorporating more specific mechanistic knowledge can increase the risk of incorporating incorrect inductive bias into the model [\[69\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0069), meaning mechanistic knowledge should only be incorporated in high confidence.

 

#### 14.2.5.2 Discrepancy Hybrid Modeling

Hybrid modeling does not always require a machine learning model for the simulation of time-varying parameters; discrepancy hybrid models take the output of the mechanistic component and correct it with a data-driven component, similar to GB EL. For instance, when applied to the mechanistic model described in [Eqs. 14.2a](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0004)–[14.2c](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0006), a discrepancy hybrid model would take the form shown in [Eqs. 14.11a](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0021)–[14.11c](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0023):

Comparing discrepancy hybrid models to hybrid models with time-varying parameters was investigated in a previous study for a chemical system, which found the discrepancy model to perform worse than other hybrid model structures for a dynamic system \[[106](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0106), [107](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0107)\].

 

#### 14.2.5.3 Machine Learning Component

As discussed in [Section 14.1.2](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-0003), a multitude of machine learning approaches have been applied to bioprocesses, all of which are potentially applicable to hybrid modeling provided the limitations of the machine learning component are not exceeded by the problem at hand. For instance, when dealing with systems with high-dimensional inputs, incorporating a dimensionality reduction-based ML model, such as PCA, could be greatly beneficial. On the other hand, if quantified model uncertainty is a critical requirement for later use, then using GP could be the preferred option due to its direct computation of output mean and variance. However, if the process is known to have time-dependent or sequential mechanisms, such as the changing composition of CHO cells [\[108\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0108), then using an RNN would be a better option, as the hidden state is able to simulate internal memory. As such, when deciding the ML component to be used, one needs to first consider not only the amount of the data available but also the ultimate goal of the hybrid model construction.

 

### 14.2.6 Dynamic Optimization Using Hybrid Modeling

As previously highlighted in [Table 14.2](#c14.xhtml#c14-tbl-0002), bioprocess models are frequently implemented for optimization purposes. Dynamic optimization in the context of bioprocesses refers to the identification of optimal operating conditions for a process over time, such as batch, fed-batch, and continuous systems. Since a number of bioprocess models incorporate Ordinary Differential Equations (ODEs), the dynamic optimization of bioprocess must incorporate a form of numerical integration within the optimization algorithm, resulting in non-convex optimization problems that are not trivial to solve. Some optimization problems also deal with a process model with high stiffness, in which case, causing numerical issues with model discretization and resorting to gradient-free optimization algorithms, such as PSO and evolutionary algorithms, despite no guarantee of convergence to even a local optimum. Generally, it is recommended to either conduct gradient-based optimization from multiple initial points or utilize gradient-free optimization to identify a good initial guess from which gradient-based optimization can be employed, thus ensuring sufficient exploration of the solution space.

 

#### 14.2.6.1 Optimal Feeding in Fed-Batch Bioprocesses

In this section, we outline an optimization framework for a fed-batch bioprocess as an example. When optimizing a fed-batch process, we can consider the degrees of freedom to be the dynamic substrate feeding rate. In this example, we propose maximizing final biomass cell density, for which the optimization problem, incorporating the hybrid model described in [Eqs. 14.8a](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0016)–[14.8c](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0018), takes the form given in Framework 14.12:

It should also be noted that optimization packages are often minimization-oriented, and minimizing the negative of a function is equivalent to finding its maximum. [Eqs. 14.8a](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0016)–[14.8c](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0018) have been modified to take the forms shown in [Eqs. 14.12c14.12c](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0026)–14.12 g to incorporate the mass balance of fed-batch operation. It should also be noted that introducing feeding can incur stiffness in the optimization framework, particularly with pulse feeding, which can pose challenges for gradient-descent optimization algorithms in some cases.

 

#### 14.2.6.2 Dynamic Optimization Under Uncertainty

Uncertainty can be incorporated within a dynamic optimization framework through the objective function or constraints, depending on the application. For example, robust optimization requires an optimal solution to meet inequality constraints subject to *all* possible combinations of uncertain parameters within their uncertainty bounds, providing applicability to biosystems where product quality needs to be guaranteed or where certain conditions endanger cultured organisms. Therefore, robust optimization algorithms tend to identify a set of “worst-case” parameters (parameters most likely to violate constraints); the optimum is decided using the “worst-case” parameters for constraints, instead of their nominal values [\[109\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0109). A study looking at robust optimization algorithms for a penicillin production case study, where cell density and substrate concentrations had maximum allowable values throughout fed-batch operation, was presented in a previous study on robust dynamic optimization [\[110\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0110). Although robust optima can be found, the solutions can be overly conservative; a similar approach that overcomes this issue is chance-constrained optimization, where a predetermined proportion of solutions are allowed to violate the uncertain inequality constraints [\[111\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0111). However, this does require assumptions to be made regarding the manner in which parameter uncertainties are distributed. Both robust and chance-constrained optimization methodologies are computationally expensive for dynamic systems, and there is no guarantee of finding a global optimum in most cases \[[112](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0112), [110](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0110)\].

A less computationally expensive approach involves sampling parameters to generate several parallel models; optimization of the nominal objective function is then subject to the constraints for all parallel models, thus approximating robustness or the meeting of chance constraints. This multi-modal approach (i.e. scenario tree-based approach) was proven to violate constraints in fewer instances than solely using the nominal parameters in a previous study [\[113\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0113); however, it did not achieve total robustness, unlike some more computationally expensive approaches that aim to solve a bilevel optimization problem to identify the “worst-case” parameters, as demonstrated in a subsequent study [\[110\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0110).

When considering the uncertainty arising from the objective function instead of constraints, uncertainty can be accounted for by introducing a penalty term that penalizes the variance of the objective function [\[114\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0114). Decreasing the penalization of variance allows the user to explore a region lacking in knowledge to possibly design new experiments, while increasing this penalty targets an optimum that is less likely to vary from model predictions. Again, generating a distribution of objective function values can be achieved by generating several models in parallel using different parameter samples, from which a mean and variance of the objective function can be calculated. Finally, given the complexity of dynamic optimization under uncertainty, this is not included in the current book chapter (neither is a detailed uncertainty analysis of hybrid model construction). However, interested readers can refer to [\[110\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0110) for a study on robust optimization of penicillin production, [\[115\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0115) for chance-constrained RL for batch process control, and [\[116\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0116) for optimization under uncertainty for beer fermentation.

 

## 14.3 Hybrid Modeling of Microalgal Lutein Production

 

### 14.3.1 Introduction to Microalgal Lutein Production

Now, in order to illustrate the potential of hybrid modeling, we will use microalgal lutein production as a case study to apply the hybrid modeling methodology explained in [Section 14.2](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-0013). Lutein is a carotenoid that has several health benefits for humans, including anticancer effects and prevention of cataracts \[[117](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0117)–[119](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0119)\]. However, humans do not synthesize lutein internally and instead rely on the ingestion of lutein from food and supplements. Although some foods naturally contain lutein, particularly fruit and vegetables [\[120\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0120), consuming lutein supplements can be more convenient and effective. The consumption of lutein supplements has helped drive the global lutein market to an estimated $369 million in 2024, with an expectation to grow to $461 million by 2029 with a Compound Annual Growth Rate (CAGR) of 6.1% [\[121\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0121). Currently, commercial lutein production is entirely sourced from marigold flower petals [\[122\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0122). However, microalgae, microscopic photosynthetic organisms that produce lutein for light harvesting [\[123\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0123), have the potential to become a commercially viable option for lutein production due to less labor-intensive harvesting, higher growth rate, and capacity for all-year harvesting (rather than seasonal) compared to marigold flowers [\[117\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0117). Despite the potential commercial viability, several limitations exist within the microalgal lutein production process, namely the low lutein content within microalgal cells, resulting in low process yields, and high costs of microalgal biomass production compared to the marigold flower, which does not require as much energy or nutrient feeding to grow [\[117\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0117).

Various options are being explored to drive microalgal lutein production toward commercial viability, one of which is heterotrophic growth (the focus of this case study), where the lutein-producing microalgae grow in the absence of light, allowing ultra-high cell densities to be achieved, thus improving the potential yield and production rate of lutein [\[124\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0124). In order to further optimize the production of lutein under heterotrophic growth conditions, experiments can be conducted to identify some optimal operating conditions, such as temperature and choice of substrate, as demonstrated in a previous study [\[124\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0124). Additionally, another consideration is to carry out a fed-batch operation and optimize the feeding strategy, which can utilize different flow rates and feed compositions. However, the potential combinations of feed rates and compositions are numerous, making the optimal feeding strategy challenging to identify experimentally due to the multitude of degrees of freedom. Model-based optimization addresses the complex nature of optimizing a fed-batch process by efficiently exploring a wide range of potential feeding conditions, therefore reducing the need for experimental trials. In this section, we demonstrate the application of hybrid modeling to an HCD culture of lutein-producing microalgae for fed-batch optimization.

 

### 14.3.2 Experimental Setup and Data Availability

The case study in this section focuses on the growth of *Chlorella sorokiniana* under fed-batch conditions utilizing glucose and urea as substrates. Urea was favored over sodium nitrate as a nitrogen source for achieving higher biomass productivity in a previous study [\[124\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0124). Glucose and urea are fed in a single combined feed continuously throughout the fed-batch process. The fed-batch reactor has an initial working volume of 2.5 L with a single feed rate capable of reaching up to 0.05 L/h. The feed was designed to permit feed concentrations of glucose and urea as high as 750 g/L and 60 g/L, respectively.

Measurements of cell density were collected every 12 hours, with measurements of glucose and urea concentrations taken every 12 hours for the first 24 hours, followed by more frequent sampling of 3–4 times per subsequent 12-hour interval, and lutein content was measured at 24-hour intervals. Two initial fed-batch experiments were conducted, both starting with the same initial cell density, glucose concentration, and urea concentration. The first experiment commenced with an initial 24-hour batch phase, followed by the maintenance of glucose concentration between 4 g/L and 8 g/L through frequent manual adjustment of feed flow rate until the 168-hour mark passed, when the experiment was terminated. Glucose and urea feed concentrations were fixed at 750 g/L and 46.5 g/L, respectively, throughout the experiment. For the second experiment, which also started with a 24-hour batch phase, the feed rate was only changed every 12 hours, with urea feed concentration being adjusted to a value between 0 g/L and 60 g/L every 12 hours until the experiment was terminated after 144 hours. The experimental data can be seen in [Figure 14.4](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0004), where lutein content has been multiplied by the cell density to show the overall change in concentration within the reactor.

 

### 14.3.3 Constructing a Hybrid Model for Microalgal Lutein Production

Ultimately, the case study aims to identify an optimal fed-batch feeding strategy that maximizes the lutein produced by the end of the process. In order to facilitate fed-batch feed optimization, a model of the fed-batch process will be constructed and subsequently integrated within an optimization framework. The model should be capable of generating accurate predictions despite limited experimental data, enabling an efficient optimization of the fed-batch process. The hybrid model built for this specific case study is constructed in accordance with the methodology discussed throughout [Section 14.2](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-0013). Primarily, kinetic modeling is conducted, which is additionally used as a benchmark for the hybrid model, before introducing an ANN to enhance the model accuracy.

 

#### 14.3.3.1 Preliminary Kinetic Modeling of Microalgal Lutein Production

A fundamental kinetic model of the case study system takes the form shown in [Eqs. 14.13a](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0031)–[14.13f](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0036):
