where *C*[*X*] represents cell density in g/L, *C*[*G*] represents glucose concentration in g/L, *C*[*N*] represents urea concentration in g/L, *L*[*C*] represents lutein content in mg/(g biomass), and *C*[*L*] represents the overall lutein concentration within the reactor. The mechanistic model relies on the assumption of Monod kinetics for substrate uptake and growth, as well as first-order cell death. The use of Monod kinetics for the backbone of the model is justified by its successful incorporation within several models of lutein-producing microalgal systems seen in literature \[[125](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0125)–[127](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0127)\]. Urea was decoupled from cell growth in [Eq. 14.13c](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0033) because the experimental data in [Figure 14.4](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0004) illustrates the ability of cells to continue growing in the presence of little to no urea; the undisclosed relationship between urea and biomass growth rate will be quantified by the machine learning component when constructing the hybrid model. It should be noted that lutein content is an intracellular concentration. Hence, dilution is accounted for in [Eq. 14.13d](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0034). The parameters in [Eqs. 14.13a](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0031)–[14.13f](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0036) are estimated using the parameter estimation framework described in Framework 14.3, subject to [Eqs. 14.13a](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0031)–[14.13f](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0036) instead of [Eqs. 14.5b](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0011)–[14.5d](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0013).

The kinetic model fitting can be seen in [Figure 14.4](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0004) with the parameter values provided in column two of [Table 14.3](#c14.xhtml#c14-tbl-0003). Despite fitting cell density well, with an R² value of 0.932 across the two fed-batch experiments, the kinetic model particularly struggled to capture the substrate concentration profiles, which is evidenced in the R² values of −1.073 and 0.123 for glucose and urea, respectively, across the two fed-batch experiments. The kinetic model fitting of both fed-batch experiments 1 and 2, shown in [Figure 14.4](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0004), generally shows the kinetic model is underpredicting the substrate concentrations, particularly beyond the first 24 hours, which means that the kinetic model is overpredicting their respective consumption rates. By the 24-hour mark, the cell density has already increased by over 600%, meaning the overprediction of consumption rates could be due to mass transfer limitations or intracellular competition as a result of increased cell density, which the mechanistic model does not explain. Since the mechanistic understanding of the process is evidently incomplete, a data-driven component can be introduced to capture the remaining relationships within the system while not requiring the additional assumptions of a more intricate kinetic model, therefore avoiding the introduction of further inductive bias. The kinetic model constructed in this section provides a foundation for the hybrid model and will henceforth be used as a benchmark for further comparison.

![Table 14.3 Kinetic model parameters and their respective time-varying mean and standard deviation.](images/c14-i0010.png)

Table 14.3 Kinetic model parameters and their respective time-varying mean and standard deviation.

 

#### 14.3.3.2 Artificial Neural Network Implementation for Time-Varying Parameters

Due to the inadequate fitting of the kinetic model, as discussed in the previous section, a data-driven component is introduced to improve the model accuracy. For this case study, a Feed Forward Neural Network (FFNN) is chosen as the data-driven model due to its ability to capture any nonlinear relationships that we may find in the fed-batch fermentation process. The first step is to identify the time-varying parameters, which in this case were found to be *μ*[max], ![v Subscript max Underscript upper G Endscripts](images/c14-i0012.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>v</mi><msub><mi>max</mi><mi>G</mi></msub></msub></math>, and ![v Subscript max Underscript upper N Endscripts](images/c14-i0013.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>v</mi><msub><mi>max</mi><mi>N</mi></msub></msub></math> (whose time-varying parameters are ![theta Subscript mu Sub Subscript max Subscript Baseline comma](images/c14-i0014.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi></msub></msub><mspace width="-0.2em"/><mo>,</mo></math> ![theta Subscript v Sub Subscript max Underscript upper G Endscripts Subscript Baseline comma](images/c14-i0015.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi><mi>G</mi></msub></mrow></msub></mrow></msub><mspace width="-0.2em"/><mo>,</mo></math> and ![theta Subscript v Sub Subscript max Underscript upper N Endscripts Subscript Baseline comma](images/c14-i0016.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi><mrow><mspace width="-0.2em"/><mi>N</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></msub></mrow></msub><mspace width="-0.2em"/><mo>,</mo></math> respectively) as these parameters presented the highest uncertainties to which the fit of the model also demonstrated sufficient sensitivity to their values. The parameter estimation framework in Framework 14.5, subject to [Eqs. 14.13a](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0031)–[14.13f](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0036), is then used to identify time-varying parameter profiles.

Following the identifications of time-varying parameter profiles, whose mean (*μ*) and standard deviation (*σ*) are shown in [Table 14.3](#c14.xhtml#c14-tbl-0003), the FFNN is trained to model the relationship between the time-varying parameters as outputs and the state variables and control actions as inputs. In this case, the state variables and control actions used as inputs to the FFNN are *C*[*X*], *C*[*G*], *C*[*N*], *F*[*G*] (the feed rate of glucose in g/h) and *F*[N](the feed rate of urea in g/h). Control actions are included in the FFNN input because the state variable values alone (at the time the parameters are updated) do not provide the full information of the system before the next parameter update occurs. The FFNN is trained using the L1 Loss function (Mean Average Error, or MAE), shown in [Eq. 14.6](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0011), with L1 regularization penalizing the absolute values of the ANN weights and biases, as illustrated in [Eq. 14.9](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0014). The L1 regularization term converges redundant parameters to a value of zero to reduce overparameterization and overfitting of the FFNN by encouraging the training to focus only on the most influential weights and biases.

The FFNN, consisting of 2 hidden layers with 8 nodes in each layer, was trained using augmented data; each augmented dataset is a copy of the training dataset with the inputs being subject to Gaussian noise. Augmenting data improves the performance of neural networks by expanding the training dataset and making the model more robust to noise, thus reducing overfitting \[[128](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0128), [129](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0129)\]. In this study, 100 augmented datasets were generated using a Gaussian noise distribution and a standard deviation of 0.01 (1% of the standard deviation of the standardized data). It is important to include enough noise to improve the FFNN robustness, while not introducing so much that it inhibits the FFNN fitting capabilities. The combination of parameter regularization and data augmentation helps combat potential overfitting using the very limited dataset of just two fed-batch experiments. Training was conducted over 40,000 epochs, as in a previous hybrid modeling study [\[130\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0130), to ensure convergence over the large augmented dataset. The precision plots for the augmented dataset training are shown in [Figure 14.3](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0003), which illustrates the strong fitting capabilities of the FFNN, which converged to an MAE (or L1 loss) of 0.014 and R² values of 0.999, 0.998, and 0.999 for the standardized time-varying parameters ![theta Subscript mu Sub Subscript max](images/c14-i0017.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mrow><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></msub></math>, ![theta Subscript v Sub Subscript max Underscript upper G Endscripts](images/c14-i0018.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi><mrow><mspace width="-0.1em"/><mi>G</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></msub></mrow></msub></math>, and ![theta Subscript v Sub Subscript max Underscript upper N Endscripts](images/c14-i0019.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi><mrow><mspace width="-0.1em"/><mi>N</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></msub></mrow></msub></math>, respectively.

![Figure 14.3 Precision plots of the standardized time-varying parameters theta Subscript mu Sub Subscript max, theta Subscript v Sub Subscript max Underscript upper G Endscripts, and theta Subscript v Sub Subscript max Underscript upper N Endscripts from the training of the FFNN using 100 augmented datasets.](images/c14f003.png)

Figure 14.3 Precision plots of the standardized time-varying parameters ![theta Subscript mu Sub Subscript max](images/c14-i0020.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mrow><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></msub></math>, ![theta Subscript v Sub Subscript max Underscript upper G Endscripts](images/c14-i0021.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi><mrow><mspace width="-0.1em"/><mi>G</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></msub></mrow></msub></math>, and ![theta Subscript v Sub Subscript max Underscript upper N Endscripts](images/c14-i0022.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi><mrow><mspace width="-0.1em"/><mi>N</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></msub></mrow></msub></math> from the training of the FFNN using 100 augmented datasets.

To illustrate the improvement made by introducing a data-driven component, we must compare the fitting of the benchmark kinetic model to the hybrid model. [Figure 14.4](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0004) shows the fitting of both the initial kinetic model and the overall hybrid model, which improved the mean R² value from 0.219 to 0.974 across the two fed-batch experiments. The first fed-batch experiment (shown in [Figure 14.4](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0004)a) saw a large improvement in the mean R² value, going from 0.263 to 0.962. The second fed-batch experiment (shown in [Figure 14.4](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0004)b) saw a slightly larger improvement in the mean R² value, going from 0.174 to 0.986. In terms of the simulated state variables, the smallest improvement in R² value was from 0.932 to 0.996 for cell density, meaning the original kinetic model provided a good estimation of the yield of cells from the glucose fed to the reactor. Since the overall lutein concentration is found to be strongly linked to cell density, this saw a similar change in R² value from 0.892 to 0.965, which further supports the decision to not implement a time-varying parameter for lutein content in [Eq. 14.13d](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0034). However, urea and glucose saw much larger improvements in fitting with their R² values increasing from 0.123 to 0.972 and −1.073 to 0.963, respectively, which accounts for the vast majority of the overall fitting improvement. The hybrid model is able to improve the fitting of the substrate concentration profiles because the FFNN can account for changes in parameter values that may be caused by various phenomena, such as metabolic activity or mass transfer limitations, without the need for a detailed physical model. On the other hand, the benchmark kinetic model is limited to the assumed structure and therefore lacks generalizability in comparison to the hybrid model.

![Figure 14.4 Hybrid model fitting compared to the benchmark kinetic model of fed-batch experiment 1 (a) and fed-batch experiment 2 (b).](images/c14f004.png)

Figure 14.4 Hybrid model fitting compared to the benchmark kinetic model of fed-batch experiment 1 (a) and fed-batch experiment 2 (b).

Since the implementation of an FFNN introduces additional parameters, the corrected Akaike Information Criterion (AICc) can also be accounted for to compare models of differing sizes, as demonstrated in a previous hybrid modeling study \[131\]. For fed-batch experiment 1, the hybrid model improved the AICc from a value of 521.0 for the kinetic model to 419.3 for the hybrid model, with fed-batch experiment 2 seeing a similar improvement in the AICc from 460.1 to 381.3, therefore demonstrating that the introduction of an FFNN is justified and has not inappropriately increased the model complexity.

The drastic improvement in the fitting of the dynamic model highlights the potential of incorporating machine learning to capture dynamics that preliminary mechanistic modeling may overlook. Since the model is sufficiently accurate, it is ready to be integrated within an optimization framework to design experiments that maximize the production of lutein, the results of which are discussed in the next section.

 

### 14.3.4 Dynamic Optimization of Microalgal Lutein Production

The dynamic optimization framework aims to maximize the final lutein mass in the reactor at the end of the fed-batch process spanning 5 days (120 hours) with feeding updated every 12 hours to allow for automated operation. The overall optimization framework is illustrated in Framework 14.14:

For the purpose of this case study, a computational experiment has been conducted to examine the optimization results of the current hybrid model using a more comprehensive hybrid model validated over a wide range of operating conditions as the “ground-truth.” [Figure 14.5](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0005) shows the results of optimization Framework 14.14, which predicted a final lutein production of 290.3 mg, with an actual final concentration of 366.0 mg. For comparison, the second fed-batch experiment used for hybrid model construction was also designed with 12-hour feeding stages and achieved a total lutein production of 466.8 mg. Although this is a reduction in overall lutein production due to the shorter batch time, the optimized experiment takes place over a shorter time horizon (120 hours instead of 144 hours) and achieved the highest lutein yield of 0.702 mg/(g glucose) in comparison to the yields of 0.611 mg/(g glucose)^− and 0.675 mg/(g glucose) achieved in fed-batch experiments 1 and 2, respectively. In terms of the predicted feed rate, the steadily increasing feed rate shown in [Figure 14.5](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0005) does make sense from a physical point of view because the increase in cell density will have a higher demand for substrate to maintain the larger cell density. Both glucose and urea feed concentrations maintained their maximum permitted values of 750 g/L and 60 g/L, respectively, thus ensuring sufficient substrates are provided for growth.

The model prediction mismatch in the latter stages of the simulation in [Figure 14.5](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0005) highlights where further information is required to better train the model. Dynamic models can be particularly susceptible to error propagation (small errors early in the simulation that snowball into a larger offset further along the simulated time horizon). For example, the largest errors in the glucose and urea concentration profiles shown in [Figure 14.5](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0005) exist beyond a time of 100 hours, emphasizing the need for improved training in the latter stages of the process. One cause of this mismatch could be the prediction of cell density, the fit of which has an R² value of 0.799, where the hybrid model initially over-predicts cell growth, leading to the over-predictions of substrate consumption rates. Subsequently, the over-prediction of substrate consumption rates means that the substrate concentrations are generally under-predicted from a time of 25–30 hours onward, resulting in an underprediction of cell growth. The suboptimal prediction of cell density is likely to be due to the training dataset; despite augmenting the data with 100 new datasets, [Figure 14.3](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0003) shows that the time-varying parameter ![theta Subscript mu Sub Subscript max](images/c14-i0028.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mrow><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></msub></math> has a noticeable gap in the augmented training dataset where no training data exists for time-varying parameters between standardized values of 0.5 and 1.5, despite the use of a penalty term that penalizes the deviation of time-varying parameters in the objective function shown in [Eq. 14.5a](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0010). Moreover, the increasing cell density throughout the process increases the sensitivity of the system to propagated errors, for example the glucose consumption rate in fed-batch experiment 1 increased from 1.91 g/L/h to 6.97 g/L/h from when the feeding commenced at the 24-hour mark to the final time of 168 hours, meaning simulation errors have a larger effect on simulated trajectories later on in the time horizon. A similar trend is shown in the feeding profile in [Figure 14.5](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0005), which reflects the increased glucose consumption rates in the optimization result over time, thus increasing the sensitivity of the model to errors in the prediction of substrate uptake. The worst performing component for prediction was urea, with an R² value of −0.115. However, this is due to two main limitations of the dataset; (1) there exist gaps in the training for ![theta Subscript mu Sub Subscript max Subscript Baseline comma](images/c14-i0029.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mrow><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></msub><mspace width="-0.1em"/><mo>,</mo></math> as aforementioned, which directly affects urea (as the consumption rate is shown to be directly proportional to cell density in [Eq. 14.13c](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0033)), and (2) both fed-batch experiments used for training saw the urea sit at low concentrations for prolonged periods, meaning the FFNN anticipates a high consumption rate of urea (and therefore ![v Subscript max Underscript upper N Endscripts](images/c14-i0030.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>v</mi><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi><mrow><mspace width="-0.1em"/><mi>N</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></msub></math>) regardless of the FFNN inputs, which will not always hold true. The low urea concentrations in the training dataset will also inhibit the ability of the FFNN to recognize the effects of urea on growth – the only information the data provides is that growth can still occur when subject to low urea concentrations. Similarly, the glucose concentration in fed-batch experiment 1 remained in a narrow region between 4 and 8 g/L beyond a time of 36 hours, which again limits the ability of the FFNN to adequately capture the effects that glucose has on the time-varying parameters. The poor predictive capabilities for urea and glucose emphasizes the need for data covering a broad range of operating conditions.

![Figure 14.5 Hybrid model predictions against the ground-truth data using the optimal feeding strategy deduced from the optimization framework described in Framework 14.14.](images/c14f005.png)

Figure 14.5 Hybrid model predictions against the ground-truth data using the optimal feeding strategy deduced from the optimization framework described in Framework 14.14.

Although the predictive performance may seem suboptimal during certain short phases of the process, it must be emphasized that only two fed-batch experiments were available for training, making the construction of a high-fidelity model extremely challenging. So, in this context, the hybrid model predictions are satisfactory. In cases where a limited number of experiments can be designed, careful DoEs should be conducted to maximize the information obtained from each experiment. In order to improve the hybrid model predictions in the future, constraints could be added to reduce the excess remaining substrates at the end of the experiment to improve the process yield. In addition, feed strategies that differ more from existing experiments could be tried, through the use of a penalty function in the optimization framework objective that encourages the exploration of a wider range of operating conditions for when the model is updated, thus highlighting the importance of Model Based DoEs (MBDoE) in model training and the subsequent process optimization. In its current state, the most effective way to utilize this hybrid model would be with online updating of the data-driven component from real-time data, as retraining the FFNN can be done quickly and accurately.

 

## 14.4 Summary

The chapter began by highlighting some key literature that illustrates a variety of ML applications to bioprocess development and optimization. An observation was made that existing models generally fall within the spectrum between mechanistic (“white box”) and purely data-driven (“black box”) modeling, with their respective strengths and weaknesses explained in depth. In order to simultaneously address the limitations of both mechanistic and data-driven modeling and utilize their respective strengths, the authors present the concept of hybrid modeling (or “grey box”) for the integration of ML within a mechanistic model. Several applications of hybrid models in bioprocessing from literature are explored, demonstrating extensive capabilities for the enhancement of bioprocesses.

The chapter then outlines a comprehensive methodology for constructing hybrid models, commencing with a mechanistic model based on mass balances and simple kinetic laws. For the cases where a mechanistic model performs in a dissatisfactory manner, sensitivity and uncertainty analysis are used to identify the most uncertain parameters, which are then reformulated as time-varying functions. Machine learning models can then be trained to estimate the time-varying parameters using experimental state variables and control actions as inputs. Detailed procedures are provided for training ANNs, including regularization, data augmentation, and partitioning into training, validation, and test sets. Bootstrapping is also introduced as a strategy for quantifying uncertainty in hybrid model predictions and improving hybrid model robustness.

The methodology described in this chapter is then applied to a detailed case study on lutein production by *Chlorella. sorokiniana* microalgae under heterotrophic fed-batch conditions. Initial mechanistic modeling based on Monod kinetics could not accurately predict glucose and urea concentrations, despite performing well for cell density, and so an FFNN was introduced to model three key time-varying parameters: maximum specific growth rate, maximum specific glucose uptake rate, and maximum specific urea uptake rate. The hybrid model significantly outperformed the purely mechanistic model, improving mean R² values across key state variables from 0.219 to 0.974.

Finally, the hybrid model was incorporated within a dynamic optimization framework to maximize lutein production over a 120-hour fed-batch operation. The optimization degrees of freedom were provided as the dynamic feed flow rate and substrate feed concentrations, demonstrating how model-based optimization can assist in efficiently identifying optimal operating conditions. Overall, the modeling and optimization of the lutein-producing microalgal fed-batch process demonstrate the potential of hybrid modeling for dynamic bioprocesses, particularly under conditions of limited data availability. Although not explicitly explored in this chapter, it is important to note that online model updating can be employed to incorporate new data and enhance predictive accuracy. Equally critical is the availability of informative and diverse datasets to ensure robust hybrid model training.
